articles.title: Researcher Preferences and Research Findings
articles.authors: Nate Breznau
articles.abstract: Empirical research produces findings that are influenced by the preferences of the researchers. Researchers choose their research question, how they collect or manipulate data and which models they employ. Every decision is an opportunity for a researcher’s preferences to enter the research production function. Recent ‘many analysts’ studies shed light on this phenomenon whereby researchers given the same data to test the same hypothesis arrive at different results. This chapter reviews types of bias in the research process stemming from researchers’ preferences. For example, desires, prior worldviews, motives, ideologies and learned behaviors can all influence the rational pursuit of knowledge. Some preferences are incentivized in the competitive academic market for science others stem from political motives. The process is complex as different preferences can interact with one another in the research process. The chapter concludes with recommendations for consumers of research findings and institutions of science.

articles.title: A Lack of Robustness in Robustness Checking from Auspurg and Brüderl
articles.authors: Nate Breznau; George J Borjas
articles.abstract:
In a comment on our work on ideological bias in the production of research findings (Borjas and Breznau 2026), Auspurg and Brüderl argue that our findings are based on “fragile evidence” and contain a “coding error” that, when corrected, removes the statistically significant results we presented (Auspurg and Brüderl 2026). In this response we address each of their claims carefully. 

In our published paper, we explicitly acknowledged the limitations of our findings which are based on secondary data and a small sample. After examining Auspurg and Brüderl’s claims, we conclude that they have not presented any new evidence that warrants any correction to our conclusions. We also make a claim of our own. We applaud efforts to examine results in the social and behavioral sciences for robustness. However, we note that Ausprug and Brüderl have published reproductions and robustness checks of more than 10 studies and in every case they find that the original study is not robust. Assuming even a poor rate of robustness in the social sciences, their collective work seems to produce an extremely biased distribution of results, suggesting that their work may itself be biased by something other than checking the robustness of empirical findings.

articles.title: Scientific Misconduct and the Neo-Feudalisation of Knowledge: A Conceptual Analysis of a Mutually Reinforcing Relationship
articles.authors: Kris A. Willems; Wynand van der Walt
articles.abstract: Scientific misconduct is conventionally understood as an individual ethical failure: a deviation from the norms of honest inquiry by researchers acting in bad faith or under excessive pressure. This paper argues that each such framing, while not incorrect, is analytically insufficient. Drawing on the sociology of science, political economy, and research integrity literatures, it proposes a conceptual framework in which scientific misconduct and neo-feudal knowledge structures co-form a mutually reinforcing feedback system. The framework is grounded in the concept of the modern clerisy–the credentialed scientific class whose authority shapes policy, technology, and public narratives–and examines what happens when members of that class, under systemic pressure, begin to mirror the power structures they are nominally tasked with transcending. The paper identifies two reinforcing pathways: misconduct erodes the epistemic legitimacy on which democratic knowledge systems depend, while neo-feudal structures–characterised by gatekeeping, the privatisation of knowledge, and metric-driven hierarchies–incentivise the very practices that generate misconduct. Together, these pathways suppress epistemic diversity, concentrate knowledge authority within elite networks, and produce global inequities in knowledge production. The paper concludes that reform must be both structural and cultural: better systems and better stewards of knowledge are not alternatives but prerequisites for one another.

articles.title: Emotions in the Lab: An Umbrella Review of Emotion Inductions
articles.authors: Amanda Kvarven; Anna Marie Connysdotter Karlsson; Daniel Västfjäll
articles.abstract: Emotion inductions are widely used to investigate how affective states influence cognition, judgement, behaviour, and physiology, yet induction procedures are often treated as interchangeable. This umbrella review provides an overview of emotion induction procedures and synthesises evidence from 24 meta-analyses and systematic reviews identified through searches of Scopus and PsycINFO. Video-based inductions were among the most widely used and effective procedures, while virtual reality emerged as a promising alternative. Negative affective states were generally easier to induce than positive affective states, with fear, anxiety, and disgust showing particularly high induction success. However, substantial heterogeneity was observed across reviews, which differed considerably in how inductions were classified and evaluated. Common concerns included inconsistent emotion labels, overlap between emotional states, variation in manipulation checks, demand characteristics, and inconsistencies in neutral control conditions. Overall, the literature appears highly fragmented from a methodological perspective. Differences in induction procedures, classification systems, and outcome assessment may contribute to heterogeneity in findings and complicate evidence synthesis. Greater standardisation and systematic evaluation of emotion induction methods are needed to strengthen the methodological foundations of emotion research.

articles.title: The PRISMA family of reporting guidelines for systematic reviews: initiatives to better support development and implementation, and future challenges and opportunities
articles.authors: Joanne McKenzie; Evan Mayo-Wilson; Sue E Brennan; Daniel George Hamilton; Yemisi Takwoingi; David Moher; Matthew James Page
articles.abstract: Incomplete and inaccurate reporting of research can prevent research from being used. Reporting guidelines aim to circumvent this by providing recommendations that support researchers in writing complete and accurate accounts of their work. While reporting guidelines have many benefits, challenges exist for both developers and users. In this article, we outline initiatives implemented to address challenges within the PRISMA (Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic reviews and Meta-Analyses) family of guidelines and highlight opportunities for future work.

articles.title: Who Owns, Publishes, and Governs Diamond Open Access? Institutional Arrangements Among Journals Using Open Journal Systems
articles.authors: Natascha Chtena; Juan Pablo Alperin; Mikael Laakso
articles.abstract: Diamond Open Access (OA) is frequently defined in the negative—no fees for readers, no fees for authors—but this characterization captures only the financial surface of a model whose deeper ambition is community-led, nonprofit stewardship of scholarly knowledge as a public good. What distinguishes diamond OA from other fee-free publishing models is not only how journals are financed, but also how they are institutionally organized—who owns them, who publishes them, who governs them, and how these responsibilities are distributed among the actors involved in journal publishing. Yet the institutional arrangements of diamond OA journals remain among the least studied dimensions of the diamond landscape—in part because they resist easy categorization and in part because they are difficult to observe from the outside. Drawing on 1070 responses to a global survey of journals using Open Journal Systems (OJS)—the most widely adopted publishing platform in the diamond OA ecosystem—we examine how journals identify owners and publishers, allocate governance authority, and describe the institutional relationships through which publishing is organized. We find that the institutional organization of Diamond OA journals varies substantially by region and often does not conform to conventional models. Although academic departments are the most commonly reported owners, and editorial teams most often hold authority over editorial appointments and operational decisions, journals frequently identify multiple owners and/or publishers, while ownership and decision-making authority do not consistently coincide. Respondents also report organizations serving as owners and publishers outside their usual functions. Drawing on institutional bricolage, we interpret these patterns not as signs of organizational deficiency or incomplete formalization, but as adaptive configurations of informal arrangements, institutional dependencies, and negotiated responsibilities that make diamond publishing possible. We discuss the implications of these findings for how diamond OA journals are classified, understood, and supported through policy.

articles.title: A novel view of microfinance: implications of the neuroscience of decision-making
articles.authors: Rebecca Kanter; Antara Haldar; A. David Redish
articles.abstract: Microfinance institutions (MFIs) are commonly understood to succeed through structural mechanisms such as group lending, joint liability, peer monitoring, and repayment incentives. However, these explanations fail to account for the wide variation in outcomes among institutions employing similar contractual structures. We propose a new theoretical framework that reconceptualizes microfinance success as fundamentally dependent on the institutional cultivation of trust. Drawing on emerging neuroeconomic models of decision-making and cooperation, we argue that MFIs operate as assurance systems in which repayment and continued lending depend on mutually reinforced expectations of cooperation between borrowers and institutions. Within this framework, trust functions not as a byproduct of preexisting social capital, but as a psychological precursor to cooperative decision-making that can be intentionally structured through institutional design. We identify three distinct but interacting forms of trust—deliberative, instinctual, and procedural—through which institutions shape borrower expectations and stabilize cooperative equilibria. Through comparative analysis of major MFIs including Grameen Bank, BRAC, ASA, BancoSol, Bank Rakyat Indonesia, Equity Bank Kenya, and SKS Microfinance, we find that long-term institutional success is better explained by trust-generating architectures than by lending modality alone. Current global microfinance datasets inadequately capture these institutional dimensions, limiting the field’s ability to explain institutional resilience, scaling, and failure. Reframing microfinance through the lens of trust and neuroeconomic decision-making offers new implications for institutional design, financial inclusion policy, and the evaluation of development interventions under conditions of uncertainty.

articles.title: Bargaining for leisure time in the household: the case of the Kipsigis
articles.authors: Angarika Deb; Daniel Major-Smith; Monique Borgerhoff Mulder
articles.abstract: We study a bargaining model of household decision-making, where inequality in outside options—the resources one could access if intra-household cooperation fails—should provide bargaining power and shape distribution of labour between partners. This model predicts that individuals with stronger outside options should negotiate more favourable allocations of housework and have more leisure time. We test these predictions among the Kipsigis, an agro-pastoral society in Kenya characterised by patriarchy and a patrilocal social system. We use measures of social, material and embodied wealth as proxies for outside options, examining whether these predict leisure inequality. Contrary to the bargaining model, we find no positive relationships between any of the wealth measures and leisure inequality, instead seeing either null or negative associations. These results suggest that factors beyond individual bargaining power—particularly gender norms prescribing household roles and the structural constraints of pastoral production—might shape household labour allocation among the Kipsigis. In addition, we see that Kipsigis women enjoy less leisure on average than men, a stark difference from our previous analysis of hunter-gatherers, where men and women had equal leisure. We discuss implications for evolutionary approaches to gender relations, and the need for acknowledging ethnographic complexity in adoption of bargaining approaches across diverse cultures.

articles.title: Longitudinal Profiles of Parental Self- and Child-Focused Emotion Regulation
articles.authors: Gesine Jordan; Kristina Stockinger; Christine Schiltz; Samuel Greiff; Ziwen Teuber
articles.abstract: Parenting is an emotion-eliciting experience that requires parents to navigate the dual demands of regulating their own and their children’s emotions, drawing on regulatory strategies such as reappraisal and rumination. However, patterns of self- and child-focused reappraisal and rumination and their associations with parental exhaustion, children’s internalizing problems, children’s academic achievement, and parent–child relationships remain underexplored. Our preregistered three-wave online study targeted U.S. parents of sixth–ninth graders (N = 1,046; 51.53% mothers; Mage = 43.22). We employed latent profile analyses and latent transition analyses. Results revealed three profiles of parental self- and child-focused emotion regulation strategies, stable across a 4-month timeframe: Reappraisers (T1 ≈ 9%, T2 ≈ 7%) showed high use of self- and child-focused reappraisal, self-ruminators (T1 ≈ 25%, T2 ≈ 31%) reported high self-focused rumination and low use of other strategies, and average regulators (T1 ≈ 66%, T2 ≈ 61%) showed moderate use of all strategies. In addition, reappraisers reported the lowest levels of parental exhaustion and children’s internalizing problems and the highest parent–child relationship closeness. By contrast, self-ruminators reported the highest levels of parental exhaustion and children’s internalizing problems and the lowest parent–child relationship closeness. However, profile membership did not predict children’s academic achievement. The study provides important insights into distinct subgroups of parents on the basis of their combined use of self- and child-focused emotion regulation strategies, highlighting the differential relations of these strategies on parental well-being and child outcomes.

articles.title: Diversity, Intersectionality and Representativeness in Brain Health Research
articles.authors: Matthew Raymond; Jai Shah; Kelly Anderson; Sinan Guloksuz; Nev Jones; Sherif Karama; Laurence Kirmayer
articles.abstract: Advancing equity in brain health research requires systematic attention to diversity and representativeness across the full research enterprise, from priority-setting and study design to knowledge translation. This paper, part of a series developing a cultural-ecosocial framework for brain health research, examines the conceptual foundations, current gaps, and practical strategies for integrating diversity and representativeness in neuroscience and mental health research. We review key dimensions of diversity relevant to brain health, analyze ongoing failures of representativeness in neurobiological and clinical research, and discuss how these failures compound structural health inequities. Drawing on recent developments in the field—including recommendations for responsible use of race and ethnicity in neuroimaging, the emergence of community-based participatory neuroscience, new international calls for global collaboration on equity in brain science, and insights from psychiatric genomics and race-based data collection—we outline specific recommendations for researchers, funders, and institutions. We situate these within the broader cultural-ecosocial framework introduced in companion papers in this thematic issue, connecting diversity and representativeness to social determinants of brain health, intersectionality, and ethical obligations toward marginalized communities. An Appendix provides practical guidelines for considering diversity and representativeness in brain health research design, consistent with transcultural psychiatric principles

articles.title: A call for greater transparency in piloting
articles.authors: Isaac J Handley-Miner; Agata Bochynska; Brett Buttliere; Kai Li Chung; Mahmoud Medhat Elsherif; Christopher James Graham; Neele Henriette Heiser; Hannah Loenneker; Bjørn Sætrevik; Yashvin Seetahul
articles.abstract: A pilot study is a preliminary investigation conducted before a full-scale research study. Although piloting is a common and valuable part of the research process, pilot studies are not systematically reported (or even acknowledged) in the psychology literature. This paper argues that establishing norms and guidelines for regularly reporting pilot studies can improve many aspects of psychological research. Specifically, reporting pilot studies can help researchers avoid systematically excluding part of the research process from the scientific record, reveal selection biases in research designs that may affect the generalizability of findings, evaluate others’ research more accurately, learn from other researchers’ successes and failures, uphold ethical responsibilities, and improve the methodological practice of piloting. We conclude with three concrete suggestions for near-term changes to help pilot reporting become standard practice: scientific communities and institutions should develop simple pilot reporting templates; journals should establish clear pilot reporting guidelines for authors; and authors should acknowledge when pilot studies were run and share relevant materials and data. Current reporting standards favor conclusive and polished research narratives, but such narratives are the end product of a complex scientific process that should also be shared. A truly transparent science should spotlight processes, like piloting, that underpin the conclusions scientific papers draw.

articles.title: StreetArt4Sustainability: Mapping Sustainable Development Goals to Street Art
articles.authors: Patricia Arriaga; Maria Henriques Campos; Catarina Pereira; Sara Fernandes; Erin Michelle Buchanan
articles.abstract: Street art has been increasingly recognized for its potential to communicate themes aligned with the United Nations' 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development. This paper uses the StreetArt4Sustainability dataset, comprising 556 street art images, to examine perceptions of their alignment with the 17 Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs). Across two studies, SDG attributions were evaluated in terms of diversity, reliability, similarity, and co-occurrence structure. In Study 1, a stimulus sampling design was used, with 262 participants each rating a random subset of 40 images. In Study 2, three coders evaluated all artworks in relation to the SDGs using a deductive thematic coding approach. Findings revealed that survey participants attributed a broader range of SDGs to each artwork than coders; agreement was also higher among coders than among participants. Network analyses also showed structural differences: participants’ data yielded two broad clusters, labeled social and environmental based on their SDG composition, whereas coders’ data revealed a third cluster comprising SDGs associated with economic themes. Despite the differences, the two samples converged on which SDGs were most and least frequently endorsed, and on the SDGs occupying the most central positions within each network. Overall, these evaluations offer a methodological framework for assessing visual art in relation to the SDGs by combining complementary indicators for multi-label classification and providing a validated resource for advancing research on visual communication, sustainability perception, and the role of public art in supporting awareness of global development goals.

articles.title: Open Pilot Trial of a Single Session Consultation Service for Clients at StrongMinds Uganda
articles.authors: Rosco Kasujja; Ian Sotomayor; Peter Birungi; Morris Ndeezi; Erica Szkody; Jessica L. Schleider
articles.abstract: The need for mental health services in Sub-Saharan Africa far exceeds the availability of support, creating long waitlists for the few services that are in place. To address this crisis, implementing evidence-based, single-session interventions for individuals seeking treatment may provide timely relief. StrongMinds—a mental health charity organization serving youth and adults in Uganda—piloted a Single-Session Consultation (SSC) service for new treatment-seekers with elevated depressive symptoms, as indicated by a score on a screener survey suggesting the presence of at least mild depression. To optimize its reach and fit with StrongMinds’ service delivery model, the SSC was delivered by trained lay providers in both individual and group-based formats. Within two months (September-October 2023), the SSC was delivered to 200 Ugandan adults with elevated depression symptoms (ages 16-86; 73% female) upon initial outreach for StrongMinds’ group psychotherapy services. SSC clients reported significant improvements in hopelessness and depression symptoms at 2-week (ds = -0.73, -1.12) and 1-month follow-ups (ds = -0.96, -1.44), while waiting for group psychotherapy. SSC clients reported high SSC satisfaction (M = 4.47/5), and intervention effects did not significantly differ by delivery format (i.e., individual vs. group format). Results suggest the SSC’s acceptability, feasibility, and utility as a low-intensity, scalable intervention for adolescents and adults in Uganda on waiting lists for longer-term psychotherapy.

articles.title: Human vs AI Emotion Classification of Faces Expanded
articles.authors: LuLu Eisenberg; Kendra Leigh Seaman
articles.abstract: With the recent explosion of artificial intelligence (AI) in everyday life, questions have emerged about the abilities of AI to handle underrepresented groups. This study combines two recently developed resources—the Faces Expanded dataset and Python Facial Expression Analysis Toolbox (Py-Feat)—to compare human and AI emotion classification of images from underrepresented racial and age groups. The results showed a moderate positive correlation between human and AI performance, with humans outperforming AI in emotion classification. The relationship between human and AI performance was strongest for images displaying happiness and weakest for images displaying fear. These findings emphasize the importance of incorporating racial and age diversity into both facial stimuli and AI training datasets. This study contributes to the ongoing discussion about the limitations of AI in psychological research and its potential applications in real-world scenarios.

articles.title: Two practices that understate the mental health risks associated with adolescent social media use
articles.authors: Jonathan Haidt; Zachary M Rausch
articles.abstract: Why do researchers analyzing the same body of evidence reach different conclusions about whether social media use poses risks to adolescent mental health? We offer a partial explanation: two common practices can lead researchers to underestimate harm and reach divergent conclusions. First, studies often do not account for risk elevations, relying instead only on correlation coefficients, which are more prone to misinterpretation. Second, researchers often rely on highly blended analyses that combine heterogeneous exposures (e.g., multiple digital activities, including “TV watching”), outcomes (e.g., depression with life satisfaction), and populations (e.g., girls with boys), and then treat weak aggregate associations as evidence that specific risks are negligible. This is especially problematic when the central question is whether heavy social media use is associated with internalizing symptoms among adolescent girls. We illustrate how sequential blending can transform a large and clinically relevant association into a negligible one, which helps explain the persistent disagreement in the literature. We conclude by urging researchers to present their findings in more practically interpretable terms, including elevated risks, and to investigate heterogeneity across platforms, usage levels, populations, and outcomes.

articles.title: Behavioral effects of interactions between oxytocin and sex hormone-related proxies: a systematic review
articles.authors: Charlotte Felicia Kroll; Nicolas Kurtenbach; Arno Riedl; Koen R. J. Schruers; Dennis Hernaus
articles.abstract: Central oxytocin has been widely implicated in modulating social behavior and cognitive functions, yet evidence in humans remains subtle, heterogeneous, and difficult to replicate. Interactions between oxytocin and sex hormones as a key biological moderator may partly account for the variability in findings. This review systematically synthesizes experimental and observational behavioral findings on interactions between oxytocin and sex hormones as well as their related proxies (menstrual cycle stage, hormonal contraceptive use, and participant sex) during social and nonsocial tasks. A comprehensive search across four databases yielded n=63 included studies that examined interactions in participants aged 18 years and over, covering both clinical and nonclinical samples. Methodological approaches and details on hormonal variation and validation were systematically extracted, and results were clustered into conceptually coherent task domains. Overall, oxytocin x (proxy) sex hormone interactions were infrequently observed, with no domain yielding robust or consistent findings. There is some evidence of sexually dimorphic effects of oxytocin administration on social processing, a potential modulation by age, and suggestive PTSD-specific effects. Given the strong biological plausibility of oxytocin x sex hormone interactions, the absence of robust evidence for these interactions in the behavioral studies reviewed likely reflects methodological challenges such as imprecise hormonal operationalizations, and limited statistical power. Progress in this field may require more rigorous hormonal assessments, adequately powered factorial designs, dual causal manipulation (where feasible), and more complete reporting of sex and hormonal characteristics to determine when and how oxytocin and sex hormones jointly shape human social and nonsocial task behavior.

articles.title: bbtkv3: An Open-Source Suite for Timing Measurement and Analysis with the Black Box ToolKit v3
articles.authors: christophe pallier
articles.abstract: Experimental psychologists require sub-millisecond accuracy in  measuring stimulus presentation and participant response times. The Black Box ToolKit (BBTK) is a widely used hardware solution for such  measurements. One limitation is that the software provided along the BBTK by the vendor is specific for Windows. We developed a   cross-platform suite of command line tools and a library designed  to interface with the BBTK v3. These tools included serial port  detection, sensor threshold adjustment and automated event  capture. Additionally, it includes an interactive shell for manual  device control and a statistical analysis tool that computes event  durations, jitter, and latencies from captured data. Built in Go,  the suite is distributed as self-contained binaries for Windows,  macOS, and Linux. The source code and a library for embedding BBTK  control in Go applications are available under the GPL-3.0 licence  at https://github.com/chrplr/bbtkv3

articles.title: A Model Fit Approach to Test the Adequacy of Interval-Level Measurement in  Psychometric Models
articles.authors: Ellie Bastos Degobi; Víthor Rosa Franco; Sanford R Student
articles.abstract:
Psychometric models often treat latent variables as interval-scaled, but seldom test this assumption. We propose a model-comparison framework contrasting three increasingly 
restrictive models: the Isotonic Ordinal Probabilistic Model (ISOP), an ordinal representation; the Additive Conjoint Isotonic Probabilistic Model (ADISOP), an additive 
structure without parametric form; and the Rasch model, which assumes a logistic form. Because ISOP and ADISOP lack a nominal parameter count, model selection relies on 
bootstrap-estimated effective degrees of freedom, applied to AIC, BIC, HQC, and a bootstrap-analogue of DIC. A fully crossed simulation varied item number, sample size, and 
response categories across 45 conditions. AIC, BIC, and HQC often supported an additive representation for polytomous data, typically via ADISOP, but favored ISOP in some longer 
dichotomous-test conditions even when data were Rasch-generated. The bootstrap-analogue DIC showed a different pattern and failed computationally in some conditions. An empirical 
illustration using the Brazilian National High School Examination likewise showed disagreement across criteria. These findings support model comparison as a way to make 
measurement-level assumptions empirically testable, while showing that agreement across criteria is more informative than reliance on any single index.

articles.title: How Open is that Journal? Developing and Validating JORPE: An AI-Assisted Tool for Evaluating Open Research Support
articles.authors: Roni Tibon; Josefina Weinerova; Rowan Meijer
articles.abstract: The growing adoption of Open Research practices has created a need for scalable and transparent methods to evaluate how academic journals support openness and reproducibility. Existing frameworks primarily assess the presence of transparency policies but often overlook the extent to which journals facilitate their implementation through infrastructure, guidance, editorial processes, and publication formats. In this proof-of-concept study, we introduce the Journal Open Research Policy Evaluator (JORPE), an AI-assisted framework that automatically extracts, evaluates, and benchmarks journal policies using a multidimensional rubric. The rubric was informed by a manual review of 152 psychology journals and iteratively refined through comparisons between AI- and human-generated assessments. Stability was evaluated across 10 independent AI executions for 10 journals. Agent-generated scores showed excellent reliability, with an intraclass correlation coefficient (ICC(3,10)) of .993 for total scores and values exceeding .93 across all rubric dimensions. Comparisons with human ratings demonstrated substantial agreement, with a significant discrepancy observed for only one dimension. Analysis of disagreements informed rubric refinements that improved convergence between AI-generated and adjudicated scores while highlighting the complementary strengths of human and AI evaluation. The revised framework was subsequently applied to generate reports for 361 Q1 psychology journals indexed in SCImago, revealing substantial variation in journal support for Open Research, particularly for preregistration, registered reports, and broader Open Research publication formats. JORPE provides a transparent, scalable, and regularly updatable approach to evaluating journal policies and offers a flexible framework that can be adapted to different disciplines and evolving Open Research practices.

articles.title: Orthographic Learning Without Phonology: Lexical Configuration and Engagement of Novel Words in Deaf and Hearing Adults
articles.authors: Vera Varga; Denes Toth; Valéria Csépe
articles.abstract: Skilled reading relies on orthographic representations that compete during visual word recognition, and the establishment of these orthographic representations is assumed to depend on phonological recoding. This study investigated whether orthographic learning, both lexical configuration and lexical engagement, can occur in the absence of well-defined phonological representations. We compared deaf (N = 26) and hearing (N= 26) adults matched for age and education as they learned novel written words paired with unfamiliar object through visual exposure in a picture–word matching task. Learning was assessed through three tasks: a delayed picture–word matching task (measuring orthographic–semantic associations), a spelling recognition task (measuring lexical configuration), and a masked priming lexical decision task (measuring lexical engagement). Results showed that both groups acquired and retained new orthographic–semantic associations, although retention was weaker in the deaf group. No significant group differences were found in spelling recognition, indicating that accurate orthographic representations can form without phonological input. Neither group showed evidence of lexical competition in the masked priming task, suggesting that full lexical integration had not occurred. Overall, these findings suggest that while phonological access may support some aspects of word learning like retaining orthographic-semantic associations, it is not necessary for the initial acquisition of orthographic representations.

articles.title: Why we should be using real world data to improve pharmacotherapy in psychiatry
articles.authors: Declan M Quinn; Jane McGrath; Robert Whelan
articles.abstract: Psychiatric pharmacotherapy is often effective for patients. For example, symptoms of attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) are typically ameliorated by stimulant medications. However, identifying the best medication for an individual or their optimal dose can be difficult because clinical visits and retrospective symptom reports only capture snapshots of the underlying dynamic, context-dependent treatment trajectories. Real-world data approaches, obtained from smartphones and wearable technologies, can potentially provide a rich source of information for individual optimization of pharmacotherapy, yet they are infrequently used. First, these tools enable remote, high-frequency monitoring of medication efficacy and side effects, tracking core symptoms plus comorbid psychopathology, sleep, and autonomic function throughout titration. Second, densely sampled cognitive task data and ecological momentary assessment offer a route to understanding changes to neurocognitive mechanisms in response to medication. Third, real-world data can help redress the persistent sex disparities in pharmacotherapeutic research and practice by characterizing how symptoms and treatment response interact with sex-specific life events. We conclude with recommendations for future research and practice.

articles.title: Mechanisms Linking Smartphone and Social Media Use to Adolescent Mental Health and Wellbeing: A Qualitative Study of Adolescent, Teacher, and Parent Perspectives
articles.authors: Amie Randhawa; Brynna Dodge; Peymane Adab; Hareth Al-Janabi; Sally Fenton; maria michail; Breanna Morrison; Paul Patterson; Samuel Perry; Alice Sitch
articles.abstract:
Background: The impact of smartphones and social media on adolescent mental health and wellbeing are key concerns for families and policy makers. Much previous research has focussed on screentime, which does not capture the multi-functional nature of these technologies, and the mechanisms of influence. This study aimed to explore adolescent, parent and teacher perspectives on how different types of smartphone and social media use influence mental health and wellbeing outcomes.
Methods:  Adolescents (aged 12-15, N=82), school staff (N=46), and parents (N=49), recruited from 7 English Secondary Schools, participated in focus groups exploring adolescent uses of smartphones and social media, and associated mental health and wellbeing outcomes. 
Findings: Thematic analysis revealed six mechanisms of influence of adolescent smartphone and social media use on their mental health and wellbeing; displacement; sustained engagement; algorithmic content exposure; emotional and behavioural regulation; knowledge acquisition; and constant connectivity. There was broad agreement across participant groups on most themes, with each group providing a more nuanced perspective. 
Conclusions: This study provides a new taxonomy of mechanisms that explain how adolescents’ uses of smartphones and social media influence mental health and wellbeing outcomes. It highlights the benefits and harms associated with a wide variety of smartphone and social media use behaviours, across physical, cognitive, social, and emotional wellbeing domains. These findings can be used as a decision-support tool to inform clinical practice, intervention development and guidance on adolescent smartphone and social media use for families, clinicians and researchers.

articles.title: The Relationship between Distressing Life Events and Positive and Negative Mental Health
articles.authors: Pauline Hartmann; Antonia Döring; Xiao Chi Zhang; Jürgen Margraf; Marcella Lydia Woud
articles.abstract: Background and Objectives: Previous research on distressing life events primarily emphasized negative mental health outcomes. However, there has been a growing focus on positive mental health factors in recent times. To reflect this broader perspective, the present study investigated the relationship between distressing life events, including emotionally impactful or potentially traumatic experiences, and positive mental health, life satisfaction, subjective happiness, and depression, anxiety, and stress. Design and Methods: The sample included N = 426 students who participated in an online study testing protective and risk factors in the context of mental health and reports secondary analyses of these data. Results: Correlational analyses including the full sample showed that experiencing a distressing life event was linked to lower levels of positive mental health and life satisfaction, and higher levels of depression, anxiety, and stress. Post-hoc group comparisons supported this pattern. Among those who experienced a distressing life event, higher current distress due to the event correlated with lower levels of positive mental health, life satisfaction, and subjective happiness, and higher levels of depression, anxiety, and stress. Conclusions: This study showed robust correlations between the experience of a distressing life event and levels of both positive and negative mental health. These findings underscore the emotional and psychological impact of adverse life events, highlighting the potential value of targeting transdiagnostic protective factors, such as positive mental health and resilience, in approaches aimed at preventing and reducing mental health problems following distressing life events.

articles.title: Blissful Ignorance: A Motivated Cognition Perspective on Information Avoidance
articles.authors: Gabriela Czarnek; Katarzyna Jasko; Arie Kruglanski
articles.abstract: Extant models of willful ignorance—defined as the intentional choice not to seek or use information—typically invoke varying sets of underlying motives. In contrast, we treat willful ignorance as a case of epistemic behavior explained by a broader model of belief formation: Lay Epistemic Theory (Kruglanski, 2004). Drawing from that model, we argue that information avoidance stems from two overarching epistemic motivations: the need for specific certainty (a directional motive) and the need for non-specific certainty (a non-directional motive). Under particular conditions, these motivations may lead individuals to avoid or suppress information. This approach offers conceptual clarity by embedding information avoidance within belief formation processes and provides a unified framework that generates novel insights and testable hypotheses.

articles.title: "Like Solving a Puzzle": Psychology Students' Experiences of Data Wrangling and Analysis
articles.authors: James Edward Bartlett; Gaby Mahrholz; Ashley Elizabeth Robertson; Wilhelmiina Toivo; Holly Neill; Heather Woods; Dale J. Barr
articles.abstract: Data wrangling is an essential skill for reproducible research and graduate employability, but research methods curricula typically emphasise learning a decision tree of statistical tests over preparing raw data for visualisation and analysis. Our exploratory mixed methods study evaluated psychology students’ ability to analyse a processed versus unprocessed dataset and explored their experiences of the analysis process. Forty-two participants used either a processed dataset requiring minimal preparation (n = 25) or an unprocessed dataset requiring multiple wrangling steps (n = 17) to address the same research question. We collected quantitative data on the results that participants could produce and qualitative data on their experiences at each stage of the analysis process. 92% of participants using the processed data and 76% using the unprocessed data successfully produced the correct result, with attrition notably higher for those given the unprocessed data. A content analysis highlighted that students found the problem solving element of data wrangling rewarding but reported challenges in identifying the appropriate wrangling steps and choice of analysis without prescriptive instructions. The key implication of our findings is that psychology research methods curricula should provide scaffolded training in data wrangling and reproducible workflows prior to their independent research project.

articles.title: Person Perception and Artificial Intelligence: Modeling Human Social Judgment
articles.authors: Tiffany Matej Hrkalovic; Travis J. Wiltshire
articles.abstract: Person perception, the rapid social judgments people make about others' traits, emotions, and intentions, is increasingly being automated through artificial intelligence. From algorithmic hiring tools that score facial expressions and vocal tone to call center software that monitors emotional cues in real time, AI systems are now being designed to replicate and scale human social judgment. This chapter examines the psychological and cognitive foundations underlying these processes, the computational frameworks that operationalize them, and the challenges that emerge when human perceptual biases and unresolved theoretical debates are embedded into automated pipelines. It argues that such systems do not transcend person perception but institutionalize it, inheriting the assumptions, cultural norms, and systematic errors of the human judges on whose annotations they are trained. The chapter concludes with a research agenda oriented toward more transparent, theoretically grounded, and ethically accountable development and deployment of socially intelligent AI systems.

articles.title: No Evidence for an Illusory Near Space Advantage for Affordant Objects
articles.authors: Avni Rani Jansari; Aditi Jublie
articles.abstract: Our study investigated whether perceptual sensitivity for affordant objects is modulated within the illusory spaces. This was done using a horizontal Ponzo illusion which creates the perception of illusory peripersonal and extrapersonal space while holding the retinal size constant. In two experiments, the participants completed a visual search task in which targets were presented in either of the illusory spaces. The target was either an affordant object (a mug) or a non-affordant geometric shape (a triangle). In the first experiment, we found that the perceptual sensitivity for the affordant object was better in illusory far space, while perceptual sensitivity for the non affordant shape remained relatively stable across the spaces. However, when the illusion's direction was reversed in the second experiment to see if the findings were a result of visual hemifield or not, the effect of the affordant object disappeared. Together, these findings suggest that the role of spatial context on affordant object perception is inconsistent across visual field arrangements and may reflect an interaction between affordance processing and lateral attentional biases rather than a general perceptual advantage of PPS.

articles.title: No need to invoke ‘unconscious attention’ to explain the perceptual advantage of targets presented to the same eye as a preceding cue
articles.authors: Surya Gayet
articles.abstract: Claims about unconscious processing can profoundly impact theories of awareness, but require careful exclusion of simpler low-level explanations. Fuentes and Valle-Inclán (2026) report faster detection of targets presented to the same eye as a preceding monocular cue and interpret this effect as evidence that unconscious eye-of-origin information guides reflexive attention. Here, I argue that this conclusion is not warranted. Cue validity is fully confounded with transient shifts in ocular dominance caused by the presentation of the cue (i.e., flash suppression; Wolfe, 1984). The temporal dynamics of the reported validity effect are consistent with such an ocular-dominance account. Moreover, the assessment that eye-of-origin information was indeed inaccessible to consciousness does not meet current standards for establishing unconscious processing. Considering the existence of a more parsimonious interpretation of the data, based on well-established low-level visual phenomena, this set of experiments cannot be taken as evidence for unconscious guidance of reflexive attention.

articles.title: Prospective associations between sibling psychopathology in adolescence and their link to functional brain connectivity
articles.authors: Valerie Karl; Tilmann von Soest; Lars T. Westlye; Christian K. Tamnes; Tobias Kaufmann
articles.abstract:
Background: Siblings of adolescents with psychopathology are at elevated risk of developing psychopathology themselves, yet the role of sibling psychopathology on subsequent mental health and brain functional development has been largely overlooked. Adolescence may represent a particularly vulnerable period for such influences because it is characterized by heighted neural plasticity and peak onset of mental disorders. 
Method: Using longitudinal sibling data from the Adolescent Brain Cognitive Development (ABCD) Study (N = 3954, 49.2% female, age range = 9.3 - 16.1), we first examined prospective within-person associations between self-reported sibling general psychopathology across eight time points using random intercept cross-lagged panel models (RI-CLPM). Next, we tested whether past and recent sibling psychopathology exposure was linked to cortical functional connectivity at age 14 in a subsample (N = 1400) using supervised machine learning. 
Results: Within-person analyses revealed that higher sibling psychopathology during early adolescence (age = 11.5) predicted lower psychopathology in the other sibling at the subsequent timepoint (age = 12.1) whereas higher psychopathology during mid-adolescence (age =13.5) predicted later higher psychopathology in the other sibling (age 14.2). We did not find evidence for an association between sibling psychopathology exposure and functional connectivity after correcting for multiple comparisons. 
Conclusions: Together, these results suggest that sibling psychopathology relates to both resilience and increased risk for adolescent psychopathology in an age-specific manner. Further research is needed to clarify underlying mechanisms and identify how family-based interventions and support may reduce psychopathology risk during adolescence.

articles.title: Developing ADLib: Co-producing accessible qualitative data collection tools with learning disabled researchers and participants
articles.authors: Kayleigh Doyle; Laura Fox; Mo Hakim; Dan Newton; Harry Roche; Mary Peachey; Elliot Negru; Fran Copping; FinnMcLellan; Kathryn Asbury
articles.abstract:
Co-production is a collaborative process in which researchers, communities, and other interested parties work together to create knowledge and solutions to problems in society. Everyone involved in co-production is an equal creator and sharer of knowledge, and everyone’s perspective is combined to shape a shared understanding of the topic. In learning disability (LD) research, co-production is particularly important because it ensures that research is done with and for people with a learning disability. By engaging in co-production, the creation and sharing of knowledge will better represent the priorities of the community, and be more inclusive and accessible to their preferred modes of communicating and being. This collaboration helps address the longstanding “epistemic injustice” experienced by people with learning disabilities, whose knowledge and perspectives have often been overlooked or undervalued in research. 
This paper begins by introducing the Accessing Disability Library (ADLib). We then describe our multi-layered process of co-production on an 18-month ESRC-funded project focused on developing sustainable data infrastructure to support researchers in meaningfully including LD children and young people in their work. We present this process in four stages: (1) building the co-production team; (2) co-producing an informed consent approach; (3) co-producing data collection tools; and (4) co-producing the library. Comments and reflections from members of the co-production team are woven throughout the paper. By sharing both the challenges and successes of adopting a co-production approach in learning disability research, we hope to encourage other researchers in the field to move beyond tokenistic consultation. In doing so, we aim to support a shift away from epistemic injustice and towards more collaborative, inclusive research infrastructures.

articles.title: Turn to chatbots for sharing feelings or seeking solutions? Differential associations of preferences for chatbot-mediated self-disclosure and instrumental help-seeking with adolescent interpersonal behaviors in the United States and Hong Kong
articles.authors: Huinan Hu; Mojtaba Habibi Asgarabad; Enyi Jen; Ho Nam Cheung
articles.abstract: This study examined the association between different conversation topic preferences with AI chatbots (self-disclosure, instrumental help-seeking) and adolescents’ prosocial behaviors and bullying via the mediating role of coping styles, as well as potential cultural differences. A total sample of 2023 adolescents from the United States (US) and Hong Kong (HK) were included in the analysis. A major finding was that the preference to seek instrumental help from AI chatbots showed stable positive associations across different cultures, relating to more adaptive coping and positive behaviors. By contrast, the associations of the preference for self-disclosure with AI chatbots showed cultural differences, relating to more adaptive coping and positive behaviors in HK adolescents, but more maladaptive coping and negative behaviors in US adolescents. These findings enrich the current understanding of human-AI interactions from a cross-cultural perspective and have practical implications for designing AI chatbots and guiding adolescents’ usage of AI chatbots.

articles.title: Children's Play and Independent Mobility in 2025: Results from the British Children's Play Survey.
articles.authors: Paul McCrorie; Lily FitzGibbon; Bryony Longdon; Rachel Jane Nesbit; Brooke Elizabeth Oliver; Helen Frances Dodd
articles.abstract:
Understanding trends in how much, where, and how adventurously children play, and when they are granted independent mobility, is critical for supporting public health policy, urban planning, and health and wellbeing interventions. This study presents findings from the 2025 British Children’s Play Survey, a nationally representative survey of parents and caregivers of children aged 5–11 years living in Britain (n = 1,974), providing an updated assessment of the previous survey conducted in 2020.
Averaged across the year, children spent approximately 3.4 hours/day playing, with over half of this occurring outdoors (52%) and 13% in nature. Children spent the most time playing at home and the least time playing on streets near home. Playgrounds, greenspaces, and indoor play centres consistently afforded the highest levels of adventurous play, while streets and home environments were least adventurous. Parents/caregivers reported that children were typically allowed out alone at a mean age of 10.84 years, over one year later than they themselves reported for their own childhood (9.70 years).
Play behaviours and independent mobility were patterned by socio-demographic and geographic factors. Boys accumulated more total, outdoor, and adventurous play than girls. Regional differences were evident, with higher play levels in London and Scotland, and distinct age-related patterns, including declines with age outside of London and a curvilinear positive pattern within London, with increases from around age 9. Parental attitudes were differentially associated with outcomes: engagement with risk was positively associated with all play outcomes, while tolerance of risk was associated with earlier independent mobility.
Overall, findings reinforce the value of repeated population-level monitoring over time, indicating broad continuity since 2020, regional variation and persistent generational differences in independent mobility. Supporting access to diverse play environments and improving parental understanding of the benefits of engagement with risk may help enhance opportunities for adventurous play.

articles.title: An Inductive Reasoning Model of Temporal Self-Perception
articles.authors: Johannes Ullrich; David Joachim Grüning; Joachim Krueger
articles.abstract: How do people perceive their selves across time? To shed light on the question of how continuity and growth relate to each other, we extend the inductive reasoning model (IRM; Krueger et al., 2024-a, 2024-b) from social perception to temporal self-perception. Based on the robust empirical patterns showing that people perceive their present selves to be (a) positive and (b) more similar to their future than to their past selves, the IRM makes precise predictions about how much the positivity of the future self will exceed the positivity of the past self (i.e., subjective growth). We find support for the IRM in (re-)analyses of six datasets from Western samples (total N = 8,679). Moreover, we find evidence for additional self-enhancement in that subjective growth is greater than predicted; people enhance their future self, but do not diminish the positivity of their past self. Lastly, we discuss opportunities for future research, such as the use of individual differences in model parameters as correlates of mental health, aging, or culture.

articles.title: Multimodal large language models encode implicit gender bias
articles.authors: Ayse Sueda Nisanci; Carl Michael Galang; Marcel Brass
articles.abstract: Value-aligned multimodal large language models (MLLMs) appear explicitly unbiased, yet they still encode implicit biases. Quantifying implicit biases is essential for pursuing fairness in MLLMs. However, measuring them remains an open challenge. Here, we propose reverse correlation, a widely used data-driven technique in psychology for capturing mental representations and stereotypes, as a method for uncovering implicit biases in MLLMs. Applying this technique, we investigated whether state-of-the-art MLLMs, GPT-5.4 and Claude-Opus-4.8, reflect stereotypical gender biases in visual templates of leaders and followers reconstructed from 75,600 choices. We find that human participants perceived leader templates as more masculine and follower templates as more feminine. We further demonstrate that Claude-Opus-4.8-generated templates showed stronger stereotypical gender associations than human representations, indicating amplification of gender bias. Our findings advance implicit bias evaluation in MLLMs by establishing reverse correlation as a tool for uncovering visual stereotypes and highlighting the need to mitigate implicit biases despite explicit alignment efforts.

articles.title: The Solution in the World: Interactivity and Discontinuity Problem Solving
articles.authors: Frédéric Vallée-Tourangeau
articles.abstract: The label "insight problem" presupposes its own explanation: that these problems are solved through sudden, in-the-head restructuring. We propose “discontinuity problem” as an alternative, one that names what these problems produce, namely an impossible-then-possible transition, without presuming how it comes about. We employ the 12 Bunnies problem, a numerical discontinuity task solvable only by overlapping enclosures. Participants worked on the problem in either an interactive or control condition. Interactive participants, who could manipulate pictured bunnies and enclosures (creating solution prototypes), solved the problem more often and sooner and conceived of the overlap idea more often and earlier, than control participants. Coding of the video-recorded sessions revealed a distinction between deictic vs. symbolic counting, as well as instances where a solution was physically constructed before being recognised as one. These data illustrate that representational change is enacted through material engagement rather than computed internally and then executed.

articles.title: Measurement of American adolescents’ experiences of online harms: A nationally representative survey
articles.authors: Angela Yuson Lee; Carmen Hui Jing Lim; Xun Liu; Kang-Xing Jin; Anneke Buffone; Ravi Iyer; Zachary M Rausch; Jonathan Haidt; Nathanael Fast; Jeffrey Hancock
articles.abstract:
Importance: Concerns about the risks adolescents face online are rising, but existing research on online harms typically examines limited outcomes, rarely allows for platform-specific comparison, and lacks practical standardized measurement that would be suitable for public health monitoring.
Objective: We introduce and implement a measurement approach estimating the prevalence of negative experiences among US adolescents online, offline, and by platform.
Design, Setting, and Participants: Cross-sectional, nationally representative, probability-based survey of US adolescents aged 13-17 conducted February-December 2025 through the Understanding America Study panel. Self-reported use of 20 online platforms (e.g. Facebook, Instagram, Snapchat, TikTok, YouTube, Facetime, email etc) was assessed.
Main Outcomes and Measures: Self-reported prevalence of major risks and harms experienced in past 4 weeks, including harassment, sexual solicitation, and exposure to violent or self-harm content, as well as sleep disruption (measured online, offline, and by platform). Survey-weighted logistic regression identified associated factors.
Results: Weighted sample included 482 adolescents (mean age 15 years; 47.1% female; 65.1% White) from 47 US states. Across online and offline contexts, 44.3% witnessed harassment and 29.6% had experienced it directly in the past 4 weeks. Overall prevalence varied by gender and age: girls were more likely than boys to feel worse about themselves due to others' posts, messages, or communications (29.1% vs 15.5%), and older adolescents (ages 15-17) were more likely than younger adolescents (ages 13-14) to have witnessed discrimination against others (48.6% vs 38.5%). Online exposure exceeded offline exposure for numerous harms, including exposure to violent imagery (10.5% vs 1.6%), unwanted sexual images (13.5% vs 2.0%), and content encouraging self-harm (9.6% vs 5.1%). More than half (51.7%) reported sleep disruption due to technology use. Parental education, income, and parental controls were not significantly associated with online harm exposure (all P > .05). Platform differences in exposure to some harms were substantial, e.g., 42.8% of TikTok users and 28.3% of Instagram users attributed disrupted sleep to those platforms, compared with 11.3% of text-messaging users and 0.6% of email users.
Conclusions and Relevance: Negative online experiences are common among US adolescents and vary by platform, gender, and age. Establishing rigorous, multi-layered measurement approaches with platform-by-platform, social media versus other digital environments, and online versus offline comparisons is essential for transforming fragmented evidence into actionable data that can guide effective decisions by youth, parents, platforms and
regulators.

articles.title: Catatonia recovery separates two intervention axes that constrain electroconvulsive therapy
articles.authors: Hiroki Saito
articles.abstract: Catatonia recovers through capacities returning in a fixed dependency order, and benzodiazepines and electroconvulsive therapy work without a known target. On an evidence-coupled bistable cascade over that order we take three quantities to be externally accessible: the root capacity, the coupling between capacities, and accumulated evidence. Here we show that evidence has no external port and the other two act on disjoint regions. While every capacity is below threshold, a maximum principle forbids non-negative diffusive coupling, on any graph and either direction, from crossing the switching surface, so acute conversion needs an excursion, whereas an additive excitatory drive converts on its own. Above one exact criterion, the prevailing threshold squared over four, propagation separates into immediate, metastable and confined. On the modelled branch coupling alone shifts the resting first stage, so a treatment effective in both states is predicted to have separable excursion and coupling components, identifiable in model coordinates.

articles.title: Seeing the world through others' minds: Determining the role of executive functions in social cognitive processes
articles.authors: Katerina Michalaki; Charlotte Rebecca Pennington; Stephen Mayhew; Klaus Kessler; Daniel Shaw
articles.abstract: Our ability to infer others’ mental states (e.g., perspectives and beliefs) is integral to successful social interaction. A long-standing debate is whether mentalising relies upon specialised social-cognitive processes or more domain-general systems that coordinate our thoughts and behaviour across social and non-social contexts. In this preregistered study, we investigated this directly by determining the causal links between mentalising and three supposedly distinct domain-general executive functions (EFs): interference resolution (the suppression of task-irrelevant information), set shifting (the flexible switching between cognitive states) and memory updating (using new information to update memory representations). A large sample (N=369) completed an online battery of three experimental tasks that measured each of the EFs and a fourth that measured mentalising – our ability to infer how the world appears from someone’s else viewpoint (level-2 visuospatial perspective-taking; VPT-2) and acknowledge that others’ belief about the world may align with or diverge from our privileged knowledge of reality (true- and false-belief reasoning). Two structural equation models were applied to data acquired with this battery to evaluate direct and indirect pathways between EFs and mentalising. Contrary to our hypotheses, these models suggest that better memory updating  and interference resolution increased the cognitive costs associated with VPT-2 and false-belief reasoning, respectively, while set shifting showed no significant effects on mentalising. Furthermore, VPT-2 did not mediate any of the causal pathways between EFs and belief reasoning. This study indicates that EFs contribute to mentalising in subtle and complex ways, and our experimental rigour reveals several methodological considerations for future research.

articles.title: Now we see the violence inherent in the tinkering
articles.authors: Paul E. Smaldino
articles.abstract: The concept of social tinkering is useful, but insufficient to explain the evolution of human cultural complexity due to its overemphasis on cooperative interactions. The importance of conflict, violence, and inequality in the evolution of complex cultures complicates the social tinkering hypothesis. Who gets to tinker, and what determines which products of that tinkering are selected?

articles.title: Targeting coping strategies, emotion regulation, and self-esteem in children with dyslexia to support mental health: A randomised-controlled trial of Clever Kids
articles.authors: Mark Edward Boyes; Kirsten Melville; Mandy Nayton; Hannah Pizzey; Suze Leitao
articles.abstract: Background: Children with dyslexia are at elevated risk of mental health difficulties, both internalising (emotional) and externalising (behavioural) problems. Clever Kids is a nine-week socio-emotional wellbeing programme developed specifically to support upper primary school children with dyslexia. Aims: We conducted a pre-registered randomised-controlled trial to test the efficacy of Clever Kids. Method: Seventy-eight children (Mage = 10.19 years, 54% female) with clinically diagnosed dyslexia took part in the trial. Children were randomised to either attend Clever Kids (n = 38) or to a wait-list control condition (n = 40). Coping skills, emotion regulation, self-esteem, perseverance, assertiveness, as well as mental health (internalising and externalising symptoms) were measured at pre-programme, post-programme, and at three-month follow-up using well-validated measures. Results: The predicted interactions between intervention condition and time were significant for six outcomes. Attending Clever Kids was associated with significant improvements in child-reported coping, emotion regulation, academic and social self-esteem, as well as parent-reported anxiety and depression. Effects were all maintained at three-month follow-up. Unexpectedly, being assigned to the wait-list condition was associated with improvements in perseverance at follow-up assessment. For all other outcomes, interactions between intervention condition and time were non-significant. Conclusion: Clever Kids appears a promising programme for supporting socio-emotional wellbeing of children with dyslexia. Future research should consider incorporating caregivers more explicitly into the programme and alternative delivery modes, which could expand the reach of the programme.

articles.title: Identification of Individual Animals from Position, Orientation, and Movement Sequences in the Morris Water Task with Machine Learning: Implications for Spatial Learning
articles.authors: Max Griffin Segal; Derek A. Hamilton
articles.abstract:
The Morris Water Task (MWT) has been the gold standard assessment of place learning and
memory for over four decades, yet the processes that contribute to successful navigation are not
completely understood. It is generally posited that rats learn to navigate directly to a place;
however, navigation is not perfectly direct but contains variation in swim speed and trajectory
resulting in efficient, yet suboptimal paths. Gonçalves-Garcia et al. (2024) demonstrated that path topography is quantitatively similar across trials within individual rats for a given start location, and dissimilar between rats and different start locations within rat. This suggests rats may take unique paths to the platform from each release point. If such variation reflects learned behavior, it should be possible to objectively classify (identify) individual rats using machine learning. In the present study, a recurrent neural network was trained to classify 15 rats based on trial-level time-series data of path coordinates, velocity, and orientation. Testing on unseen coordinates or combined features from the same starting locations yielded classification accuracies that were 5.93-7.26-fold greater than chance and significantly greater than data from different start locations. Classification using scalar metrics with support vector machines was unable to match these outcomes. Collectively, these observations support the hypothesis that navigation in the MWT involves learning to perform behavioral sequences.

articles.title: Voice Can Help and Hurt AI Empathy: How Context Shapes the Effects of Vocal Delivery
articles.authors: Joshua D Wenger; Daryl Cameron; Michael Inzlicht; Reza Hadi Mogavi
articles.abstract: As people increasingly turn to artificial intelligence (AI) for empathy, new modes of human–AI empathic interaction have emerged. While prior research on empathic AI has focused almost exclusively on text-based empathy, we explored how vocal delivery of empathetic messages might enhance or undermine AI versus human empathy. Across five studies (N = 1,584) we examined how the mode of expression (voice vs. text) and the empathy source (human vs. AI) jointly shape perceptions of empathic quality and experiences of feeling heard across different interaction contexts. In interactions involving pre-recorded empathic messages, vocal delivery reduced perceptions of quality and experiences of feeling heard for both human and AI empathizers, though the reduction was stronger for AI. This reduction was eliminated for human empathizers by giving empathy recipients the option to first opt in or consent to receiving empathy from a human empathizer, though the reduction remained for AI voices in this pre-recorded context. The reduction for AI voices also disappeared, and sometimes reversed into a benefit, in more immersive and personally relevant interaction contexts such as extended, live interaction with an AI chatbot. We further explored how the mode of expression impacts feelings of uncanniness, and the mediating role uncanniness plays in shaping feelings of being empathized with and feeling heard. Together, these findings demonstrate that whether voice helps or hurts AI empathy critically depends on the interaction context, and highlight uncanniness as one factor that can undercut spoken empathy in some contexts.

articles.title: Key Moments and Event Boundaries in Film Comprehension and Memory
articles.authors: Aditya Upadhyayula; Zachariah Reagh; Jeffrey M. Zacks
articles.abstract: Not all moments we experience carry equal weight. The boundaries between meaningful events (Event Boundaries; EBs) have been found to be important for comprehension and memory. Recently, it has been shown that people can reliably identify Key Moments (KMs) that are somewhat distinct from EBs and play a unique role in both comprehension and memory. Some but not all KMs are EBs, and vice versa. Both EBs and KMs are identified in terms of subjective judgments. However, thus far they have been measured using different psychophysical procedures: EBs have usually been measured concurrently with movie viewing, whereas KMs have been measured retrospectively. This difference confounds the underlying cognitive construct with the psychophysical task. Here we dissociated the subjective construct measured from the psychophysical task. Participants watched clips from the television series Sherlock, and were asked to identify either EBs or KMs, and were asked to do so either by pressing a button in real time while watching or retrospectively using a timeline interface, in a fully crossed between-participants design. The timepoints selected were compared within and across groups. Within both Realtime and Retrospective task paradigms, KM distributions were more similar to other KMs than to EBs and vice-versa, suggesting a partial dissociation between the two constructs. A large and significant effect of the paradigm was also observed: Retrospective estimates of the same construct differed from its Realtime counterparts. These findings demonstrate that people see different structure in events, depending both on whether they are looking for key moments or boundaries and whether they are monitoring the moment or looking back. These variations in the structure are cognitively significant, and important for researchers studying event comprehension.

articles.title: Cognitive Reserve and Adaptive Resilience: A Conceptual Analysis of a Cross-Species Framework for Neuropsychology and Cognitive Aging
articles.authors: Yunier Broche-Pérez; Carlos Ramos-Galarza; Diego D. Díaz-Guerra; Marena Hernández Lugo
articles.abstract: Why do some aging adults maintain effective reasoning despite substantial Alzheimer-related neuropathology, whereas others with comparable neural burden show marked impairment? Why do some nonhuman primates exposed to mild, manageable early stress later show stronger prefrontal regulation and adaptive stress responses? Although usually studied separately, these questions reflect a shared adaptive problem: how organisms maintain, recover, or reorganize function in response to biological or environmental challenges. We propose that resilience is a dynamic, evolutionarily conserved process expressed across species through stress regulation, behavioral flexibility, social buffering, environmental engagement, and functional preservation. In humans, the cumulative development of these capacities may contribute to cognitive reserve. This does not imply that nonhuman animals possess cognitive reserve in the clinical human sense; rather, several behavioral and neurobiological processes supporting human reserve may have comparative precursors in nonhuman resilience systems. Cognitive reserve is reframed as more than a neural endowment or discrepancy between pathology and performance. It is also an active behavioral and regulatory repertoire, including flexible strategy use, compensatory reorganization, sustained engagement, and social resource mobilization. The manuscript proposes a five-level framework linking biological regulation, behavioral flexibility, social regulation, environmental enrichment, and functional preservation, offering testable hypotheses for cognitive aging and translational resilience research.

articles.title: A Phenomenological Study of Adult Children’s Lived Experiences with Narcissistic Parents
articles.authors: Mina Ghasemi Rahmatabadi; Amirhossein Ghasemy; Alireza Ahangaran; Fatemeh Dehnavi; Amirmahdi Amraei; Fatemeh Mirzai
articles.abstract:
Objective:  This study explored the lived experiences of adult children raised by narcissistic parents, aiming to illuminate the long-term psychological and relational effects of narcissistic parenting.

Methods and Materials: A qualitative design based on Interpretative Phenomenological Analysis (IPA) was employed. Semi-structured interviews were conducted with 15 adult participants (aged 26–42) who self-identified as having been raised by at least one narcissistic parent. Data were analyzed using the six-step IPA framework to extract emergent and superordinate themes.

Findings: Six superordinate themes emerged: (1) Identity in the Shadow of the Parent, (2) Sibling Relationships under Narcissistic Mirroring, (3) Emotional Disconnection and Coping in Silence, (4) Control and Ongoing Parental Intrusion in Adulthood, (5) Reclaiming the Self in Adulthood, and (6) Social and Occupational Impact. Participants reported enduring feelings of inadequacy, identity diffusion, emotional manipulation, and conditional affection, alongside processes of healing, boundary-setting, and post-traumatic growth.

Conclusion: Narcissistic parenting leaves lasting emotional scars that impair identity development, emotional regulation, and interpersonal functioning in adulthood. Nevertheless, through therapy and personal resilience, individuals can reconstruct a coherent sense of self and establish healthy relational boundaries. The findings underscore the importance of trauma-informed clinical approaches for adult survivors of narcissistic parenting.

articles.title: Where are the context effects? A meta-analysis of the attraction, similarity, and compromise effects
articles.authors: Xiaohong Cai; Timothy Joseph Pleskac
articles.abstract: Adding an option to a choice set can alter how existing options are compared and systematically shift choice. The attraction, similarity, and compromise effects demonstrate such context dependence, but the empirical record is mixed. We conducted a meta-analysis of 83 studies comprising 964,766 individual choices, distinguishing changes in the target’s standing relative to a competitor from changes in its marginal choice probability. Primary hierarchical analyses yielded relative-choice estimates in the predicted direction for all three effects and, for absolute choice, increased target choice for attraction but little overall change for compromise.  Sensitivity analyses accounting for heterogeneity, precision-related effect-size inflation, and possible publication selection provided the strongest evidence for an average attraction effect in both relative and absolute choices but limited evidence for an average similarity and compromise effect. All three effects exhibited substantial heterogeneity across experiments. Moderation analyses showed that effect magnitudes varied with decoy structure, presentation format, attribute type, and decision criterion. Together, these results indicate that context effects are conditional rather than uniform: their magnitude and direction depend on how choice problems are constructed, represented, and measured. The findings challenge choice theories to explain how the canonical effects arise, why their magnitude and direction vary across experimental conditions, and which aspects of choice they alter. For interventions that seek to shape choice via context effects, reconfiguration of the choice set alone is insufficient. An effective intervention will depend on aligning the intended context effect with how the options are represented and compared.

articles.title: The working memory advantage for meaningful stimuli persists under high levels of proactive interference
articles.authors: Lauren Williams; Viola S. Störmer; Timothy F. Brady
articles.abstract: Previous work has shown that visual working memory performance is higher for recognizable and meaningful stimuli relative to meaningless, but physically matched, stimuli (e.g., Asp et al., 2021). Here, we test whether the benefit for meaningful stimuli arises due to active storage in working memory or can, at least in part, be explained by reliance on other more durable memory traces, such as long-term memory. We manipulated meaningfulness using ambiguous Mooney faces (Exp. 1) and objects (Exp. 2) vs. scrambled versions of the same stimuli. Although items were repeated 10x more often in the high interference condition than the low interference condition, we found equivalent objective and subjective effects of meaningfulness at high levels of proactive interference, suggesting that persistent passive long-term memory traces do not play a critical role for the meaningfulness advantage in working memory tasks.

articles.title: A Relationships of Noctcaelador with Measures of Psychological Dysfunction: The MMPI-2 and Cognitive Ability
articles.authors: William E. Kelly
articles.abstract: Research has not examined noctcaelador, psychological attachment to the night sky, in relation to psychological dysfunction. Previous studies have produced ambiguous results in this regard suggesting noctcaelador was related both to healthy psychological processes and possible indicators of dysfunction such as hallucinatory activity. The current research examines the relationship between noctcaelador and psychological dysfunction directly in a cross-sectional study. A sample of 44 undergraduate students (28 females, 16 males) completed self-report measures of noctcaelador, psychological dysfunction, and cognitive ability.
