Generally, noctcaelador was unrelated or negatively related to most indices of psychological dysfunction. However, there was a strong positive relationship between noctcaelador and hypomania. A substantial 28.9% of individuals high in noctcaelador also scored above the clinical cut-off for hypomania. It was surmised that some processes involved in hypomania may underly noctcaelador such as divergent thinking, unusual perceptual processes, and seeking out novelty. Less defensiveness among individuals higher on noctcaelador was also noted and discussed in the context of a psychic structural model of noctcaelador. Additional research is suggested to examine possible hypomanic processes in noctcaelador and the potential mediating effects of openness to experience.

articles.title: Associations of Maladaptive Psychological Processes and Noctcaelador in a University Student Sample: A Follow-Up Study
articles.authors: William E. Kelly
articles.abstract: Previous research among university students found that noctcaelador, psychological attachment to the night sky, was significantly related to higher levels of hypomania and lower levels of depressiveness and defensiveness. However, those findings involved a clinical measure of psychological dysfunction. The current study aimed to replicate those results utilizing a measure designed for nonclinical samples and controlling possible influences of openness to experience. A sample of 135 (71.9% female) undergraduate students completed brief measures of noctcaelador, maladaptive psychological processes, and openness to experience. Replicating previous findings, while noctcaelador was unrelated to most indices of maladaptive processes, it was significantly positively related to hypomanic processes after controlling openness to experience and gender. Additionally, noctcaelador was significantly related to scales measuring nonordinary perceptual experiences and valuing emotional expressivity after controlling gender and openness. Previous findings of relationships with depressive and defensive responding were not replicated. The results were interpreted in the context of a self-structural model of noctcaelador and previous research. Additional investigation is needed to extend these findings and understand possible mechanisms and contexts for the results.

articles.title: A No-Go Theorem for Process Theories of Consciousness
articles.authors: Aneil Mallavarapu; Chris Percy
articles.abstract: Many influential theories identify consciousness with temporally extended processes: global broadcasting, recurrent processing, predictive updating, computation. We show that such theories cannot be maintained alongside two commitments that scientific practice ordinarily assumes. The first is that a system's subsequent behaviour is fixed by its present physical condition together with influences crossing its boundary — the assumption underwriting experimental replicability, since preparing the same system under the same conditions is expected to yield the same result. The second is that consciousness makes some difference to what a system does, without which no experimental intervention can identify which attribution is correct. Two systems may reach the same present state by different routes. If consciousness depends on which route was taken, that difference either alters subsequent behaviour, contradicting the first commitment, or alters nothing and no experimental intervention can detect it. Consciousness must therefore be attributed to a system’s present state rather than to its past states. This holds for any system whose complete present local state, together with influences crossing its boundary, determines its subsequent evolution, which includes all systems whose relevant fundamental dynamics are captured in principle by models from classical physics.

articles.title: Creativity as a Bridge Between Temperament and Attachment to the Night Sky (Noctcaelador)
articles.authors: William E. Kelly; Kathryn E. Kelly
articles.abstract: Temperament reflects biologically rooted patterns of emotional and behavioral reactivity, yet the mechanisms through which temperament dispositions become specific higher-order experiential orientations remain unclear. This study examined whether creativity mediates the relationship between temperament and noctcaelador – psychological attachment to the night sky. Participants (N = 168) completed the EAS Temperament Survey, Scale of Creative Attributes and Behavior (SCAB), and Noctcaelador Inventory-4. Noctcaelador was positively associated with the SCAB Creative Engagement (r = .27, p < .01) and Spontaneity (r = .31, p < .01) scales but showed no direct associations with temperament in correlations or simultaneous regression analyses controlling for age and gender. Parallel mediation models indicated that the EAS Activity scale predicted noctcaelador indirectly through the SCAB Creative Engagement (B = .09, 95% CI [.013, .193]) and Spontaneity (B = .13, 95% CI [.046, .236]) scales. Findings support a process-oriented account in which noctcaelador emerges through the creative modulation of activation rather than direct temperament effects.

articles.title: Researchers’ Predicting Replicability in the Human Sciences
articles.authors: Kristina Vallas; John Protzko; Naomi Cotto
articles.abstract: What do researchers believe the replication rate of their field is, and what thresholds do they consider acceptable or problematic? We survey 1,826 active researchers, spanning 11 disciplines, estimating the replication rate of their own field and specify thresholds that distinguish acceptable from problematic replication rates. Across fields, researchers estimate their own field’s replication rate to be 56.2% (95% CI [55.1, 57.4]), with a median of 60%. Estimates vary across fields, ranging from 46.6% in Education to 65.4% in Economics. Median lowest acceptable thresholds range from 60% to 75%, median highest problematic thresholds range from 55% to 75%. When comparing perceived replication rates to what researchers say would be acceptable and unacceptable, all 11 fields fall below the threshold using mean perceived replication rates, and 9 of 11 fields fall below the threshold using median perceived replication rates. Using individual-level responses, between 41.0% and 59.0% of respondents classify their field as likely in the unacceptably low replication region. These findings suggest concerns about replicability extend across the human sciences. Researchers across fields report similar estimates of replication rates and similar thresholds for what they consider problematic, indicating broadly shared standards for evaluating scientific credibility.

articles.title: Mothers’ objectively measured smartphone use around their infant and longitudinal change in markers of socioemotional development during early infancy
articles.authors: Brandon T. McDaniel; Adam M Galovan; Sarah Coyne; Lara Wolfers; Rachel Pfafman; Alison K Ventura
articles.abstract: As parent smartphone use is common during caregiving, concerns have arisen over possible impacts on infant development. This longitudinal study used objectively measured maternal smartphone use, self-reported measures of infant behavior/emotions, and observed markers of socioemotional development (e.g., infant clarity of cues, responsiveness to mother during feeding) to examine whether maternal use was connected to changes in socioemotional development from 2 to 5 months of age. Participants included 163 mothers (84% non-Hispanic white) and their infants from the United States. Longitudinal structural equation modeling was used. Higher month 2 smartphone use predicted less favorable developmental change in infant behavioral responsiveness to the mother, and early increases in smartphone use marginally predicted less favorable change in clarity of infant cues but also significantly predicted increases in social responses to the mother. Month-to month increases in maternal smartphone use were significantly associated with increases in infant fussiness over time and marginally with decreases in infant happiness (according to maternal reports). Results suggest that maternal smartphone use may sometimes be tied to socioemotional development and infants may adapt their behavior to maternal use. Maternal smartphone use may warrant inclusion in anticipatory guidance as a potentially modifiable caregiving-context factor.

articles.title: What's in a Name? A Latent Variable Analysis of Positive and Negative Affect
articles.authors: Jason W. Payne; Ulrich Schimmack
articles.abstract: Two of the most widely used affect instruments label their subscales identically and are reported interchangeably, yet they do not measure the same thing. The Scale of Positive and Negative Experience (SPANE) marks the valence axis of the affective circumplex; the Positive and Negative Affect Schedule (PANAS) sits on the high-activation diagonals, where valence is fused with arousal. We quantify this divergence by decomposing both instruments into content-defined valence, activation, and discrete emotion factors, and testing which content predicts life satisfaction. Across two independent samples (N = 496 and N = 749), prediction ran entirely through valence: the arousal variance that distinguishes the PANAS from the SPANE added nothing to the prediction of a hedonic judgment. Because neither battery samples low-arousal states, this result is scoped to the high-arousal range the PANAS covers. The PANAS functions as a valence measure carrying additional arousal variance, and Positive Affect names a different construct in each instrument, a difference the shared label conceals.

articles.title: It's the Motive, Not the Strategy: Health and Weight-Control Motives Mediate How Reward and Punishment Sensitivity Shape Restraint and Dieting Success
articles.authors: Leonardo Pimpini; Nienke Jonker
articles.abstract: Reward and punishment sensitivity (RS, PS) as described by the Reinforcement Sensitivity Theory have been linked to dietary behavior; yet their mechanisms remain poorly understood. We examined whether dietary motives (health, weight-control) and dieting strategies (strict behaviors, flexible beliefs) mediate the relationship between RS, PS, restrained eating, and perceived dieting success. We hypothesized that PS is associated with restrained eating (H1a) and dieting success (H1b), and RS with restrained eating (H2a) and dieting success (H2b), with all associations mediated by dieting motives and strategies. 238 adults completed a cross-sectional online survey via Prolific (50% women; Mage = 32.7). Reward and punishment sensitivity (RPRM-Q), restrained eating (Restraint Scale), dieting success (PSRS), dietary motives (Food Choice Questionnaire), and dieting strategies (FORCES) were self-reported; mediation analyses used bootstrapped confidence intervals (PROCESS, Model 4). In line with H1a, higher punishment sensitivity predicted stronger weight-control motives and greater restrained eating. For dieting success (H1b), competitive mediation emerged: a negative indirect path through weight-control motives alongside a positive path through health motives. Contrary to H2a and H2b, reward sensitivity showed no direct effects but was linked through health motives to lower restrained eating and higher dieting success. Against expectations, dieting strategies were not significant mediators. Whether sensitivity traits translate into effective dietary regulation may depend on the motive, not the strategy: weight-control motives foster restraint but undermine dieting success, whereas health motives support it. Future work could manipulate dieting motives across levels of PS and RS to test effects on food intake and dieting behavior.

articles.title: The Role of Temperament and Personality Traits in the Development of ADHD from Late Childhood through Adolescence
articles.authors: Katherine M. Lawson; Jocelyn I. Meza; Richard Robins
articles.abstract: Individual differences in temperament and personality traits may shed light on the presentation and development of attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) across adolescence. The present study used multi-method, longitudinal data from a large sample of Mexican-origin youth (N = 674; 50% girls) to examine associations between ADHD symptoms (including combined, hyperactive-impulsive, and inattentive subtypes) and a wide range of temperament and personality traits assessed via self-, mother-, and father-reports and coded observational data. First, we found moderate one-year rank-order stabilities of combined, hyperactive-impulsive, and inattentive ADHD symptoms (r’s ranging from .27 to .51), but relatively low eight-year rank-order stability from age 10 to 17 (r = .19 for combined); eight-year stability was higher for boys than girls. Second, hyperactive-impulsive and inattentive symptoms were both negatively correlated with concurrent effortful control and conscientiousness, and positively correlated with impulsivity, negative emotionality, and neuroticism; in addition, hyperactive-impulsive symptoms were positively associated with surgency and extraversion. Third, bivariate latent growth curve models showed that the levels and slopes of effortful control (and its facets) and negative emotionality (particularly the frustration, aggression, and depressed mood facets) were significantly related to the levels and slopes of ADHD symptom trajectories. Findings from random-intercept cross-lagged panel models showed that temperament domains and ADHD symptoms had meaningful between- and within-person associations, but no significant cross-lagged associations. Associations were stronger for adolescent self-reports of temperament/personality than for mother reports. Overall, findings highlight connections between temperament and personality traits with ADHD symptoms across adolescence.

articles.title: Questionable prospective effects between cognitive triad and depression: A re-meta-analysis and comment on Huang et al. (2026)
articles.authors: Kimmo Sorjonen; Bo Melin; Marika Melin
articles.abstract: Based on meta-analytic findings, Huang et al. concluded prospective cross-lagged effects between cognitive triad (i.e., negative views of the self, the world, and the future) and depression. However, cross-lagged effects may be spurious. Here, we fitted alternative models to the same meta-analytic data and found discrepant increasing and decreasing effects of cognitive triad on subsequent change in depression, and vice versa, depending on the model used to analyze the data. Meta-analytic aggregations of these discrepant effects did not differ significantly from zero. Hence, the findings by Huang et al. may have been spurious and their conclusions premature. It is important to keep in mind that correlations, including cross-lagged effects, in observational (i.e., non-experimental) data may be spurious rather than due to genuine influence. We recommend researchers to fit, in line with multiverse methodology, alternative models to data and to base conclusions on an aggregation of findings.

articles.title: Evidence on the validity, reliability and usability of active and passive sensing of cognition for use in ambulatory studies: A systematic scoping review
articles.authors: Xiaochang Zhao; Artemis Stefani; Jannis Kraiss; Zeynep Koyuncu; Peter M. ten Klooster; Matthijs Leendert Noordzij
articles.abstract: Cognitive functions are traditionally measured as trait-like constructs in highly controlled lab settings using paper-based or computerized tasks. Growing emphasis on ecological validity and the increasing use of ecological momentary assessment (EMA) have shifted research focus towards repeated or continuous assessment of cognitive states in daily life. This includes cognitive tasks or questions delivered via mobile devices (active sensing), and objective indicators such as keystroke dynamics derived from smartphone sensors (passive sensing). However, the psychometric properties and usability of these approaches have not yet been established systematically. This scoping review evaluated the evidence on validity, reliability and usability of cognitive assessments for use in ambulatory research. In total, 88 studies were included, with most examining active cognitive sensing (n = 72) and fewer studies on passive sensing (n = 13) or both (n = 3). Among active cognitive assessments, processing speed tasks demonstrated the most consistent and robust psychometric evidence on mobile devices relative to other cognitive domains. Keystroke dynamics, among other passive sensing features, showed consistent initial associations with processing speed measures, and some evidence to distinguish between clinical and non-clinical groups. Despite these promising findings, only a few studies explicitly assessed between- and within-person reliability within EMA settings. Usability outcomes were generally positive across studies but less frequently investigated than validity and reliability. Future research should develop and adopt standardized approaches to evaluate mobile-based cognitive assessments. Eventually such measures will enable research on cognitive fluctuations and their dynamic relationships with stress, behavior and health in real-world contexts.

articles.title: Daily life stress measurement strategies: A scoping review
articles.authors: Solomiia Myroniuk; Annelieke Roest; Alysha Keuning; Maria Esanu; Isabel Mertins; Evelien Snippe; Peter de Jonge; Bertus F. Jeronimus
articles.abstract:
Aim. This scoping review of daily momentary stress measurement studies synthesizes a booming but fragmented field of stress research and introduces the stress MEasurement StrategieS (StressMess) database.
Methods. Systematic searches in Web of Science, MEDLINE, and PsycINFO identified studies of (a) stress and psychopathology (e.g., anxiety/depression) using (b) time series or ambulatory assessment designs where (c) stress was measured at least daily on two consecutive days. 
Results. We identified 12,846 articles and included 721 studies into the StressMess database, of which half in the past five years, typically with larger samples and more frequent measurements than older studies. Most participants were young adults (aged 18-24, M=67% women), from general populations in the US (55%), Germany (7%), and the Netherlands (5%). Stress was often operationalized as a stressor (27%) or stress response to adverse events (33%), and measured as characteristics of events (e.g., type, frequency, predictability, stressfulness, unpleasantness), or general momentaneous or daily stress score (27%), or as stress response via emotions (5%), or physiology (<1%). Some studies (13%) used multiple stress operationalizations. 
Conclusion. Stress is currently not a useful scientific concept because of the large heterogeneity in definitions, terminology, measurement strategies (instruments), and study design. We provide directions to improve conceptualizations and design for future studies focusing on measuring stress. The StressMess database is open source (www.stressmess.nl) to improve the understanding, prevention, and treatment of adverse (mental) health effects of stress. Stress measurement influences what stress research can identify and thereby clinical practice.

articles.title: Does the Label Matter? A Laboratory Study of Clothing Size Format and State Body Image in Women
articles.authors: Sofia Abrevaya; Camila Rossi; Rachel Rodgers
articles.abstract: Clothing size labels are a salient interface between consumers and apparel products and have been suggested to influence body image and emotional responses. This study experimentally examined whether different clothing size labeling systems—category-based versus color-based—affect women’s state body image and mood when isolated from garment fit and shopping context.  Sixty-seven women participated in a laboratory-based apparel simulation in which standardized body measurements were taken, and individualized size feedback was provided. Participants were randomly assigned to receive size feedback in a category-based (S/M/L/XL) or color-based format via a computerized interface. State body dissatisfaction, feelings of fatness, weight concern, and mood were assessed at baseline, post-measurement, and post-feedback. Participants’ attitudes toward size labeling systems and retail sizing practices were also assessed. Results showed no consistent effects of labeling condition or measurement procedure on any outcome. Across all domains, state responses were strongly predicted by state baseline body-related indices, whereas experimental condition and objective body size did not account for change over time. Secondary analyses indicated widespread dissatisfaction with existing sizing practices, independent of experimental conditions. These findings indicate that, under the specific conditions tested, no evidence was found that labeling format influenced body-related states; rather, they reflect pre-existing self-perceptions when detached from embodied and contextual cues. The results identify boundary conditions for the psychological impact of size labeling and highlight the importance of individual differences in apparel-related body image.

articles.title: Children's Play and Independent Mobility in 2025: Results from the British Children's Play Survey.
articles.authors: Paul McCrorie; Lily FitzGibbon; Bryony Longdon; Rachel Jane Nesbit; Brooke Elizabeth Oliver; Helen Frances Dodd
articles.abstract:
Understanding trends in how much, where, and how adventurously children play, and when they are granted independent mobility, is critical for supporting public health policy, urban planning, and health and wellbeing interventions. This study presents findings from the 2025 British Children’s Play Survey, a nationally representative survey of parents and caregivers of children aged 5–11 years living in Britain (n = 1,974), providing an updated assessment of the previous survey conducted in 2020.
Averaged across the year, children spent approximately 3.4 hours/day playing, with over half of this occurring outdoors (52%) and 13% in nature. Children spent the most time playing at home and the least time playing on streets near home. Playgrounds, greenspaces, and indoor play centres consistently afforded the highest levels of adventurous play, while streets and home environments were least adventurous. Parents/caregivers reported that children were typically allowed out alone at a mean age of 10.84 years, over one year later than they themselves reported for their own childhood (9.70 years).
Play behaviours and independent mobility were patterned by socio-demographic and geographic factors. Boys accumulated more total, outdoor, and adventurous play than girls. Regional differences were evident, with higher play levels in London and Scotland, and distinct age-related patterns, including declines with age outside of London and a curvilinear positive pattern within London, with increases from around age 9. Parental attitudes were differentially associated with outcomes: engagement with risk was positively associated with all play outcomes, while tolerance of risk was associated with earlier independent mobility.
Overall, findings reinforce the value of repeated population-level monitoring over time, indicating broad continuity since 2020, regional variation and persistent generational differences in independent mobility. Supporting access to diverse play environments and improving parental understanding of the benefits of engagement with risk may help enhance opportunities for adventurous play.

articles.title: Of Two Minds: A registered replication
articles.authors: Frederik Aust; Tobias Heycke; Benedek Kurdi; Pieter Van Dessel; Jeremy Cone; Melissa Ferguson; Xiaoqing Hu; Elsa Congjiao Jiang; Robert Rydell; Lisa Spitzer
articles.abstract: Several dual-process theories of social evaluation posit that implicit (or automatic) and explicit (or non-automatic) evaluations reflect distinct attitudes acquired via qualitatively different learning processes. Consequently, one may explicitly like a person but dislike them implicitly. Rydell et al. (2006) reported a striking demonstration of this dissociation: Briefly flashed negative words paired with a person described as behaving positively produced positive ratings of that person but negative Implicit Association Test scores. However, Heycke et al. (2018) could not replicate this dissociation. In two new replication attempts (N = 593) across four countries and three languages, with words flashed between 13 and 27 ms, we too found overwhelming evidence against the dissociation between directly and indirectly measured evaluations. We conclude that the dissociative evaluative learning effect reported by Rydell et al. (2006) is replicably non-replicable.

articles.title: Ethical considerations for integrating social determinants in brain health research:  A cultural-ecosocial approach
articles.authors: Axel Constant; Phoebe Friesen; Myrna Lashley; Laurence Kirmayer
articles.abstract: The integration of social determinants of health (SDH) into neuroscience and brain health research is a critical step in advancing our understanding of the complex interplay between social environments and neurobiological outcomes. However, this integration raises unique ethical challenges that extend beyond traditional research ethics frameworks. This paper examines the ethical considerations surrounding SDH data collection, management, analysis, and communication in brain health research. We organize these challenges according to a research life cycle framework, identifying specific risks at each phase: priority setting, data management, analysis, and communication. We propose a comprehensive risk mitigation framework organized around three domains of practice: (1) engagement, (2) governance, and (3) scientific practices. We present a three-tier model of ethical practice based on health equity scholarship and Indigenous research ethics perspectives, distinguishing Foundational, Equity-Informed, and Justice-Oriented practices. We conclude with recommendations to guide researchers in implementing ethical practices relevant to their research contexts while advancing health equity and protecting vulnerable populations. An appendix provides a researcher toolkit and guidance for research ethics boards.

articles.title: Burning facts: thick and thin causatives
articles.authors: Fabienne Martin; David Rose; Shaun Nichols
articles.abstract: Lexical causative verbs are traditionally assumed to pattern uniformly: they specify only a result state, leaving the manner of causing unarticulated, like the overt cause. We argue that this view obscures a fundamental division within English causative verbs. Building on Rose et al. (2021), we show that a substantial subset of causatives – thick causatives such as burn, melt, break, bury – encode information about the way a change is brought about, and that this specification yields systematic semantic and pragmatic restrictions. Thick causatives in their physical sense resist subjects that denote absences, facts, degrees, or events that fail to instantiate the appropriate productive (force- transmitting) mechanism, in contrast to thin causatives like kill, destroy, and change, which readily combine with such subjects. Using corpus evidence from a representative sample of 37 frequent English causatives, we demonstrate (i) that most thick causatives pattern like Embick’s 2009 break-causatives – compatible with strong adjectival resultatives and requiring production-based causation – while (ii) some thick causatives (e.g., bury) encode the relevant manner information via the state they lexicalize rather than via an event predicate. We develop a pragmatic competition account linking the production constraint to the directness constraint, yielding a unified explanation for the distribution of thick vs. thin causatives in English.

articles.title: Structural Order and Memory Encoding: A Recall Advantage for Postnominal Modifiers
articles.authors: Ondřej Drobil; Michael Ramscar; Jan Chromý
articles.abstract: How does the position of attributive modifiers shape memory for sentence content? Prior work suggests that modification enhances noun‑phrase representations, but evidence on adjective position is mixed and confounded by differences in modifier type. We report four experiments in Czech that directly test how prenominal vs. postnominal position affects immediate (post‑sentential) recall. Across experiments, we used open‑ended comprehension questions following written and spoken stimuli. In Experiments 1–2 (written), postnominal adjectives were recalled more accurately than prenominal ones. Experiment 3 crossed modifier position with modifier type (bare adjectives vs. genitive modifiers that canonically occur postnominally in Czech). The recall advantage for postnominal position generalized across types; no interaction emerged, arguing against an explanation based on syntactic atypicality or frequency. Experiment 4 (listening) replicated the recall advantage for postnominal position under fixed pacing. Together, the results show a robust recall benefit for postnominal modification that generalizes across modality and presentation regimes. We interpret the advantage in terms of discriminative, error‑driven learning: encountering the noun first foregrounds object features, enabling cue competition to sharpen the diagnosticity of subsequent modifiers, yielding stronger, more retrievable representations.

articles.title: Clarifying emotion recognition in neurotechnology: A scientific and technical reality check
articles.authors: Marie Luise Schreiter
articles.abstract:
Consumer neurotechnology systems that are claimed to be able to infer human emotions from facial expressions, voice, and physiological signals are increasingly deployed in domains such as marketing, education, human resources, and mental health.  As these systems have moved beyond clinical and research settings into consumer markets, their purported capacity to infer users’ internal states has become increasingly relevant to everyday life. More recently, emerging neuro-technologies have extended these claims by suggesting that emotional states can be detected directly from neural data using artificial intelligence, thereby bypassing outward behaviour altogether. These technologies are often promoted on the premise that emotions can reliably be measured objectively, enabling more precise, efficient, and equitable decision-making. However, the scientific and technical foundations underlying these claims remain contested.
In this article, we examine the scientific basis and methodological reality underlying claims regarding emotion classification in neurotechnology. We will evaluate the basic assumptions that are embedded in emotion recognition claims: That 1) emotional states can be objectively and reliably inferred from bodily or brain data and 2) emotional states are associated with stable and sufficiently specific behavioural, physiological, or neural signatures that permit reliable inference and 3) recordings from forehead, in-ear devices or consumer EEG in form of headbands, glasses, or earbuds can deliver technically good-enough signal to inform about the inner emotional conditions of an individual user. 
Based on current findings, we are sceptical about claims regarding consumer emotion recognition systems. These systems currently face fundamental conceptual, empirical, and practical limitations. We conclude that the current enthusiasm surrounding AI-based emotion recognition reflects an overconfidence in the objectivity of data-driven systems as well as current technological capabilities. A more realistic appraisal of the technical state of the art and transparent discussions of limitations of these technologies is necessary, particularly when they are deployed in high-stakes contexts or in vulnerable groups. Clarifying these limitations is essential for responsible development, evaluation, and governance of emotion recognition in neurotechnology.

articles.title: The Psychological Wellbeing Benefits of Textile Handcrafts: A Systematic Review, Meta-Analysis, and PERMA-Based Framework
articles.authors: Emma Claire Palmer-Cooper; Caitlin Foster; Anne E. Ferrey
articles.abstract:
The evidence base reporting benefits of textile handcrafts is fragmented across disciplines and methodologies. This comprehensive synthesis of peer-reviewed research examines the relationship between textile handcrafts and psychological wellbeing, identifying a unifying model to explain underlying mechanisms and outcomes. Aims and outcomes of interest were determined through co-development with public stakeholders.
A narrative synthesis of 42 studies (total N = 18,528) was complemented by meta-analysis. Qualitative findings indicated that engagement in textile handcrafts supports mood regulation, coping, self-identity, and a sense of accomplishment, alongside social and cognitive benefits. Quantitative findings demonstrated improvements in mood, coping, quality of life, cognition, and social outcomes. Social benefits were evident both in-person and online. Negative experiences were infrequently reported, and included fear of making mistakes or being judged, and frustration during skill acquisition. A meta-analysis of seven studies indicated an improvement in positive psychological wellbeing (β = 0.82, SE = 0.39, p = .040), while analysis of five studies indicated a reduction of negative psychological wellbeing (β = 0.74, SE = 0.30, p = .013).
Findings suggest that textile handcrafts can enhance psychological wellbeing, particularly for those who enjoy such activities and engage in supportive environments, and may support cultural expression, self-identity, and social connection. 
The identified mechanisms can be coherently captured by the PERMA model, offering, to our knowledge, the first suggestion for a theoretically grounded and integrative framework for understanding the benefits of textile handcrafts. Future research would benefit from higher-quality reporting of methods and results to support replication and synthesis.

articles.title: Dissociating the effects of encoding intentions and disengagement on recognition memory
articles.authors: Alexandra Lapteva; Corinna Martarelli
articles.abstract: Research on the effects of intentionality on memory has yielded heterogeneous results, with intentional encoding sometimes facilitating performance and sometimes showing no observable impact. A potential source of this variability may lie in internal disengagement states, such as mind-wandering and boredom, during encoding. In the present study, we investigated whether mind-wandering and boredom mediate the relationship between intention to remember and recognition memory. A total of 271 participants (Mage = 34.2, SDage = 7.6) completed a two-phase online experiment in which they encoded picture stimuli under intentional or incidental instructions, intermittently reporting their mind-wandering and boredom, followed by an old/new recognition task. Bayesian mediation analyses revealed that intentional encoding improved recognition accuracy, and that both mind-wandering and boredom independently predicted poorer recognition accuracy. However, encoding intention did not credibly reduce either mind-wandering or boredom, thus, they did not mediate the relationship between intention to remember and recognition accuracy. Instead, individual differences in trait mind-wandering and boredom proneness, as well as payment status, explained more variance in disengagement during encoding than the condition alone. These findings suggest that the benefits of intentional encoding for recognition memory may operate independently of changes in disengagement during encoding and highlight the importance of considering individual differences as a factor that influences recognition memory.

articles.title: Impact of early environmental risk on associations between genetic liability to externalizing and trajectories of externalizing problems in early adolescence
articles.authors: Sarah J Brislin; Maia Choi; Genevieve Fullerton Dash; Peter Barr; Holly E Poore; Natasia Courchesne; Leigh Lustig; Fazil Aliev; Danielle Dick
articles.abstract:
Objective: We examined whether environmental risk (e.g., prenatal substance exposure, poverty, trauma, discrimination) moderates the association between genetic liability and developmental trajectories of externalizing behaviors (e.g., aggression, rule-breaking) during early adolescence. 
 
Method: The analytic sample (N=10,634) was drawn from the Adolescent Brain Cognitive Development (ABCD) Study. We used latent growth curve modeling to examine the development of externalizing behaviors from ages 9 to 14, based on longitudinal parent (Child Behavior Checklist [CBCL]) and youth-reported (Brief Problem Monitor [BPM]) measures. We evaluated associations with polygenic risk associated with externalizing (EXT PGS), exposure to environmental risk, and tested whether environmental risk moderated the relationship between EXT PGS and externalizing behavior trajectories.

Results: The EXT PGS and general environmental risk were each associated with higher scores on the intercept (baseline Externalizing Problems). The EXT PGS was significantly associated with a slower decrease in youth-report of externalizing problems while general environmental risk was significantly associated with a faster decrease in externalizing problems over time. Broad environmental risk significantly amplified the association between the EXT PGS and the intercept. The association between the EXT PGS and the development of externalizing behavior (parent-report slope) was significantly moderated by state-level risk factors.

Conclusions: The EXT PGS has a significant effect on externalizing behaviors at age 9 and this association is amplified by broad environmental risk. This suggests that initiatives at both the micro (household) and macro (state policy) level can decrease the development of externalizing behavior.

articles.title: Are words perceived more clearly than nonwords? A conceptual replication and extension of Lupyan (2017)
articles.authors: Feng Wan; Jan Andrews; Ruofei Yao; Isabelle Borgstedt; Emily Anne Doucet; Joshua R de Leeuw
articles.abstract: Four experiments investigated whether previously observed differences in the perceived blurriness of words versus nonwords reflect early perceptual processes or post-perceptual cognitive factors such as memory. Building on Lupyan’s report that familiar words literally appear less blurry than scrambled letter strings objectively equally blurred, we designed a forced-choice paradigm featuring an immediate “perceptual” block, where both stimuli remained visible during the judgment, and a “memory” block, where one stimulus disappeared before participants responded. Across Experiments 1–3 using words as targets, nonwords were consistently more likely than words to be judged as blurrier than the target, with this effect generally stronger in the memory condition. Experiment 3 eliminated a same word confound present in Experiments 1 and 2, suggesting that the effect was not solely driven by stimulus repetition. However, Experiment 4, in which the target was always a nonword, failed to produce a statistically reliable lexicality effect in either block. Combined analyses across Experiments 3 and 4 indicated that the clarity advantage for word over nonword samples was stronger when words were targets than when they were samples which could be due to an upward vertical attention bias for meaningful stimuli. Together, these findings suggest that familiarity-related sharpening effects are highly sensitive to contextual and task-related factors, emphasizing the need for caution when interpreting such effects as evidence of direct top-down influences on low-level visual perception. All four experiments also demonstrated a sharpening effect of memory for both words and nonwords, consistent with previous research.

articles.title: Machine Psychometrics for Artificial Agents
articles.authors: Konstantina Sokratous; Joachim Vandekerckhove; Clintin P Davis-Stober
articles.abstract: Artificial intelligence systems are increasingly evaluated as behavioral agents, yet many evaluation practices still treat model outputs as isolated responses to be scored for accuracy, safety, bias, or preference alignment. We argue that this response-level paradigm is insufficient for systems whose behavior is generated from probability distributions and changes across contexts, versions, and interventions. Human psychometrics and cognitive modeling offer a useful foundation because they were developed to infer latent traits, capacities, preferences, and decision processes from indirect behavioral data. However, artificial agents create a different measurement regime. Their next-token and response-level probability distributions can often be inspected directly, allowing uncertainty, calibration, bias, and response instability to be modeled as latent properties rather than inferred only from overt responses. Artificial agents can also be remeasured and intervened on under controlled conditions, enabling parameter-level assessment of stability, drift, improvement, degradation, and causal sensitivity across prompts, model updates, fine-tuning, retrieval changes, and ablations. We propose machine psychometrics as a distribution-aware measurement framework for artificial agents. In this framework, computational cognitive models serve as interpretable interfaces between probability distributions and latent parameters, allowing model behavior to be compared, validated, and monitored without assuming that human psychological constructs transfer unchanged to machines. This approach shifts AI evaluation from scoring what a model says to measuring the probabilistic structure that generates its behavior.

articles.title: Autistic traits and visual imagery abilities independently predict visual working memory performance
articles.authors: Ryan Elson; Madeleine Forster; Emily Weaver; Amelia Wozniak; Claudia Danielmeier
articles.abstract: Increasing evidence shows a co-occurrence of autism spectrum disorder and aphantasia (a lack of visual imagery) with both cohorts showing reductions in visual working memory (WM). Here we explored whether visual imagery ability (measured with the Vividness of Visual Imagery Questionnaire, VVIQ, and Spontaneous Use of Imagery Scale, SUIS) mediated the relationship between autistic traits (measured with the Autism Quotient, AQ-50) and visuospatial WM in the general population. Participants who reported being more detail-oriented (higher ‘attention to detail’) and who reported fewer difficulties with communication (lower ‘communication’ scores) performed better on a WM task. Participants who reported preoccupation with one task and difficulties switching tasks (higher ‘attention switching’ scores) on the AQ-50 made more binding errors, selecting a colour associated with a different shape during encoding. These relationships were not mediated by visual imagery scores, suggesting that visual imagery does not underpin WM difficulties associated with autistic traits in our study. Despite neither VVIQ nor SUIS scores predicted WM performance separately, within a multiple regression model both higher imagery vividness and, surprisingly, less frequent use of imagery significantly predicted better WM performance. While vivid imagery may support WM performance, spontaneous, task-irrelevant imagery may instead distract from task performance.

articles.title: Rhythm Perception and Text Reading Fluency: Indirect Associations Through Pseudoword and Word Reading
articles.authors: Regina Abreu; Lara Cunha; Marta Martins
articles.abstract: A growing body of research has linked children’s rhythm processing to reading. However, it remains unclear whether rhythm processing relates differently to distinct reading skills and whether this pattern varies across levels of reading experience. We examined cross-sectional associations between musical rhythm perception and pseudoword, word, and text reading fluency in 305 European Portuguese-speaking children in Grades 1 to 4 (167 girls; Mage = 8.49 ± 1.19 years). Using structural path analysis, we tested indirect associations with text reading fluency through pseudoword reading alone and serially through pseudoword and word reading, and explored variation across grade-based levels of reading experience. Rhythm perception was positively associated with all three reading fluency measures. Adding direct paths from rhythm perception to word and text reading did not improve model fit. In the retained model, rhythm perception was indirectly associated with text reading through pseudoword reading alone and through the serial pseudoword-to-word pathway. Complementary analyses indicated that rhythm perception was most strongly associated with pseudoword reading. Multi-group analyses supported differences between Grades 1–2 and Grades 3–4, but no individual path or indirect association differed significantly between groups. Together, these findings highlight pseudoword reading as the reading skill most consistently associated with rhythm perception and suggest that decoding-related pathways may help account for its association with fluent text reading. Replication across distinct levels of reading experience and orthographies of varying consistency, together with longitudinal studies, is needed before generalizations or developmental and causal conclusions can be drawn.

articles.title: Mapping Kyrgyzstani Digital Feminism on Instagram: A Quantitative Content Analysis
articles.authors: Begimai Bekbolotova; Anaëlle Gonzalez
articles.abstract: Digital media platforms have become important spaces for feminist activism, yet little is known about how feminist actors in Kyrgyzstan use social media in their everyday communication. This study addresses this gap by providing the first systematic quantitative content analysis of feminist Instagram content in Kyrgyzstan. Drawing on a dataset of 838 posts from 17 feminist Instagram accounts between January 2022 and June 2023, the study examines the topics addressed, the use of collective action frames, differences across account types, and associations with user engagement. Results show that Kyrgyzstani digital feminism is strongly centred on gender-based violence, women’s rights, institutional failures, empowerment, and solidarity. Physical and domestic violence emerged as the most frequently addressed topic, while prognostic framing was the most prevalent collective action frame. Differences across NGOs, social projects, and influencer-activists were limited, indicating a broadly shared feminist agenda despite organisational diversity. User engagement was highest for culturally grounded content such as the slogan “Free woman means prosperous Kyrgyzstan.” The findings extend scholarship on digital feminism beyond Western contexts and highlight Instagram’s role as a key infrastructure for feminist expression, community-building, and mobilisation in Kyrgyzstan.

articles.title: Neurocognitive Foundations of Adaptive Behavior in Partially Observable Environments
articles.authors: Rasmus Bruckner; Dirk Ostwald
articles.abstract: Adaptive behavior requires acting on sensory evidence that only partially reveals relevant environmental states. Partially observable Markov decision processes (POMDPs) provide a unified framework for this problem by representing perceptual uncertainty as belief states and linking these beliefs to decision functions, policies, and learning. We review how POMDP concepts can advance computational cognitive neuroscience across two domains. First, studies of information sampling show how beliefs about latent states and environmental dynamics shape evidence accumulation and perceptual choices, while full POMDP formulations derive optimal policies or infer subjective objectives. Second, studies of reinforcement learning show how perceptual uncertainty modulates credit assignment and the updating of state and action values, often through belief-weighted approximations. We argue that POMDPs are a useful and burgeoning framework for integrating perception, decision-making, and learning, as well as for understanding the neurocognitive foundations of adaptive behavior under uncertainty.

articles.title: Systematic Measurement Error in the Intervention Outcome
articles.authors: Reeta Kankaanpää
articles.abstract: Using sum scores as outcomes in intervention studies can bias effect estimates, especially when systematic measurement error (SME) such as response styles or response shifts is present. Although both sources of SME are common in psychological assessment, their joint influence on intervention effect estimation is poorly understood. This simulation study evaluated bias across three measurement approaches: a latent variable model accounting for response style, a latent variable model ignoring both response style and response shift, and a sum-score approach. SME was operationalized as the co-occurrence of a response style induced by reversed items and intervention-induced response shifts. Response style was generated using two established bifactor mechanisms – the correlated-traits-correlated-methods minus 1 (CTC(M–1)) and random-intercept (RI) approaches, and additional conditions allowed the method factor to correlate with the growth factor. Intervention effects were estimated using second-order growth curve models for the latent variable approaches and first-order models for sum scores. Primary performance measures were mean absolute and relative bias. Under the CTC(M–1) mechanism, method factor loadings had minimal impact, whereas response shifts produced substantial bias, particularly for sum scores. Under the RI mechanism, bias in the latent variable model that ignored response style varied with the size of method factor loadings, although the overall effect of the response style remained modest. Allowing method and growth factors to correlate had little influence on bias. Across mechanisms, response shifts introduced far greater bias than response styles, and sum scores consistently performed worst. Co-occurring SME sources did not exacerbate bias.

articles.title: Self-Regulatory Strategy Use in Exam Preparation: Reflection and Automaticity Shape Successful Self-Regulation
articles.authors: Sebastian Bürgler; Marie Hennecke; Katharina Bernecker; Veronika Brandstätter; Rick H. Hoyle
articles.abstract: In a preregistered reanalysis of two longitudinal studies (N = 200, N = 294), we examined students’ self-regulation during exam preparation. Assessments included a baseline, twice-weekly measures over two weeks, a fourth-week questionnaire, and (in Study 2) a follow-up on exam grades. We replicated that larger repertoires of self-regulatory strategies across measurement occasions and using more strategies per occasion (polyregulation) were beneficially associated with several self-reported outcomes, such as study duration and perceived study progress. Many individual strategies showed beneficial associations with these outcomes, though some appeared detrimental. Associations with the objective longer-term outcome (exam grades) were scarce, possibly reflecting that many factors beyond self-regulation shape academic performance. We further examined potential variables associated with strategy use, focusing on reflective (perceived effectiveness) and automatic (habitual) strategy use. Perceived effectiveness was consistently associated with beneficial momentary outcomes, and predicted strategy use. Furthermore, automaticity and effectiveness ratings were often positively associated, and robustness checks confirmed that both contributed meaningfully to self-reported successful studying. Most importantly, higher levels of automaticity were not only associated with beneficial momentary outcomes, but also significantly associated with exam grades, underscoring the central role of habits in self-regulation.

articles.title: An Open-Source Standardized Pipeline for Equitable Observations of Interactive Behavioral Dynamics: Theory-driven Measurement, Analysis, and Masking
articles.authors: Arkadiusz Białek; Wim Pouw; James Trujillo; Fred Hasselman; Babajide Owoyele; Natalia Siekiera; Joanna Raczaszek-Leonardi; Travis J. Witshire
articles.abstract: Behavioral observation has a longstanding tradition in psychology. However, its reliance on manual coding makes observational methods costly and prone to biases that arise from the inherent limits of coding schemes and from the subjectivity of human raters. Behavioral observation research therefore has drawbacks in terms of applicability, accessibility, reproducibility, and equitability. Computer vision (CV) methods have promise in this regard. In the context of quantifying human movement, CV approaches to pose estimation are becoming increasingly precise and have the benefit of being non-intrusive, reproducible, and low-cost. With such methods, human movement in videos can be processed as multivariate time-series data, offering a basis for a more comprehensive analysis of individual, interpersonal, and social dynamics, opening up the possibility for the widespread study of diverse populations in out-of-lab real-world contexts. Fulfilling such a promise goes beyond technical progress, it requires a theory-driven implementation of new accessible observational methods made equitable to learn. To showcase this promise, we present a CV pipeline with analyses of the temporal dynamics of dyadic interactions, including a cross-cultural investigation of movement fluidity in sibling cooperation during task-focused interactions and longitudinal assessments of infant-caregiver coordination during free-play sessions. The pipeline incorporates a pedagogical computational notebook, pose estimation (YOLOv8), theory-driven linear and non-linear time series analysis, and a CV method for more privacy-aware video data archiving. Together, this pipeline showcases a promising advancement in behavioral observation methods, expanding both who can conduct research and who can benefit from it.

articles.title: Toward a Program Theory of A Singaporean Single-Session, Synchronous Chat-Based Mental Health Support for Youths: The Behavior Change Techniques Workers Use and How They Relate to Outcome
articles.authors: Gerard Chung; Lim Tse Min; Joan R. Fang
articles.abstract:
Background: Text-based chat (TBC) services are among the most accessible mental health
support for youth, yet more is known about whether they help than about how they help, that
is, what workers do in sessions. Without an account of these worker skills, TBC services cannot
be reliably trained for or evaluated. This study described the techniques chat workers use,
drawing on the Behavior Change Technique Taxonomy (BCTTv1), and linked them to user-
reported outcomes.

Methods: We analyzed 1,439 real chat sessions (44,916 worker turns) from 73 workers at
QuickChat, an anonymous, free, synchronous TBC service for youths aged 12 to 25 in Singapore.
Each worker turn was coded for the presence of 32 behavior change techniques (BCTs). We
examined how often, densely, and broadly techniques were used; how far use varied across
workers; and associations with three post-session outcomes: understanding, coping, and
perspective.

Results: All 32 techniques appeared, but practice was concentrated in a few: social support
(unspecified and emotional), problem solving, re-attribution, and framing/reframing accounted
for over half of all instances. Use varied mainly by session, not by worker, indicating skills
shared across the workforce, not individual styles. Three were positively associated with all
outcomes, namely social support (unspecified and emotional) and information about social and
environmental consequences, though effects were small.

Conclusions: Chat workers deliver change through a small set of core skills, centered on social
support and shared across the workforce. These findings offer a first step toward a program
theory of TBC to guide training and evaluation.

articles.title: Beyond the desire to know: Development and validation of the School Curiosity Inventory
articles.authors: Xin Tang; Haoyan Huang; Liyuan Peng
articles.abstract: While curiosity in school is particularly essential for school-age students’ learning and well-being, its conceptualization and assessment remain limited. The present study aimed to develop a school curiosity inventory that (a) covers multi-dimensional curiosity tailored to school contexts, (b) captures curiosity about students’ own future development, and (c) validates the meta-level facet of curiosity attitude and regulation as a unique construct. Three sub-studies were conducted to develop and validate this inventory, using Chinese student samples. Study 1 (N=1046, age=12-19) established the initial factor structure with a series of exploratory and confirmatory factor analyses, identifying seven sub-dimensions from two domains: learning, social, sensational, and self-development curiosity (motivation domain), as well as curiosity attitudes in positive and negative sides, and curiosity regulation (meta-curiosity domain). Study 2 (N=720, age=14-18) refined the seven-dimension inventory into a brief 27-item form, demonstrated its good temporal stability and measurement invariance through a two-month test-retest survey, indicated these dimensions to be partly overlapped with but different from the similar constructs in general curiosity measures, and demonstrated their greater relative importance for subsequent learning and well-being outcomes than the similar constructs. Finally, Study 3 (N=705, grade=7th-8th) reconfirmed the seven-dimension structure and mapped its nomological network with social-emotional and regulation-related skills with moderate correlations. Together, this study broadens the conceptualization of students’ curiosity to a multi-domain construct under dual-processes, and provides theoretical and practical frameworks for future school curiosity research.

articles.title: The Limits of Normality Effects on Causal Judgments: Evidence from Continuous Causes
articles.authors: Kaylee Miceli; Nina Van Rooy; Felipe De Brigard; Kevin O'Neill
articles.abstract: Statistical normality robustly influences causal judgments of binary causal variables (events which either do or do not occur): people judge statistically abnormal events as more causally responsible when causes are jointly necessary for an outcome, but as less responsible when causes are individually sufficient. However, whether this pattern extends to continuous causes, which vary in degree, remains unknown. Across two experiments (N = 1,184 U.S. Prolific participants), we examined this question using a learning paradigm in which participants learned the statistical properties of two continuous causes before making a final causal judgment. We manipulated normality via variance (Experiment 1) or mean (Experiment 2). Despite successful manipulation checks, we found strong evidence that causal judgments were unaffected by normality in both experiments, with no corresponding effects on confidence. These findings suggest that normality effects, while seemingly robust in the field of causation, may be specific to causal structures involving binary variables.

articles.title: The Role of Community Pharmacists in Identifying and Managing Insomnia and Facilitating Access to Cognitive Behavioural Therapy for Insomnia (CBT-I) – a Systematic Review
articles.authors: Adebunmi Ogunnowo; Gurprit Lall; Aiste Steponenaite
articles.abstract: Insomnia affects approximately 10% of the global adult population; however, the recommended first-line treatment, cognitive behavioural therapy for insomnia (CBT-I), is difficult to access for patients. Community pharmacists have recently expanded their role beyond dispensing medications to include management of chronic diseases. They are now seen as the most accessible health care professionals; however, their role in chronic insomnia management or CBT-I facilitation has not been systematically synthesised. This systematic review aims to synthesize available studies to determine the role of community pharmacists in chronic insomnia and their use of CBT-I in practice. Five databases (PubMed, Scopus, MEDLINE, PsycINFO, and Web of Science) were searched from inception to August 2025. Out of 129 screened articles, nine met the inclusion criteria. They were synthesised narratively and showed three main themes: pharmacists can deprescribe inappropriate hypnotics and sedatives, identify insomnia through counselling, and in some cases deliver or signpost CBT-I. Whilst one study showed that pharmacist-led CBT-I reduced Insomnia Severity Index scores from 18.2 to 7.9 (p < 0.001), the most consistent findings across studies were a lack of standardised protocols, absence of referral pathways, and time constraints - a ‘structural void’ that prevents routine implementation. Despite pharmacists' ability to perform those roles, the interventions hardly ever happen in real-life practice. The findings suggest that having capable pharmacists is not enough to close the CBT-I access gap, especially because the profession appears ready but is not well-equipped, and standardised approaches to screening with clearly defined roles and sustainable payment methods are needed.

articles.title: Evaluation in early visual processing – evidence from deep neural networks
articles.authors: Ivan Ivanovich Ivanchei; Inès Mentec; Axel Cleeremans
articles.abstract: An important question in affective science is whether valence assignment, i.e., evaluating a perceived object as positive or negative, occurs after perception or whether it is intrinsic to it. Recent theories propose that valence assignment, or simply evaluation, may be embedded within conscious perception. To test this idea, we combined deep neural network (DNN) modeling with representational similarity analysis (RSA) to identify which levels of visual processing contribute to valence assignment. To measure valence, we used a “Birthday” task in which participants selected or rejected one of three emotionally neutral everyday objects (e.g., cups, lamps) as a birthday gift. We presented the task under varying instructions: no additional instruction, utility-based, aesthetic-based, and under time pressure (choice deadline of 0.8 s from the stimulus onset). Perceived valence distances between objects were captured as representational dissimilarity matrices (RDMs) and compared with DNN activation distances across layers. Across conditions, valence distances correlated with differences in the first DNN layer, reflecting low-level visual processing. However, this relationship could not be explained by individual features such as contrast or luminance, implying a more integrative perceptual basis. When choices involved objects from distinct categories, valence judgments primarily reflected perceived utility, yet aesthetic instructions biased them toward similar visual computations. These findings indicate that valence assignment is partially built into perceptual processing, with higher-level task demands flexibly shaping its expression. This supports a view of conscious perception as inherently valenced, yet context sensitive.

articles.title: Discrete Shifts in Symptom Networks During Psychotherapy for Chronic Depression – A Regime-Switching Network Analysis
articles.authors: Jonas Petter; Lea Schumacher; Jan Philipp Klein; Elisabeth Schramm; Martin Härter; Martin Hautzinger; Levente Kriston
articles.abstract: The network approach to psychopathology conceptualizes mental disorders as systems of interacting symptoms rather than consequences of a latent factor. Recent developments have focused on modeling changes in symptom networks over time, where most approaches assume that these changes occur continuously. We propose an alternative by modelling discrete shifts between network states using hidden Markov models (HMMs). We conducted a secondary analysis of a multicenter randomized trial comparing disorder-specific and non-specific psychotherapy for chronic depression (n = 254). We identified two distinct states with the HMM: a low-symptom level state showing weaker symptom connectivity and a high-symptom level state with stronger positive connections. While participants typically remained in the same state across consecutive time points (80-88% of the time), transition probabilities differed between treatment groups. In particular, participants receiving disorder-specific psychotherapy showed higher probability of transitioning from the high-symptom to low-symptom state compared to the non-specific psychotherapy (19.5% vs. 12.0%). The regime-switching approach to analysis proved feasible and theoretically plausible, offering practical advantages for treatment evaluation within the network framework. By examining differences in network structure during healthy versus disordered states, this method provides insights into symptom dynamics that could inform both research and clinical applications.

articles.title: Participatory Choice Architecture: Three Mechanisms for Co-Designing Digital Environments
articles.authors: Vincent Beermann; David Joachim Grüning; Jonas Bozenhard; Ralph Hertwig; Maximilian Kiener
articles.abstract: Choice architecture is inevitable in digital environments, yet its design rests on a structural asymmetry: A few designers shape the environments that everyone else inhabits. The literature on the ethics of nudging has addressed this asymmetry chiefly through requirements of transparency and easy resistibility, but rarely questioned the underlying dichotomy between those who design choice environments and those for whom the environments are designed. This article argues that the dichotomy is itself a contingent design choice rather than a necessity of choice architecture, and that participatory design—in which users co-author the environments that shape their behavior—can substantially attenuate that asymmetry. Drawing on competence- and opportunity-based accounts of autonomy, we develop the normative case for participation and identify three commitments it requires: explainability, constitutive trust, and inclusion. To operationalize these commitments, we propose three design mechanisms: active knowledge sharing, collective deliberation, and openly configurable architectures with preconfigured templates. The mechanisms are illustrated through examples from existing digital environments, including self-nudging tools, crowd-sourced annotation, and civic-technology platforms. We close with a research agenda centered on testing whether, and if so where, participatory architectures outperform top-down equivalents in terms of sustained behavior change and perceived legitimacy.

articles.title: Affective Responses Across Three Airport Areas: Exploratory Associations With Sensory Sensitivity
articles.authors: Shuhei Iimura; Nao Niwa; Kaishu Iijima; Hiroto Yamamoto; Yuko Yotsumoto
articles.abstract: Airport environments contain multiple sensory and spatial demands, yet little is known about immediate affective responses within specific airport areas. Using a small exploratory within-subject field design, we examined changes in negative affect and state anxiety among 28 university students during fixed 7-min stays in a seating area, quiet rooms, and a food court at an international airport. A brief stay in the quiet rooms was associated with reduced anxiety, and this change remained statistically significant after correction for multiple comparisons. In exploratory correlation analyses, p values were adjusted using the Benjamini–Hochberg false discovery rate procedure. Several associations between sensitivity and negative affect remained statistically significant after adjustment. Higher sensitivity was associated with higher negative affect before the seating-area stay and both before and after the food-court stay, as well as with a larger decrease in negative affect in the seating area. However, area × sensitivity interactions were not statistically supported, and the correlational findings do not establish that sensitivity moderated affective changes across the airport areas. The findings provide preliminary evidence concerning immediate affective experiences in naturally occurring airport environments.

articles.title: The orbitofrontal-anterior temporal network complements the attention network for where to look in social situations
articles.authors: Nico Marek; Radha Nila Meghanathan; Stefan Pollmann
articles.abstract:
Human neuroimaging experiments have consistently found dorsal and ventral attention networks subserving spatial shifts of covert attention or eye movements. However, these experiments used abstract, artificial stimuli for better experimental stimulus control and clearly defined instructions about where to attend or what to search for. This clearly is not an adequate model of eye movement control in natural environments full of semantic and social information.

Here, we show that during movie viewing, activation of the dorsal and ventral attention networks was complemented by activation patterns in orbitofrontal and anterior temporal cortex, previously not implicated in human eye movement control, supporting individual decisions where to look. This effect was largely driven by looking at faces.

We compared similarity relationships between eye fixation patterns on the one hand and brain activity patterns on the other hand. Searching for between-scenes changes in activation patterns that mirrored changes in fixation patterns, we were able to identify the attention networks defined by previous experiments with artificial stimuli. In contrast, interindividual differences in fixation patterns, indicative of endogenous decisions about where to look, were mirrored by activation pattern differences in orbitofrontal and anterior temporal cortex, particularly for scenes presenting faces.

Thus, we could precisely replicate the role of the attention networks in a more natural viewing environment. Crucially, we also showed that previous lab experiments, lacking the complexity of free viewing in a naturalistic environment, overlooked the importance of the orbitofrontal - anterior temporal network for individual differences in active vision. Our findings show that the orbitofrontal - anterior temporal network needs to be considered in studies of active vision, particularly in social situations.

articles.title: A recipe for an ESM study: An illustrative example of a comprehensive design
articles.authors: Franziska Schutzeichel; Marlene Keil; Peter J. de Jong; Klaske A. Glashouwer; Marije aan het Rot
articles.abstract: Despite their wide application, designing Experience Sampling Method (ESM) studies remains challenging partly due to complex and interdependent methodological decisions, such as sampling schedules, response formats, and technological platforms. The existing literature provides valuable frameworks but often mentions methodological options without concrete examples; this article aims to bridge this gap in practical guidance. Informed by the existing ESM literature, we illustrate our decision-making process while designing an ESM study on the temporal associations between momentary life meaning, eating disorder symptoms, and negative affect. While grounded in our specific research questions, this paper provides practical guidelines on how to decide among various methodological options for researchers across psychological fields. We outline key decisions, practical considerations, and challenges encountered during the study’s development. Our paper provides a practical checklist to support researchers in designing ESM studies from scratch and in reporting essential aspects in their manuscripts, promoting transparency and replicability. By illustrating a real-life example of setting up our own study, we aim to guide researchers in navigating the complexities of ESM design.

articles.title: The Linear Relationship Between Visual Imagery and Alexithymia Breaks When Imagery Is Absent: Complete Aphantasics Are No More Alexithymic Than Typical Imagers
articles.authors: Maël Delem; Marine MAS; Olivier Luminet; Gaën Plancher; Perrine RUBY
articles.abstract: Several studies have suggested a link between aphantasia (reduced or absent visual mental imagery) and alexithymia (difficulty identifying and describing one's feelings, together with an externally oriented thinking style), but results and interpretations differ across studies, and no consensus has emerged. We pooled data from five independent studies (N = 1478: 147 complete aphantasics, 141 hypophantasics, 1115 typical imagers, 75 hyperphantasics) who completed the Vividness of Visual Imagery Questionnaire and the twenty-item Toronto Alexithymia Scale, and compared six candidate models, from linear and categorical baselines to several non-linear alternatives (GAM, Segmented and Floor-group models), to determine the shape of the relationship between visual imagery vividness and alexithymia, rather than assuming it in advance. The best fitting and most interpretable model (floor-group) showed  that among all participants capable of some degree of visual imagery (from hypo- to hyperphantasics), alexithymia declined as visual imagery vividness increased, consistent across all three TAS-20 sub-scales. Complete aphantasics broke this linear relationship entirely: rather than showing the highest level of alexithymia, as the linear relationship would predict, their scores were lower than that of hypophantasics and did not meaningfully differ from those of typical imagers. This discontinuity, specific to the total absence of visual imagery, was corroborated by an equally well-fitting segmented model, held up across all five studies individually, and is inconsistent with prior work treating any degree of reduced imagery as equivalent. Our results support the idea that some components of alexithymia are related to the level of visual imagery vividness in people that experience visual imagery. However, in people with complete aphantasia, alexithymia levels may depend on other processes. In other words, having no visual imagery at all does not seem to be associated with increased alexithymia levels, while having very weak visual imagery does.

articles.title: Causal Effects of Beliefs About Errors on Primary School Students’ Reactions to Errors and Knowledge Acquisition: Evidence from Three Experimental Field Studies
articles.authors: Jana Spear; Donna Bryce; Cara-Sophie Enste; Andrew Martin; Robert Grassinger; Markus Dresel
articles.abstract: Errors occur frequently during educational practice and hold substantial potential for personal improvement. However, learning from errors does not happen automatically; rather, students must react adaptively to their errors and modify the learning process accordingly. Such adaptive reactions to errors involve maintaining learning motivation and functional emotions as well as engaging in cognitive and behavioral adjustment. Although previous research has identified positive beliefs about errors as a potential determinant of adaptive reactions to errors, most evidence is correlational, and experimental investigations—particularly among primary school students—remain limited. Therefore, we conducted three experimental field studies in which we positively manipulated the beliefs about errors in an experimental group which was compared to an active control group. In an authentic learning situation, the utilization of a digital learning environment enabled the observation of both learning behavior and immediate learning progress. In samples of third- and fourth-grade students, Study 1 (N = 282) and Study 2 (N = 238) were conducted in math, while Study 3 (N = 230) focused on German as a first language. The experimental manipulation successfully affected the beliefs about errors in a sustainable manner in all three studies. In turn, positive beliefs about errors improved self-reported adaptive reactions to errors, which was mostly maintained until a follow-up assessment. Additionally, positive beliefs about errors led to a more adaptive learning behavior and greater knowledge acquisition in Study 3. These findings provide novel insights into how positive beliefs about errors influence effective learning from errors.

articles.title: Reasoning Beyond Reality:  A Mental Model Theory of Counterfactuals
articles.authors: Marco Ragni; Ruth M.J. Byrne; Luise Mevius; Philip Nicholas Johnson-Laird
articles.abstract: The sentence: If he had been the thief then he would have fled, is interpretable as a counterfactual conditional: he is neither the thief nor did he flee.  Theorists often presuppose that counterfactuals are subjunctive conditionals of this sort.  We present a new theory of counterfactuals based on mental models.  Four experiments corroborated it, and its computational implementation simulates its dual systems of intuition and deliberation. As it assumes, no linguistic cue in English signals that a sentence is counterfactual.  Depending on its context, any assertion can describe a factual or a counterfactual domain, whether it is indicative or subjunctive (Experiment 1).  Assertions can have mixed moods with one indicative clause and one subjunctive clause, e.g.: She paid her mortgage or she would have moved.  People reason that this disjunction implies that she did pay her mortgage and did not move (Experiments 2 and 3).  Any sort of compound assertion based, say, on and, if, and or, can have a counterfactual interpretation.  It yields inferences from models in both factual and counterfactual domains, and from a model in one domain to its denial in another domain. Their difficulty depends on the number of intuitive models of their premise (Experiment 4).  We discuss how counterfactuals can elicit certain correct inferences more readily than factual assertions do, how verifications of counterfactuals can depend on mental simulations using kinematic models, and whether alternative theories of our results are feasible.  We conclude that factuals and counterfactuals can have the same language, models, and inferences.

articles.title: Trade-off between performance and human-like perception in face recognition models
articles.authors: Sobhan Hojjati; Dina Keshvari Ghadikolai; Alireza Shakeripour; Zahra Bahmani Dehkordi; Kazuhisa Shibata; Hakwan Lau; Ali Moharramipour
articles.abstract: Deep learning models for face recognition are widely adopted in cognitive neuroscience, yet it is not well understood whether their excellent performance means they “see” faces like humans. Here, we collected a substantial dataset of human face-similarity judgments to assess how well prominent face recognition models align with human perception. We found that models with high—but not the highest—recognition performance are often best aligned with human similarity judgments. We further tested to what extent a linear transformation could better align model representations with human perceptual similarity. Models with superior recognition performance benefited the least from this transformation, suggesting a deeper mismatch with human perception. Notably, enforcing this alignment reduced recognition performance for higher-performing models but gave low-performing models a slight recognition boost.
