articles.abstract: Based on the dual-process model of entertainment experiences and motivated cognition, we propose that specific affective states such as surprise, curiosity, and confusion (so-called epistemic emotions), as well as empathy, are involved in eudaimonic entertainment experiences while reading political news. We further assume that these emotions are related to normatively desirable outcomes such as deliberation within, information seeking, and knowledge acquisition about political topics. To test the hypothesized model, we conducted a between-subjects online experiment (N = 407) that used different stimuli to induce the emotions of interest while simultaneously varying news topics. Structural equation modeling revealed that the data mostly supported our hypotheses. Overall, we find that through these affective states, even soft news can enable normatively desirable outcomes. All data and materials can be accessed from https://osf.io/82gqu/.

articles.title: Time-Based Cognition and Working Memory Explain Changes in Delay Discounting Through Adolescence
articles.authors: Camille Phaneuf-Hadd; Leah Somerville
articles.abstract: Individuals of all ages face choices between immediate but smaller and delayed but larger rewards. In a decision process known as delay discounting, people tend to devalue options that are realized farther into the future. Several candidate cognitive mechanisms have been proposed to underpin such choices: inhibition (overriding a prepotent response), prospection (orienting to the future), working memory (manipulating information held in mind), reward motivation (activating behavior for reward), and time perception (subjectively judging time horizons). These mechanisms change through adolescence, in tandem with delay discounting decisions becoming more patient from childhood to adulthood. However, the cognitive mechanisms principally responsible for developmental increases in patience remain contested. By measuring delay discounting alongside indices of inhibition, prospection, working memory, reward motivation, and time perception in the same participants (N = 159, 10-20 years, collected in the United States), the present study examined whether these mechanisms – alone or in combination – explained age variability in reward- and time-based choice in different stakes contexts. Mixed- effects modeling revealed that patience indeed increased with age, especially for higher- than lower-magnitude decisions. Dependency modeling identified dissociable and overlapping drivers of age-related changes in delay discounting: prospection mediated patience in lower-magnitude decisions whereas working memory mediated patience in higher-magnitude decisions; time perception mediated patience in both. Although compressed time perception supported older participants’ more patient choices overall, distinct cognitive mechanisms may become available during adolescence to underscore willingness to wait for larger later rewards, depending on decision stakes. These findings advance understanding of how multiple constituent processes scaffold the development of value-based choice.

articles.title: Linguistic diversity as a two-step process: Grounding polysemy in universal neural networks and expanding it by cultural learning
articles.authors: Marit Lobben; Laura Bakke; Tor Endestad
articles.abstract:
This paper advances a new account of linguistic typology grounded in the hypothesis of neural reuse, namely that languages selectively recruit pre-existing neurocognitive systems for grammatical purposes. The proposal is tested through a case study of the Mandarin classifier zuò (座), combining cognitive semantic analysis with fMRI evidence. The semantic analysis shows that zuò forms a highly structured polysemy network organized around scene-based construal, progressing from anchored entities and perceptual salience to bounded environments, landmarks, navigable spaces, and goal-directed schemas.
To examine whether this organization reflects underlying neural systems, an fMRI experiment contrasted zuò with a non-scene classifier. Processing zuò alone—prior to any scene-denoting noun—activated regions associated with scene perception and navigation, including the parahippocampal place area, retrosplenial cortex, and occipital place area. This indicates that a grammatical morpheme can recruit a scene-selective cortical system, supporting the view that polysemy may be constrained by shared neural architecture.
At the same time, the full semantic range of the classifier cannot be derived from neural structure alone. Several extensions depend on lived experience and culture-specific knowledge, suggesting that neural reuse provides a scaffold that is subsequently elaborated through usage and cultural models. The findings support a typological perspective in which languages differ in whether and how they recruit available neural systems, thereby shaping the emergence of grammatical categories and polysemy networks.

articles.title: Ecological Constellations of Risk and Opportunity: Linking Household Deprivation and Neighborhood Opportunity to Adolescent Girls’ Mood Disorders and Cortical Thickness of the Superior Frontal Gyrus
articles.authors: Ava Reck; Estelle Berger; Madeleine Goldberg; Ann-Marie Barrett; Jolinda Smith; Nicholas B. Allen; Jennifer H Pfeifer
articles.abstract: Household neglect and neighborhood opportunity are each linked to youth mental health and neural development, yet less is known about their co-occurrence, limiting understanding of layered ecological risk. Using a person-centered approach, this study identifies profiles of household neglect and neighborhood opportunity and examines longitudinal associations with adolescent mood disorders and superior frontal gyrus cortical thickness. Longitudinal data from 156 adolescents (100% female at birth, aged 10–13 at baseline [M = 11.54, SD = 0.80], 73.72% White, average income-to-needs ratio of 2.79) were used in the current analysis. Latent profile analysis identified distinct profiles of household neglect and neighborhood opportunity at baseline. Associations between profile membership, mood disorder prevalence, and superior frontal gyrus cortical thickness were examined across five time points, each approximately 18 months apart. A four-profile solution fit the data best: (1) Moderate Neglect/Moderately Low Opportunities, (2) Low Neglect/Moderately High Opportunities, (3) High Neglect/Very Low Opportunities, and (4) Low Neglect/Very High Opportunities. Profile 3 showed higher mood disorder prevalence than Profile 2 at baseline and than Profile 1 at time three; Profile 4 also exceeded Profile 1 at times three and four, indicating elevated risk at both extremes of the opportunity spectrum. Profile 3 exhibited thicker superior frontal cortical thickness than Profile 1 at times one, two, and four, and than Profiles 2 and 4 at time four. Results underscore the importance of multi-level, context-sensitive approaches to prevention and intervention for youth exposed to intersecting environments.

articles.title: Complex systems approach to social science
articles.authors: Merlijn Olthof
articles.abstract: The complex systems approach is an alternative paradigm for studying human behavior. In this paradigm, the study of human behavior centers around complex systems principles that are applied across various subfields. This entry provides an introduction to the complex systems approach focusing on the study of transitions, networks and multifractal scaling. A brief reflection on the field concludes the entry.

articles.title: A crosslinguistic corpus phonetic analysis of intrinsic vowel duration
articles.authors: Eleanor Chodroff; Miao Zhang
articles.abstract: This study investigated the crosslinguistic distribution of intrinsic vowel duration, the observation that high vowels tend to be shorter than low vowels, using a large-scale corpus phonetic approach. Previous studies have reported a durational difference but have been limited by small speaker samples and narrow language coverage. Nevertheless, this observation has been debated to reflect an automatic consequence of the vowel height difference, or to be under speaker control. We reconsider this dichotomy in terms of competing pressures of target uniformity and enhancement in phonetic realization. Target uniformity would be consistent with a systematically shorter duration for high than low vowels and no systematic asymmetry between front and back vowels. In contrast, enhancement would predict larger, more variable durational differences between high and low vowels. To address the empirical gap, we analyzed duration contrasts among /i/, /u/, and /a/ in inter-obstruent contexts from over 60 languages, 80 language–length contrasts, and 16 language families in the VoxCommunis Corpus using automatic and manual vowel segmentations. Linear mixed-effects models assessed duration differences across vowel height and backness, incorporating rate-normalized and raw measures, while by-speaker analyses probed individual consistency. High vowels were shorter than low vowels in approximately 90% of language contrasts and significantly so for almost 80%. Crucially, no consistent durational bias emerged between high front and high back vowels. These findings suggest that intrinsic vowel duration is better understood as a statistical universal emerging from the balance between uniformity and enhancement in phonetic realization, rather than as a purely automatic universal.

articles.title: Recycling Rivalry: Social Identity Appeals Increase Recycling When Combined with Intergroup Comparison
articles.authors: Hege Landsvik; Jareef Martuza; Sveinung Jørgensen; Lars Jacob Pedersen; Siv Skard
articles.abstract: While many people recycle at home, they are less likely to do so in public, where high waste production meets a diffusion of individual responsibility. We examine whether social identity can close this gap. Across two preregistered season-long field experiments at a Norwegian Premier Division football stadium, we test the separate and combined effects of ingroup identity appeals and intergroup comparison on the recycling behavior of football supporters. In Study 1 (N = 5,712), an ingroup identity appeal did not increase recycling relative to an outgroup appeal, suggesting that standalone identity appeals are insufficient to shift behavior. When the ingroup appeal was combined with a ranking of clubs by their recycling rate, recycling rates were more than two times higher than in any other condition. Study 2 (N = 6,598) replicated this effect against a no-intervention control. Study 3 (N = 761), a post-game survey among Study 2’s participants, showed that supporters exposed to the combined intervention reported greater motivation to recycle and greater perceived importance of contributing to the ingroup’s success. These findings extend social identity theory by showing that identity appeals increase recycling when group performance is tied to a concrete metric of success, which an intergroup comparison can supply, making the behavior a way to pursue positive group distinctiveness.

articles.title: Effect-Based Assessments of Intergroup Comparability  – The Practical Impact of Measurement Non-Invariance & Differential Item Functioning on Psychological Tests and Scales
articles.authors: Tizian Maria Benedikt Schuhbeck; Melanie Viola Partsch; Philipp Sterner; David Goretzko
articles.abstract: To assess psychological tests and scales for violations of intergroup comparability – termed Measurement Non-Invariance (MNI) in factor analysis and Differential Item Functioning (DIF) in item response theory – statistical testing has emerged as the dominating approach, but inherently fails to differentiate between major and negligible violations. To address this, upwards of 27 effect size measures for both MNI and DIF have been proposed over the last decades, using vastly different conventions in naming and notation, with no clear consensus on interpretation. This arguably constitutes a severe hindrance for the much needed popularization of a non-dichotomous assessments of intergroup comparability. We address this limitation by introducing a unifying taxonomy that encompasses all previous measures as instances of just four fundamental types: Expected Difference (ED), Expected Absolute Difference (EAD), Total Expected Difference (TED) and Total Expected Absolute Difference (TEAD), which are universally applicable, irrespective of the underlying measurement model. Furthermore, we construct corresponding effect directions and derive formulas to calulate MNI/DIF-induced biases in commonly used mean difference effects, such as Cohen’s d & Cohen’s f. We provide a dual illustration using both FA and IRT models on real-world data.

articles.title: Unified Definition of Psychological Stress and the Cognitive Integration Model
articles.authors: Haixia Gu; Yangyang Lei; Yun Zhang; Chao Chen; Chunyu Liu
articles.abstract: Psychological stress is central to health and diseases. Yet heterogeneous definitions and insufficient theoretical integration lead to findings that are difficult to replicate or compare, ultimately hindering their translation into practice. To address this problem, we aimed to identify the fundamental and conceptually distinct components of psychological stress and integrate them into a unified definition and model. We systematically reviewed 67 existing definitions of psychological stress from previous publications and identified their core components. We quantified both the use frequency of each component and patterns of co-occurrence across the literature. We also reviewed major theoretical models to evaluate how comprehensively each model captured those core stress-related components. Existing definitions and theories were found to capture only partial aspects of the stress process, resulting in a fragmented conceptualization. To reconcile these fragmented perspectives and establish a cohesive foundation, we synthesize these core components into a novel framework. We redefine psychological stress as a perceived imbalance between stressors and available resources, with stressors arising from internal needs or external demands and corresponding internal and external resources. Cognitive appraisal is central to the stress process. Notably, internal needs represent an important class of stressors, yet they have received less attention than external demands in the past. To situate this definition within the broader stress process, we propose a Cognitive Integration Model (CIM). The CIM specifies how stressors and resources are dynamically integrated through cognition to generate psychological stress, whereas coping and responses are positioned as downstream components that provide feedback regulation and link stress to health outcomes. These components across the entire stress process may be jointly shaped by genetic and environmental factors. Together, this unified definition and model provide a common framework for integrating stress research across diverse theories, terminologies, and methods. This framework reframes psychological stress not as a purely environmental exposure, but as a product of gene–environment interaction.

articles.title: Parenting Behavior in Relation to Children's Socio-Emotional Skills: A Latent Profile Analysis
articles.authors: Sonja Kälin; Nora Tilda Kunz; Niamh Oeri
articles.abstract: Parenting is closely linked to children’s social-emotional development, including externalizing behavior, peer relationships, and emotion regulation. However, most existing research has examined these associations using single parenting behaviors or predefined parenting styles, thereby neglecting the complex co-occurrence of different parenting practices. To address this limitation, the present study applied a person-centered approach using Latent Profile Analysis (LPA) to identify distinct parenting profiles and explore their associations with child socioemotional skills. Based on reports of parenting behavior from parents of N = 254 kindergarten children (51.2% female, M = 6.0 years, SD = 0.62), three parenting profiles emerged: supportive (66%), engaged-disciplinary (22%), and harsh (12%). Associations with teacher-rated outcomes showed that children exposed to engaged-disciplinary parenting displayed more peer problems. In comparison, children assigned to the harsh parenting group showed more behavioral problems and, unexpectedly, stronger emotion regulation skills. The findings underscore the need to tailor support to specific subgroups of parents with distinct parenting behaviors, to strengthen positive parenting behaviors, and, in turn, promote the development of children.

articles.title: Real-Time Monitoring of Emergency Response Team Cognition
articles.authors: Bjørn Sætrevik; Camilla Konglevoll; Rebecca Vederhus
articles.abstract: Emergency response team members must have aligned and compatible mental models of the incident they are handling and of the work the team is doing. Being able to monitor team members’ mental model similarity during performance may allow a team leader to direct the team’s work in a way that increases team cognition. The current study collected data during 14 scenario training sessions for second-line emergency response teams (N = 134 participant recordings). The similarity of team member mental models about incident and teamwork were measured at freeze-points during scenario performance. In a preregistered replication of a previous finding, we found that mental models were more consistent within than between teams, indicating that some teams had better team cognition. We also developed and field-tested a team cognition monitoring tool, which presented real-time calculation of the team’s mental model similarity. At freeze-points during the exercise we provided half the team leaders with a report about the similarity of their team’s mental models at that point. Aligned with preregistered hypotheses, the teams achieved more similar mental models (when excluding the team role with most variation) when the leader could monitor the similarity. This indicates that similarity reports could be used to evaluate and enhance team cognition in emergency response teams, and team leaders could benefit from real-time monitoring of the team’s mental model similarity.

articles.title: Effects of a Neuroticism Intervention Over One Year
articles.authors: Peter Haehner; Amanda Jo Wright; Rosalie Andrae; Christopher James Hopwood; Wiebke Bleidorn
articles.abstract:
Introduction: Personality interventions recently gained increasing interest as promising tools to improve people’s lives. Although initial evidence on the effects of these interventions is promising, their longer-term effectiveness has yet to be established. 
Methods: Using data form the Changing How I Live Life (CHILL) Study, we examined the effects of a digital neuroticism intervention over 1 year. In this study, participants (N = 475) were randomized to an active control group or intervention groups targeting different levels of neuroticism. Furthermore, participants reported on different aspects of perceived intervention utility at the 1-year follow-up. 
Results: Participants significantly decreased in their neuroticism from pre-intervention to the 1-year follow-up regardless of whether they were randomized to the intervention groups (d = -0.40 to -0.53) or the active control group (d = -0.41). Intervention effects did also not differ among groups targeting different levels of neuroticism. Nonetheless, participants were relatively happy with the intervention and reported a high willingness to pay money to get access to a similar app. 
Conclusion: This study provides novel insights into the durability of intervention-induced neuroticism changes, but future research is needed to better understand the mechanisms and boundary conditions of volitional personality changes with and without interventions.

articles.title: Self-regulation shapes who benefits from large language models
articles.authors: Xiangbin Teng; Sirui Ren
articles.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) promise to broaden access to expertise, yet their benefits are uneven: the same model can scaffold a novice, accelerate an expert, or produce polished work that masks shallow understanding. We apply the established framework of self-regulated learning to human–LLM interaction and argue that loop quality emerges from the user–task–interface system rather than residing in the user alone. Productive loops involve three observable moves: steering sets goals and standards; monitoring evaluates fluent but fallible output; and repair tests, critiques, and revises it. Weak loops can create a synthesis trap in which users offload comparison and integration, producing false mastery—better assisted performance without corresponding transfer, confidence calibration, or error detection—and accumulating verification debt. The framework predicts that LLMs will widen differences between users when verification burden is high and regulatory support is weak, but narrow them when tasks are verifiable and interfaces externalize standards, evidence, and checks. We propose constraint density, monitoring calibration, and repair depth as process markers linking interaction traces to independent outcomes. This account turns divergent findings into testable predictions and motivates cognitive workbenches designed to preserve verification, agency, and transfer.

articles.title: An integrative framework for the human sense of control
articles.authors: Alireza Modirshanechi; Peter Dayan; Eric Schulz
articles.abstract: From managing daily schedules to making major life decisions, how much we feel in control of our lives is central to our behavior and well-being. Yet, there is currently no precise, unifying account of what it means to feel in control. Here, we propose that humans feel in control when they are prepared to tackle future tasks. We formalize this perspective via a precise yet interpretable measure of controllability that quantifies three key factors: (i) the range of available actions, (ii) the certainty or (iii) the possibility of achieving desired outcomes. This measure unifies previous conceptions of control and successfully predicts human preferences in three experiments in which participants either rate their sense of control or prepare themselves to seek rewards or avoid punishments. Our framework offers a principled foundation for understanding how environmental structure shapes the human sense of control, paving the way towards an integrative science of agency.

articles.title: Activities, Motivational Congruence, and Well-Being:  Cross-Sectional and Longitudinal Evidence
articles.authors: Taylor G. Hill
articles.abstract: A consistent observation across positive psychology is that similar activities do not benefit everyone equally, yet it remains unclear whether well-being depends more on activity content or on motivational congruence. Two preregistered studies examined associations between activities, motivational variables, personality, and well-being using cross-sectional (N = 392; 1,179 personally meaningful activities) and longitudinal (N = 350; 1,012 orientation–experience observations) data. In Study 1, behavioural activity categories showed little association with well-being, whereas hedonic and eudaimonic orientations showed consistent positive associations across outcomes. Motivational motives showed smaller but generally positive associations, and interaction effects between motives and orientations were limited, suggesting that these components contributed relatively independently rather than through strong cross-sectional congruence effects. Personality moderation effects were selective and modest. In Study 2, greater orientation–experience congruence most consistently predicted subsequent life worthwhileness, whereas evidence for life satisfaction was weaker. Congruence was associated primarily with competence need satisfaction, with little evidence of associations with autonomy or relatedness. Hedonic and eudaimonic experiences each showed independent positive associations with well-being, although their interaction was negative rather than synergistic. Across both studies, the findings suggest that activity categories alone provide limited insight into well-being, whereas motivational variables (and particularly within-person orientation–experience congruence) show more consistent associations with well-being.

articles.title: The crossword effect: A recall advantage for words encoded in alignment with their spatial associations
articles.authors: Christoph Scheepers; Ricarda Senger
articles.abstract: Across two preregistered experiments, we demonstrate that free word recall improves when words are encoded in alignment with their spatial associations. Experiment 1 compared words with a strong horizontal association (e.g., railway) to words with a strong vertical association (e.g., rocket) and established that the latter were more likely to be recalled when presented vertically rather than horizontally during encoding. No such benefit was observed for horizontally associated words. Experiment 2 extended these findings by showing a vertical encoding advantage also for spatially neutral words (e.g., foam), which was smaller than for the vertically associated words but larger than for the horizontally associated words in Experiment 1. Beyond suggesting a general vertical encoding advantage in free word recall, the results support Barsalou's (1999) Perceptual Symbol Hypothesis, which posits that word meanings are grounded in perception and action. Our findings demonstrate that access to word concepts in short term memory is modulated by sensorimotor processes during encoding, specifically horizontal versus vertical reading.

articles.title: Stability and Change of Spirituality following Childbirth: Longitudinal Evidence Swiss Household Panel Data Using Multiple Propensity Score Matching Analyses
articles.authors: Friedemann Trutzenberg; Michael Eid
articles.abstract:
Introduction: The birth of a child typically transcends parents’ daily lives and is frequently described as a spiritual experience. Yet, little is known about medium- or long-term effects of becoming parents on individuals’ spirituality. Spirituality is commonly conceptualised more broadly than religiosity and can refer to an ori- entation towards something divine, no matter whether this is a religious being or a non-religious entity. Its lifespan development and responsiveness to life events are not yet systematically understood, and existing evidence often does not allow for causal conclusions. Addressing this research gap, our study seeks to provide robust causal insights on the medium-term stability and change of spirituality following childbirth.

Methods: Using longitudinal pre- and post-birth spirituality data from the Swiss Household Panel (SHP), we compared participants who had become parents for the first time between 2015 and 2018 with propensity score (PS)-matched child- less and multiparous parent controls.

Results: Across multiple robustness conditions regarding covariate selection, manifest and structural equation modelling analyses suggested a high average medium-term stability in spirituality (r ≥ 0.87; ρ ≥ 0.95) and no average spiritual change following childbirth among the first-time parents (N = 138) compared to the matched controls.

Discussion: Given this high average stability, future research should focus on differential trajectories rather than average effects to better understand which individual and situational characteristics influence the development of spirituality following life events.

articles.title: Detecting political misinformation: A boosting intervention tested on Donald Trump’s statements
articles.authors: Lucca Pfruender; Ewout Meijer; Merijn Volmer; Leonie Hannah Shoshana Loewy; Bruno Verschuere
articles.abstract:
Misinformation has become an unavoidable part of political reality, eroding institutional
trust. We tested whether a simple booster intervention can improve misinformation detection
compared to intuitive judgments. The booster conditions instructed people to focus on the
level of detail in a politician's message while allowing them to weigh in factual knowledge.
Americans (n = 588) judged the veracity of statements made by Donald Trump, which were
fact-checked as true or false. False statements were judged less detailed than true statements,
and the booster interventions increased misinformation-detection accuracy by 4 to 6
percentage points over intuitive judgments. Political statements as short as one sentence
differed in detail depending on whether they were true or false, and this could be used to
boost voters’ ability to detect misinformation, at least in Donald Trump’s statements.

articles.title: How Prompting and Editing Shape Psychological Ownership in AI-Assisted Creative Writing
articles.authors: Niki Pennanen; Pyry Kanerva; Christian Guckelsberger
articles.abstract: Large language models are increasingly used as writing partners, but their use complicates whether writers experience the resulting text as genuinely their own. Such psychological ownership is especially relevant in AI-assisted writing because it contributes to the immediate and extended experience of AI use, and users may sign, share, revise, or be held accountable for texts whose content was partly generated by AI. Prior work shows that greater human input can increase ownership, but it remains unclear how ownership is shaped by two common forms of involvement: steering generation through prompting, directly revising generated text, and their combination. We report a preregistered mixed factorial experiment (N=273) in which online participants wrote short stories either without AI assistance or with AI assistance under one of two prompting styles (single-prompt vs. iterative), crossed with editing or not editing the AI-generated text. Editing increased ownership, especially for single-prompt generation. Iterative prompting increased ownership when editing was unavailable, but not when editing was available. These findings suggest that iterative prompting and post-generation editing are partially substitutable routes to psychological ownership, each providing opportunities for control and self-investment at different phases of the writing process. Fully manual writing nevertheless produced substantially higher ownership than all AI-assisted conditions, a gap that persisted in exploratory covariate analyses adjusting for effort, perceived story quality, and intrinsic motivation. The results suggest that AI writing tools should avoid one-shot delegation workflows when ownership matters, and instead support users in both steering and directly revising co-created text.

articles.title: Growth Trajectory Profiles of Self-concept of Abilities, Intrinsic Value, Utility Value, and Emotional Cost in Math Across Grades 4 to 8
articles.authors: Mathilda Sandman; Anna Widlund; Jaana Viljaranta; Rebecca Lazarides; Wendy Symes; Johan Korhonen
articles.abstract:
Background: Previous research has consistently shown that students’ math motivation declines across the school years. However, less is known about individual differences in these developmental trajectories. 
Aim: This study investigated the development of students’ math self-concept of abilities, intrinsic value, utility value and emotional cost from Grades 4 to 8 at the average level and by identifying distinct growth trajectory profiles. Profile membership was further related to gender and performance. 
Sample: The sample comprised 875 Finnish students (53 % girls) from Grades 4 to 8 using an accelerated longitudinal design. 
Method: Latent growth curve models and growth mixture modeling were utilized. Gender differences were analyzed using the 3-step approach and differences in math performance were examined using the BCH method.
Results: On average, self-concept of abilities, intrinsic value, and utility value declined whereas emotional cost increased over time. Three trajectory profiles were identified: Positive declining reflected the normative developmental pattern, while students in the Struggling profile showed lower initial motivation, increasing emotional cost, and the lowest math performance. Further, students in the Fading interest profile, predominantly boys, maintained high self-concept and performance despite low/moderate utility value and steeply declining intrinsic value. 
Conclusion: The average developmental trends concealed individual differences in students’ motivational development. While most students followed the expected decline, distinct profiles showed that motivation can develop differently across students and have different implications for academic performance.

articles.title: The Role of Individual Differences in the Effects of PC and VR Simulations on Elementary School Students’ Learning and Curiosity
articles.authors: Valdemar Aksel Stenberdt; Géraldine Fauville; Cecilie Fenja Strandsbjerg; Adéla Plechatá; Ingo Zettler; Guido Makransky
articles.abstract: Curiosity is related to important academic outcomes. Yet, current research suggests that children’s curiosity decreases during formal schooling, and research exploring theory-informed interventions to increase curiosity remains limited. Building on a synthesis of prior research, the SIM-Curious framework is introduced, identifying pathways to support curiosity-driven learning with simulations. Then, results of a pre-registered, randomized field trial (N = 217, Mage = 13.22 years, SD = 0.94) are presented, examining the overall effects of simulations and the relative effects of media (Virtual Reality vs PCs) in promoting curiosity and knowledge. Students’ specific state curiosity and knowledge increased, but there were no significant main effects of media. Higher prior specific state curiosity indirectly influenced follow-up knowledge through question-asking during the simulation. Individual differences in trait curiosity, prior knowledge, in-simulation question-asking, and post-simulation specific state curiosity influenced post-intervention information-seeking. The results are discussed in light of the SIM-Curious framework and illustrate its promise.

articles.title: A scoping review of the sexual health and wellbeing of LGBTQIA+ people affected by cancer.
articles.authors: Daniel Brown; Pierre Roscher; Karina Rune
articles.abstract:
Background
Sexual health and wellbeing are critical components of quality of life following cancer, yet they remain under-addressed in care. LGBTQIA+ people affected by cancer face additional challenges due to heteronormative healthcare systems, minority stress, and limited access to inclusive, culturally responsive services.
Aims
This scoping review aimed to map the extent, nature, and characteristics of research on the sexual health and wellbeing and sexual healthcare experiences of LGBTQIA+ people affected by cancer.
Methods
Databases (PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, and CINAHL) were searched up to September 2024. Eligible studies included peer-reviewed research on LGBTQIA+ individuals affected by cancer. Data were charted using both manual and AI-assisted extraction, and analysed thematically.
Results
Forty-nine reports representing 29 studies were included, involving approximately 3,800 participants. Research was dominated by cisgender sexual minority men with prostate cancer. Seven key themes were identified: sexual function and adaptation, healthcare heteronormativity, psychosocial wellbeing, chosen family, interventions, measurement, and intersectional disparities. Sexual dysfunction was common but experienced differently across groups, often requiring adaptation rather than restoration. Heteronormative care limited inclusive communication and tailored support. LGBTQIA+ individuals reported higher psychological distress, with social and chosen family support playing a key role in adjustment. There was a lack of tailored interventions and inclusive measurement tools, and limited representation of diverse subgroups.
Conclusions
Significant gaps exist in understanding and addressing the sexual health needs of LGBTQIA+ cancer survivors. Inclusive, queer-informed frameworks, improved measurement tools, and targeted interventions are needed to support equitable and person-centred care.

articles.title: A Test of the 2 × 2 Model of Perfectionism in Predicting Distress among Licensure Examination Reviewees
articles.authors: Renz Louis T. Montano; Jan Patrick G. Gutierrez
articles.abstract: Perfectionism has been consistently linked to psychological distress, yet most evidence in the Philippine context relies on cross-sectional designs, limiting temporal conclusions. Licensure examinations in the Philippines, such as the Psychometrician Licensure Examination mandated by Republic Act No. 10029 (2009), represent a high-stakes evaluative context that may amplify perfectionistic tendencies. The present study tested the 2 × 2 model of perfectionism among 315 licensure examination reviewees, examining how Evaluative Concerns Perfectionism (ECP) and Personal Standards Perfectionism (PSP) predicted Time 2 overall distress, anxiety, and depression after a one-month interval. ECP was a significant positive predictor of all three outcomes, whereas PSP was not. Consistent with the 2 × 2 model, Pure PSP did not differ from Non-perfectionism, while Pure ECP and Mixed Perfectionism are associated significantly greater distress, anxiety, and depression than Non-perfectionism and Pure PSP. Notably, Pure ECP and Mixed Perfectionism did not significantly differ, lending support to the aggravating factor hypothesis. These findings underscore that ECP, rather than PSP, drive psychological distress in high-stakes evaluative contexts.

articles.title: Unique and common qualifiers in the lexical differentiation of blue and brown in American English: Corpus evidence at the vision–language interface
articles.authors: David Henry Peterzell; Anke Marit Albers; Sean Isamu Johnson; Galina Paramei
articles.abstract:
While humans perceive color as a nearly continuous spectrum, most languages categorize hues using a small set of basic color terms (BCTs). Several languages (e.g., Russian, Greek, Italian) lexicalize two or more basic ‘blue’ categories, distinguishing light from dark blue, a distinction English is usually said to lack. No basic split for English blue has been found, yet speakers may differentiate blue shades in everyday usage by attaching modifiers such as “light” and “dark” to blue more than to other color terms. Using the Corpus of Contemporary American English (COCA; ~560 million words, five genres), we extracted the 11 English BCTs with their most frequent preceding collocates and quantified chromatic specification, correcting for non-chromatic uses of the color words and their qualifiers. Although light blue and dark blue do not function as separate basic categories, blue attracts chromatic specifiers more often, and a far wider variety of unique ones (navy, cobalt, cerulean), than any other BCT, a lead we link to its communicative prominence and chromatic richness. Brown is the other heavily qualified term, but its qualification runs through common, largely achromatic modifiers rather than unique specifiers, a pattern we link to its status as a constitutively dark, lightness-defined color whose subcategories are largely lightness variants. The central contrast replicates on the current, larger COCA release (~993 million words, eight genres) using an independently constructed classification of qualifiers. We argue that color-term basicness is gradient rather than discrete, and that corpus structure offers a naturalistic window onto the vision–language interface.
Keywords: color categorization; basic color terms; color names; blue; brown; corpus linguistics; COCA; vision-language interface

articles.title: The Positively Reconstructed Self-Voice: The Mental Representation of One’s Own Voice is Brighter and Clearer than Recorded Voice
articles.authors: Yusuke Suzuki; Naoki Kuroda; Masayoshi Nagai
articles.abstract: People experience discomfort hearing their recorded voices due to the discrepancy with their internal representation. While attributed to bone-conduction amplifying low frequencies, simulating this hypothesis has yielded inconsistent results. Challenging this view, we explored the self-voice mental representation using psychophysical reverse correlation, a data-driven approach without prior assumptions. Across two experiments, Japanese adults (Study 1: n = 24; Study 2: n = 54) selected one of two randomly spectral amplitude-modulated voices that sounded more like their own. Voices reconstructed from these judgments yielded significantly higher own-voice likeness ratings than recordings or bone-conduction simulations. Acoustic analyses revealed these representations contradicted bone-conduction predictions (“lower and deeper”), emerging as “brighter and clearer” (increased spectral centroid and F1 frequency) and emphasizing “individual identity” (selectively amplified formants). Although limited to the sustained vowel /a:/, a generalized filter approximated the self-voice for novel speakers, suggesting a common mechanism underlying self-voice representations across individuals.

articles.title: Time to Divest?: Perceived Inconsistencies between universities’ environmental policy and actions reduce staff and students’ intentions to engage in pro-environmental behaviours
articles.authors: Alice M Davis; Paulina Schenk; Hiu Laam Tse; Sabine Topf; Jeremy I Skipper
articles.abstract: Many universities have environmental policy statements that are decidedly pro-environmental. However, some of their past actions may be perceived as inconsistent with these commitments. For example, one university previously invested £21 million in companies and intermediaries that produce fossil fuels, which are known to contribute to environmental devastation and global warming. In line with its policy statement, the university also promoted initiatives to encourage staff and students to adopt pro-environmental behaviours (PEBs). How might the perception of inconsistency between environmental policy and actual practice affect the efforts of members of the university community to enact individual PEBs? To address this question, in two studies we tested the hypothesis that university community members would be less likely to engage in PEBs if they were made aware of inconsistencies between environmental policy and actions. Consistent with this hypothesis, we found that staff and students were less likely to say they intend to adopt PEBs in the coming week when told about inconsistencies, compared to a group told that university environmental policy and actions are consistent. Furthermore, there were a number of interactions with attitudes, knowledge, and situational factors in both studies, mostly showing fewer PEBs when policy was inconsistent. These results imply that perceived inconsistencies between environmental policy and actions could lead university staff and students to engage in fewer PEBs. Interpretation of statistical interactions further suggests that when individual attitudes are not strong, community members—especially students—reference the university’s inconsistency and decide to perform fewer PEBs than they might otherwise. Given increasing global awareness of environmental problems, this interpretation leads to the suggestion that universities should either consider adding caveats to their environmental policy statements or bring their actions in line with those policies (e.g., by divesting fossil fuel holdings—as this university ultimately did).

articles.title: At The Mercy of Politics? When Policy Change  Undermines the Credibility of Public Managers
articles.authors: Mads Pieter van Luttervelt; Mathias Østergaard-Nielsen; Anders Grøn
articles.abstract: Politicians often change policies—sometimes unexpectedly—but how it affects the bureaucracy remains largely unknown. We argue that changing policies can undermine the credibility of public managers in the eyes of the street-level bureaucrats. Testing this argument causally in the real world is challenging as it requires unanticipated policy change that only affects part of the bureaucracy and a pre- and post-change measurement of relevant constructs. To overcome these challenges, we leverage a quasi-experimental design by exploiting that a nationwide reform in Denmark’s education sector was unexpectedly changed for half of the country’s high schools. We find a long-term negative causal effect of policy change on the credibility of public managers, when they showed commitment to the initial policy. The effect is driven by street-level bureaucrats whose policy preferences align with the initial policy. We discuss trade-offs for policy makers and managers when initiating or responding to policy changes.

articles.title: Book Review: A Marxist Critique of the Ruined University, by Krystian Szadkowski and Jakub Krzeski, Springer, 2025.
articles.authors: Anıl Kandemir
articles.abstract: This abstract summarizes a review of Krystian Szadkowski and Jakub Krzeski’s A Marxist Critique of the Ruined University (2025), a pivotal theoretical intervention that reconceptualizes the modern decline of higher education. Rather than lamenting the loss of historical academic ideals, the reviewed text posits that the university is experiencing a profound ontological crisis driven fundamentally by the imperatives of global capital accumulation. The review highlights how the authors map the academy's systemic reorganization into a primary node for value reproduction, where knowledge and academic labor are continuously co-opted to serve market interests. To navigate this crisis, Szadkowski and Krzeski deploy a Marxian "integral critique" composed of three dialectical stages: in (diagnosing internal institutional mechanisms and exploitation), against (resisting internal hierarchies), and beyond (identifying emerging social relations). The review traces the book’s eleven chapters through conceptual, foundational, tactical, and reconstructive clusters. It emphasizes the authors' uncompromising dissection of the "Academic Robinson"—a mode of subjectivation marked by hyper-individualization—and the alienating forces of neoliberal metricization that fundamentally transform institutional habitus. Crucially, the review notes that the book avoids deterministic pessimism by offering an affirmative, emancipatory blueprint. By moving beyond mere melancholic observation, the authors envision a post-capitalist "university of the common" anchored in horizontal governance, alternative property relations, and collective social production. Ultimately, the review concludes that this robust analytical toolkit successfully bridges abstract philosophical diagnosis with the urgent material need for transformative praxis and collective solidarity among academic laborers.

articles.title: Bioplastics as a Sustainability Promise: Promises and (Dis)illusionments of a ‘Technological Fix’ in Germany
articles.authors: Yannick Kalff
articles.abstract: Bioplastics have emerged as a beacon of hope for sustainable alternatives to conventional,petroleum-based  plastics. They promise sustainability by technically addressing the issues associated with plastics – waste burden, emissions, and dependence on oil. This makes them a ‘technological fix,’ recommending simple technical solutions to complex challenges but overlooking the intricate reality. The article empirically demonstrates that the disappointments with bioplastics are not solely due to technical reasons but stem from neglected societal, social, economic, or ecological factors. These factors range from the material properties of early bioplastics, monocultures and land competition for the use of renewable resources, to their economic competitiveness. From the technological promise of sustainability and the dashed hopes for bioplastics, it follows that the technological fix fails because it is tied to the path dependencies of fossil plastics. Without social innovations in societal use of plastics, departing from these paths is difficult.

articles.title: The Impact of Inflation on Income Distribution in Nigeria. An Empirical Approach (1990–2023)
articles.authors: Adriel Ekozin; Felix I. Ifada; James A. Adesokan
articles.abstract: The study examined the impact of inflation on income in Nigeria for the period of 1990–2023. The study made use of four explanatory variables, which are: external remittance, interest rate, inflation rate, and exchange rate on income in Nigeria. The data were obtained from various issues of the Central Bank of Nigeria (CBN) Statistical Bulletin, journals, as well as financial indicators. Augmented Dickey-Fuller (ADF) and Johansen cointegration tests were employed to confirm the stationarity of the series and the long-run relationship among the series. The findings indicate that remittances positively impact economic growth and income distribution, supporting household consumption and investment. Higher interest rates increase the cost of borrowing, limiting access to credit, reducing investment, and negatively impacting income distribution. High inflation reduces household purchasing power, particularly affecting low-income earners, thereby worsening income distribution. The study therefore concluded that remittances play a crucial role in boosting real GDP and improving household welfare, emphasising the need for policies that facilitate their inflow. Conversely, high interest rates, inflation, and exchange-rate volatility negatively impact economic growth and exacerbate income inequality. The study therefore recommended that the Central Bank of Nigeria should implement policies to reduce transaction costs and encourage diaspora investments. The apex bank should also promote financial-sector reforms to lower borrowing costs and boost investment. The government should enhance domestic production to stabilise prices and reduce inflationary pressures.

articles.title: Changing governments, stable elites? Executive personnel continuity in global perspective
articles.authors: Marco Improta
articles.abstract: In political science, government change is typically understood as a shift in who holds power, even though new cabinets may formally include many members of the previous governing elite. In this study, I differentiate institutional turnover from personnel turnover by reconstructing transitions between successive governments using the WhoGov dataset. I introduce an Executive Personnel Continuity Index (EPCI) that measures the similarity between outgoing and incoming ministerial rosters. I argue that leader succession functions as an executive reset: new leaders have incentives to establish control, reward loyalists, and signal political change. Party organizations, however, can insulate incumbent ministers from replacement. I test these expectations using descriptive evidence, country and transition-year fixed effects, equal-country weighting, entropy balancing and a transition-centered comparison with the outgoing government's own pre-transition continuity. Across the principal specifications, leader replacement is associated with a decline of approximately one-third in executive personnel continuity. The decline is limited under same-party succession, substantially larger across party boundaries and greatest under complete partisan alternation. The findings therefore indicate that a change in government translates into a substantive transformation of the elite mainly when it also unsettles the leadership and party bases of executive power, and this has significant consequences for political systems worldwide.

articles.title: Shaping the notion of #wellbeing in the therapy culture context: an analysis through Instagram narratives
articles.authors: Ainara Larrondo-Ureta; Simón Peña-Fernández; Jordi Morales-i-Gras
articles.abstract:
Purpose – The aim of this paper is to (1) identify textual and visual themes and sub-themes associated with the #wellbeing hashtag on Instagram, (2) assess their varying levels of engagement and (3) investigate gender bias present in the analysed visual narratives.
Design/methodology/approach – This study employs a range of big data analysis techniques to investigate various dimensions of wellbeing on Instagram. Initially, a sample of 9,844 posts was processed using data mining and text analysis methods to identify and categorise significant hashtags, which facilitated the classification of posts into thematic clusters through hierarchical clustering. Engagement was then assessed using non-parametric statistical tests. Additionally, computer vision models were used to analyse and classify visual narratives, grouping images into communities based on visual similarities. Finally, gender representation in the images was examined using object detection models.
Findings – The study reveals that the discourse around #wellbeing on Instagram is predominantly feminised and focuses primarily on mental, psychological and spiritual aspects. Therapeutic and positive psychology narratives are the most prevalent and engaging, while physical activity and nutrition play a relatively secondary role. Two major macro-narratives emerge: firstly, mental health and emotional wellbeing, often featuring hashtags related to therapy, self-discovery, spirituality and motivational quotes; secondly, though less prominently, themes and visual narratives concerning physical activity and healthy habits, emphasising exercise and nutrition.
Originality/value – The study identifies, for the first time in the academic literature, key themes and subthemes in the textual and visual narratives on wellness on the social media (Instagram), offering evidence for its feminisation. These findings contribute to the academic discussion on the implications of the notion of wellbeing on Instagram in relation to “therapy culture”. This idea can be applied to other social media, as well as to other areas, such as working life, where diverse individualities and groups also coexist.

articles.title: “ChatGPT has helped me more than 15 years of therapy”:   AI therapy and moving beyond para-social interaction to conceptualising AI chatbots as a significant other.
articles.authors: Stephanie Alice Baker; Michael James Walsh
articles.abstract: There is a growing body of literature that assesses the risks and ethical challenges associated with AI therapy and the integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into healthcare. Much of this research examines the risks and harms associated with parasocial relationships and projecting sentient qualities onto AI chatbots. This article makes a novel contribution to this literature by examining AI therapy from an ethnographic perspective, examining how people strategically use prompts to reduce the perceived risks associated with AI therapy. Analysing TikTok videos (n = 840) to understand how content creators use AI to support their mental health, our study found that most people use AI therapy for personality analysis and self-improvement rather than medical treatment and diagnosis. Although users demonstrated reflexivity and agency in their therapeutic engagement with AI, we introduce the concept of AI as a ‘significant other’ to highlight the impact of AI therapy.

articles.title: Taxation of the Digital Economy in Nigeria: A Conceptual Review
articles.authors: Adriel Ekozin; Simeon Funminiyi Akinpelu; Igbinosun Friday Ese
articles.abstract: This study examined the taxation of the digital economy in Nigeria through a conceptual review, focusing on challenges, prospects, and policy implications of taxing digital activities including e-commerce, fintech, streaming services, online advertising, and social media commerce. The purpose was to critically analyse how Nigeria’s legal and regulatory frameworks, administrative capacities, and technological tools interact to facilitate revenue mobilisation from digital economic activities. A qualitative conceptual research design was employed, relying entirely on secondary data from academic journals, government reports, Finance Acts, and international frameworks, with data analysed through content and thematic analysis and supported by descriptive statistics from government and global sources. Findings revealed that while Nigeria’s digital economy has expanded rapidly, compliance with tax obligations remains moderate, with informal platforms and cross border transactions limiting effective revenue collection. Legal recognition of significant economic presence is crucial for capturing digital taxes, yet enforcement gaps and limited technological monitoring hinder compliance, with fintech platforms integrated into formal banking systems showing higher adherence than informal social media commerce. The study contributes a structured conceptual framework linking digital activities, regulatory clarity, administrative enforcement, and revenue outcomes, while identifying critical policy and practical gaps. The findings imply that improving technological monitoring, strengthening legal frameworks, and enhancing stakeholder engagement are essential for increasing compliance, offering insights for policymakers and laying the foundation for future research on sustainable digital taxation strategies in Nigeria.

articles.title: Machine-translated ParlSpeech V2 dataset: Full-text corpora of 3.5 million parliamentary speeches from seven countries translated into English
articles.authors: Štěpán Štěpán Jabůrek; Adam Černý; Christian Rauh; Jan Schwalbach
articles.abstract: Machine-translated ParlSpeech V2 contains complete full-text vectors of more than 3.5 million parliamentary speeches in the key legislative chambers of Austria, the Czech Republic, Germany, Denmark, the Netherlands, Spain, and Sweden, covering periods between 21 and 32 years. The data include speeches machine-translated into English using open-source OPUS-MT models. Original language speeches from ParlSpeech V2 (Rauh & Schwalbach 2020) are present alongside the English translation. Meta-data include the original information on date, speaker, party, and partially agenda item under which a speech was held. The accompanying release note provides a more detailed guide to the data.

articles.title: Enabling justice in nature-positive transformations: Insights from agricultural, forestry, and health transitions
articles.authors: Aniek Hebinck; Thomas Fransen; Dalia D'Amato; Ben Delbaere; Symke Nieboer; Lara Lebleu; Stella Piipponen-Doyle; Valentina Vaglica; Hans Keune; Opi Outhwaite
articles.abstract: Transformations within the biodiversity nexus are increasingly expected to deliver not only environmental outcomes but also enable justice. Yet, how justice is experienced and shaped within such transformation processes remains unclear. This paper examines how justice is experienced and shaped in practice across three nature-positive transitions in Europe: efforts to make agriculture, forestry, and healthcare more supportive of biodiversity and human wellbeing. Drawing on a relational approach to justice and insights from just transitions, the analysis shows that policy rarely explicitly aims to enable justice. Instead, policies often indirectly aim to promote justice through low-conflict and incremental pathways. Across the cases, procedural dimensions dominate in policy approaches to enable justice, while distributive and recognition dimensions are addressed unevenly and less consistently in the policy frameworks analysed. At the same time, justice appears to be shaped and experienced less by individual policy instruments than by broader structural conditions, including institutional arrangements, property relations, and dominant knowledge frameworks, which influence how policies are implemented and whose interests they serve. Building on these findings, the paper conceptualises justice as a relational and context-dependent phenomenon, produced through interactions between actor framings, institutional arrangements, and transition dynamics. This highlights key tensions between ambition for just transformation and governance approaches that prioritise incremental and low conflict pathways, with important implications for both research and policy.

articles.title: Harm Through the “#RizzCam”: Smart Glasses, Ambient Capture and Invisible Harassment
articles.authors: Milica Stilinovic; Ben Egliston; Wenqi Tan; Marcus Carter; Joanne E. Gray
articles.abstract: In online safety research, harassment is commonly understood as involving overt and unwanted acts that create a hostile environment for individuals or groups. Smart glasses, or wearable digital devices that are often indistinguishable from ordinary eyewear but can record video, audio and location data in real time, enable new forms of online harassment and gender-based harms that may not be recognised by current online safety or platform governance frameworks. Drawing on an interpretive content analysis of 350 point-of-view Instagram videos posted by individuals self-associated with the pick-up artistry (PUA) community, we examine how smart glasses can be used to harass women through what we call ambient capture. Ambient capture includes clandestine recording of people and social interactions within public, semi-private and private spaces. We argue this can constitute harassment when it is targeted at women and shared online without their consent. In our study, we found videos using ambient capture practices to harass women that had gone undetected by Instagram’s content moderation systems. These findings suggest online safety regimes and content moderation approaches should be assessed to ensure they account for the more invisible forms of harassment introduced by smart glasses and other wearable technologies.

articles.title: From science-policy to science-policy-society: enabling transformative change in practice
articles.authors: Aniek Hebinck; Mara de Pater; Anita Lazurko; Gijs Diercks; Dalia D'Amato; Amanda Krijgsman; Heli Saarikoski; Hans Keune; Symke Nieboer; Julia Wittmayer
articles.abstract: Transformative change is widely recognised as necessary to address interconnected, persistent sustainability crises. Yet, despite growing experimentation with co-production and societal engagement, dominant science–policy arrangements remain largely assessment-oriented and geared toward incremental optimisation. While the 2024 IPBES Transformative Change Assessment was a landmark articulating drivers and principles of transformation, less attention has been paid to how science–policy interfaces themselves must reorganise to enable transformative action. This perspective addresses that gap. We argue that enabling transformative change requires reconfiguring the science–policy interface toward a science–policy–society interface embedding collaboration, experimentation, and collective learning. Drawing on insights from transformative research and our own transdisciplinary experiences, we propose three institutional conditions: (1) embracing the contested nature of transformative change as a productive space; (2) shifting research and policy from incremental improvements to transformative futures and emerging alternatives; and (3) institutionalizing reciprocal, action-oriented collaboration that enables sustained experimentation and collective agency. These conditions must be reinforced through institutional reforms in agenda-setting, funding and evaluation logics, and mechanisms ensuring continuity and societal memory. We conclude that institutional reform and transformative practice co-evolve, positioning science–policy–society configurations as enabling infrastructures for sustainability transformations.

articles.title: Accounting for Compositional Bias in Unexpected Event During Survey Designs
articles.authors: Klara Müller
articles.abstract: Political events may affect not only people’s political attitudes and behavior but also who responds to surveys. If events change who participates, estimates from event-focused designs may reflect changes in sample compositions rather than genuine opinion change. This is particularly challenging for designs like the Unexpected Event during Survey Design (UESD), which identifies causal effects by comparing respondents interviewed immediately before and after an unexpected event. I develop an analytical framework that extends established UESD best-practices, which successfully address observable differences between these samples, by sensitivity analyses to assess the potential impact of unobserved compositional bias. I illustrate the framework using the 2015 Charlie Hebdo terrorist attacks to estimate rally-around-the-flag effects and demonstrate its broader applicability by replicating 14 published UESD studies on terrorist events and rally-type outcomes. Across cases, political events affect sample compositions, but accounting for observable differences rarely changes estimated effects. Further, unobserved compositional bias would typically need to be implausibly strong to overturn substantive results. The proposed framework provides tools to assess and mitigate compositional bias, which strengthens causal inference in UESD and other event-focused designs.

articles.title: A Bayesian Model to Estimate Male and Female Fertility Patterns at a Subnational Level
articles.authors: Riccardo Omenti; Monica Alexander; Nicola Barban
articles.abstract: Accurate subnational fertility estimates are crucial for shaping policy decisions across diverse sectors, including education, health care, and social welfare. However, these estimates are difficult to obtain in small populations, in which data on births classified by maternal and paternal ages may be lacking or inadequate. In this paper, we describe a Bayesian model tailored to estimate the Total Fertility Rates (TFR) for both men and women at a subnational level. The model relies on population counts from age-sex pyramids and jointly models mortality and fertility patterns while accounting for uncertainty and spatiotemporal dependencies. Testing the model with simulated data that mimic Australian regions, as well as with real data from US counties, Mexican states and Nigerian regions, demonstrates its ability to generate reasonable TFR estimates. The estimates produced have straightforward applications to the study of subregional reproductive disparities, and the proposed modeling framework can be extended to investigate subnational fertility patterns across other countries with limited or fragmented birth data.

articles.title: Constrained Agency under Existential Threat: Immigrant Entrepreneurship and Expulsion
articles.authors: Robertson Khan Tengeh
articles.abstract: Structural and socio-cultural constraints have long shaped African immigrant entrepreneurship in South Africa. The organised anti-foreigner campaigns of 2025–2026 echoed the earlier expulsions in Ghana (1969) and Nigeria (1983). What made them different was that the host society itself became the organised source of existential threat. This article aimed to develop a theoretical framework accounting for how entrepreneurial agency changes when organised political mobilisation simultaneously threatens physical safety, legal presence, and venture survival. The framework was developed as a conceptual model by drawing on constrained agency theory alongside scholarship on institutions, social movements, scapegoating, and moral panic. Rather than being tested with primary data, it was illustrated through historical and contemporary African cases. CAT-ET suggests that when constraints become existential, agency tends to shift towards either adaptive persistence or strategic exit. Two interacting mechanisms were specified: functional institutional inaccessibility under violence, whereby protective institutions remained operational but selectively inaccessible, and the entrepreneur-as-symbol dynamic, whereby immigrant ventures became politically constructed as emblems of economic grievance. CAT-ET reframed organised expulsion as a recurring political-economic process and offered a basis for comparative research across the Global South.

articles.title: Understanding moral trade-offs in pandemic response: A discrete choice experiment on avian influenza policies
articles.authors: Nicholas Smeele; Charlotte Nina Maria Waltz; Anja Schreijer; Pearl A. Dykstra
articles.abstract: Pandemic preparedness requires navigating trade-offs between health, economic, and social impacts; choices that often involve moral tensions. This study investigates how the Dutch public evaluates such trade-offs in the context of a potential outbreak of highly pathogenic avian influenza (HPAI). Using a discrete choice experiment (DCE) administered to a representative sample of 1,045 respondents from the LISS panel, we examined preferences across six policy outcomes: mortality, lasting physical and mental injuries, postponed healthcare, social restrictions, and one-off tax payments. A latent class logit model identified four distinct preference profiles, revealing substantial heterogeneity in moral and economic reasoning. Two classes exhibited taboo trade-off aversion (TTOA) when values such as life or human dignity were traded against monetary costs. Respondents displaying TTOA emphasized solidarity and governmental responsibility, while cost-sensitive groups prioritized economic efficiency. These findings highlight that public acceptance of pandemic policies depends not only on effectiveness and cost but also on perceived moral legitimacy. Accounting for TTOA in economic evaluation can improve the ethical considerations and societal acceptability of future pandemic preparedness strategies.

articles.title: Beyond Encampment? Understanding Attitudes Toward Refugee Integration
articles.authors: Mae MacDonald; Adam G Lichtenheld
articles.abstract: Most of the world's refugees live in low- and middle-income countries, where debates center on integrating those already present rather than admitting new arrivals. Yet existing research focuses largely on admission in high-income countries. We provide one of the first nationwide assessments of attitudes toward integration in the Global South, drawing on a survey of 3,326 Kenyans fielded after a reform was passed but before implementation, with embedded experiments varying policy dimension and refugee group. Support for integration is high, but citizens are less supportive of allowing refugees to leave camps than granting economic inclusion or creating integrated settlements, and support varies significantly by refugee nationality. Opposition is driven primarily by fears of crime, terrorism, and the spread of conflict. Ethnic kinship and close contact predict support, while economic factors matter little. These findings suggest that integration is politically feasible, but insecurity associated with free movement remains the largest concern.

articles.title: Macroeconomic Volatility and Organizational Performance: A Contingency Theory Perspective from the Nigerian Corporate Sector
articles.authors: Adriel Ekozin; Philip Shakede Sanni; Friday Izen Ohiokha
articles.abstract: Macroeconomic instability has continued to shape the operating environment of firms in Nigeria, creating uncertainty that affects business outcomes. This study examines the effect of macroeconomic volatility on organizational performance in the Nigerian corporate sector, while also considering the role of firm-level characteristics within a contingency theory framework. A longitudinal panel design was adopted, using secondary data obtained from the Central Bank of Nigeria, the World Bank, and financial reports of selected firms listed on the Nigerian Exchange over the period 2010–2024. Panel regression techniques were employed, including fixed and random effects models, with the Hausman test used to determine the appropriate specification. The findings indicate that macroeconomic volatility, particularly inflation, exchange rate fluctuations, and interest rate changes, has a significant negative effect on firm performance, while economic growth exerts a positive influence. The results further show that firm-level factors such as size, liquidity, and leverage significantly moderate this relationship. Firms with stronger financial capacity are better able to absorb macroeconomic shocks, whereas highly leveraged firms are more vulnerable to instability. The study concludes that organizational performance in Nigeria is influenced not only by external economic conditions but also by how firms adjust their internal structures and strategies. By applying contingency theory, the study provides a more nuanced explanation of performance differences across firms. The findings offer useful insights for managers seeking to improve resilience and for policymakers aiming to strengthen the business environment.

articles.title: El dolor que no se hereda: la intransmisibilidad de la acción indemnizatoria del daño moral (comentario a la sentencia de la Corte Suprema de 27 de julio de 2026, rol N° 32.205-2025)
articles.authors: Andrés Gabriel Varas Quijón
articles.abstract: La Primera Sala de la Corte Suprema, en sentencia de 27 de julio de 2026 (rol N° 32.205-2025, redacción del abogado integrante Álvaro Vidal Olivares), acogió un recurso de casación en el fondo y declaró que la acción indemnizatoria del daño moral que la víctima no ejerció en vida es intransmisible a sus herederos. El caso —una paciente a la que, por omisión de la pausa de seguridad, se le extirpó el riñón sano y se le dejó el tumoral, falleciendo semanas después— había sido resuelto en ambas instancias por la tesis contraria. La Corte funda la intransmisibilidad en dos pilares: la naturaleza personalísima del interés lesionado, que hace intransferible el fundamento mismo de la acción, y la finalidad compensatoria de la indemnización, que sólo puede cumplirse en la persona que padeció el daño; la sede normativa es sucesoria, y descansa en el adjetivo «transmisibles» de los artículos 951 inciso segundo y 1097 inciso primero del Código Civil, reforzado por el criterio biográfico de avaluación del artículo 41 de la Ley N° 19.966. De allí extrae dos corolarios: ni el contenido pecuniario de la prestación ni el ingreso de la acción al patrimonio del causante determinan su transmisibilidad. La tutela de los cercanos queda reconducida íntegramente al daño por repercusión o rebote —derecho propio y originario, que exige probar vínculo afectivo estrecho y no puede acumularse con la pretensión hereditaria—, mientras el daño emergente reclamado iure hereditatis quedó firme. Este trabajo reconstruye el caso y su iter, sistematiza la ratio decidendi y sus consecuencias, sitúa la decisión en el vaivén jurisprudencial chileno de las dos últimas décadas y en el espejo comparado —donde Francia e Italia habrían transmitido con estos mismos hechos—, y cierra con un decálogo de litigación. La tesis, para quien demanda: el Código hace de los herederos los continuadores de la persona del causante, pero se sucede el patrimonio, no la biografía.

articles.title: The Rise and (Partial) Retreat of DEI Claims in Recruiting
articles.authors: Janet Xu; Reuben Hurst; Shanshan Liu
articles.abstract: In recent years, and especially after the 2020 Black Lives Matter protests, U.S. employers increasingly affirmed commitments to diversity, equity, and inclusion (DEI). Donald Trump's second administration has sought to reverse this shift. Yet how far pro-diversity language actually rose in employers' recruiting, and how much of that rise has since been undone, has not been established. Drawing on the universe of U.S. online job postings between January 2016 and February 2026-371.1 million postings from 2.7 million employers-we find that pro-diversity claims appeared in 7-12% of job postings until mid-2020, then rose 152% to a peak of 25.4% postings on the eve of the 2024 election. They fell 21% thereafter, to 19.9% by February 2026. Declines were sharper among federal contractors but proportionally similar for Democratic-and Republican-leaning employers. The reversal is unprecedented, yet partial: it has undone roughly a third of the post-2020 rise, but pro-diversity claims remain twice as common as they were pre-2020.

articles.title: “Ascending dragon or blasting the dragon vein?”: How Chinese netizens construct environmental meanings in digital publics
articles.authors: Yingnian Tao; Mark Ryan
articles.abstract: Corporations’ sustainability communication is increasingly challenged by digital publics. Yet research on how netizens contest corporate sustainability narratives, and thereby construct environmental meanings, remains largely confined to Western contexts. This study addresses this gap by examining Chinese netizens’ discursive responses to a controversial fireworks display in the Himalayas staged by international mountaineering brand Arc’teryx. Comments from the seven most popular Weibo posts were selected to compile a corpus (140,584 tokens),  and analysed through corpus-assisted discourse analysis, particularly keyword and concordance analysis. Findings show that netizens mobilise multiple meaning systems to express strong disapproval, including scientific ecological knowledge, perceptions of environmental governance failure, spiritual-cultural references, consumer action, and nationalism. These interconnected meaning systems converge around a distinctive feature of Chinese digital environmentalism: a nature-centred view of human-nature relations and harmony. The study extends understanding of digital environmentalism beyond Western contexts by showing that environmental meanings in Chinese digital spaces are place- and culture-based, intertwining ecological concerns with emotion, spiritual wellbeing, perceptions of justice, and national interests.

articles.title: Gender Bias and Stereotyping in Portrayals of Female Physicists: An International Analysis from 2019-2022
articles.authors: Rishika Porandla
articles.abstract: This research quantifies the presence of pervasive gender biases and discriminatory depictions within the field of physics through the analysis of media representations. Utilizing a dataset spanning 2019-2022 in Mali, India, Peru, and Singapore, the study employs natural language processing techniques to identify instances of biased language, particularly indicative of assumptions of biological determinism (BD) and childhood socialization (CS). Findings reveal more pronounced BD/CS-insinuating diction in lower HDI regions, ranging from 21% in Mali to 0.8% in Singapore. Female physicist representation in academic literature averaged 11.9%, with first authorship rates varying from 0.2% in Mali to 23.2% in Singapore. Negative depictions persisted despite a 27% increase in references to female physicists, highlighting the need for targeted interventions to counteract prejudice and foster inclusive environments within the physics community in order to promote gender equity and harness diverse perspectives in advancing research, development, and scientific innovation.

articles.title: Social network involvement in abortion care-seeking and abortion outcomes among a population-based sample in Nigeria
articles.authors: Selena Anjur-Dietrich; Funmilola Olaolorun; Elizabeth Omoluabi; Philip Anglewicz; Suzanne Bell
