The results showed that parents' awareness of child abuse was moderate but there were significant gaps in their knowledge of child abuse law, such as the Child Rights Act, and of non-physical forms of child abuse. It was reported that parents' knowledge of child abuse was significantly and positively related to their educational level and socioeconomic status was significantly related to their understanding and awareness of child protection issues. The study recommended that there is a need for enhanced parental education and alleviation of socioeconomic inequalities to boost child protection systems in Nigeria. It calls for increased public education initiatives, community outreach parenting education initiatives and policy-level support for prioritising the inclusion of child protection education within adult literacy, health promotion and social welfare initiatives.

articles.title: A qualitative analysis of the construction of responsible dog ownership in UK stakeholder policy and educational literature.
articles.authors: Carri Westgarth
articles.abstract: A variety of campaign and policy messages in the field of dog ownership and canine welfare centre upon the fundamental concept of ‘responsible’ ownership. However, what this is perceived to entail is unstudied, and important if the design of interventions to promote it are to be effective. Therefore, this study aimed to explore the meaning and stipulations of ‘Responsible Dog Ownership’ (RDO) within UK stakeholder literature focused on education of dog owners and the animal professionals who manage them. Primary literature concerning RDO and canine codes of practice in the UK was collected (10 documents), along with a google search for UK hits for ‘responsible dog ownership’ (16 documents). An inductive thematic analysis was performed on the 26 documents. Owners were described as having a duty, requiring commitment, to provide personalised care for the dog, by seeking out the advice of qualified professionals. Actions were required to keep the dog under control, healthy (physically and behaviourally), in a suitable environment, with appropriate identification, and not allowing the dog to foul. Perceived responsibility of the owner extended to carefully considering where and how they source a dog. Clarity of current guidance on RDO is challenging due to the advice to do different things depending on the dog and context. Owners and the professionals they seek advice from are also failing to meet the clear stipulation to use reward-based training techniques and not use aversive, punishment-based methods. This study for the first time distils multiple varied guidance into one clear set of recommendations, including a suggested ‘Are you a responsible dog owner?’ checklist. This can be used as a framework by policymakers and educators to construct more detailed localised guidance around the duties and expected behaviours of dog owners in regard to UK law and wider societal perceptions.

articles.title: From National Accounting to Macroeconomic Flows
articles.authors: Woongki Lee
articles.abstract: This study develops a macroeconomic framework that integrates the household, business, government, and foreign sectors. At the center of the analysis is the circulation of value and funds across the economy through cash flows associated with issuer-holder financing. The framework clarifies the relations among major macroeconomic aggregates. In particular, by treating money creation as part of value supply, it provides a systematic basis for analyzing how monetary operations affect transactions across sectors.

articles.title: Firm Optimization across Capital Forms
articles.authors: Woongki Lee
articles.abstract: This study derives a model of firm optimization across capital forms and incorporates the resulting optimality conditions into asset pricing. The structure of the problem depends on how profitability is modeled. When profitability is endogenous, optimization is grounded in production decisions; when profitability is exogenous, it is organized around operating profit. These alternative assumptions yield two asset pricing frameworks, each with a factor representation derived from the firm’s decision margins. By relating these representations to established pricing factors, the study provides a structured economic basis for reinterpreting established factors through firm optimization.

articles.title: A General Framework for Equity Valuation
articles.authors: Woongki Lee
articles.abstract: This study develops a general framework for equity valuation that unifies a wide range of valuation models within a coherent structure. It is built on a reformulation of key equity-related variables that preserves their economic functions, together with three exact identities that capture the fundamental links among them. These identities make it possible to derive valuation models under both fixed and revising expectations. The resulting models include not only familiar formulations but also new ones, underscoring the value of this approach for analyzing equity valuation.

articles.title: Administrative Production of Disaster Vulnerability: Explaining Persistent Infrastructure Vulnerability through Administrative Learning in the Himalayan Region
articles.authors: Vishal Thakur
articles.abstract: Public administrations in disaster-prone low- and middle-income countries face a persistent governance question: do institutions learn from one disaster to the next, or does experience fail to translate into revised policy and practice? This study addresses that question through the Administrative Production of Disaster Vulnerability (APDV), a policy-cycle framework tracing how vulnerability is reproduced or corrected across planning, budgeting, maintenance, and reconstruction, applied to Himachal Pradesh, India. PWD infrastructure damage across two successive monsoons (2023, 2025) correlates strongly across eleven districts (Pearson r = 0.819, p = 0.002; Spearman ρ = 0.882, p < 0.001), with Mandi and Shimla the highest-damage districts both years and state-wide damage rising 55.5% despite reconstruction spending. APDV distinguishes chronic vulnerability (Mandi, Shimla), a failure to convert risk into revised practice, from acute vulnerability (Chamba, Una), limited anticipatory capacity. Findings support district-specific resilience planning and identify administrative learning capacity as a distinct governance challenge.

articles.title: Pseudo-Populism as Strategic Political Communication: A Comparative Analysis of Electoral Communication and Voting Behavior in the Philippines, Brazil, India and Türkiye
articles.authors: Shaina Tingga
articles.abstract:
The growing prevalence of pseudo-populism has reshaped political campaigns across
developing countries, where candidates increasingly employ people-centered rhetoric,
anti-elite narratives, and emotionally driven messaging to secure electoral support without
consistently advancing policies aligned with the public interest. This study examines the
influence of pseudo-populist political messaging on the voting behavior of electorates in
developing democracies through a secondary quantitative data analysis. Drawing upon
existing datasets and findings from reputable electoral surveys and political behavior studies,
the research investigates the relationship between exposure to pseudo-populist appeals and
voting preferences while considering the roles of political trust, media consumption,
education, and socioeconomic conditions. Rather than assuming that voters are inherently
susceptible to populist narratives, the study explores how structural and institutional factors
shape citizens' electoral decisions. By synthesizing quantitative evidence from multiple
developing countries, the research aims to identify common patterns in voter behavior and
assess the broader implications of pseudo-populism for democratic accountability and
electoral integrity. The findings are expected to contribute to the expanding literature on
populism by providing a comparative perspective on how strategic political communication
influences electoral outcomes and by offering insights that may support civic education
initiatives, evidence-based policymaking, and the promotion of informed democratic
participation.

articles.title: The Importance of a Clear and Unambiguous Estimand for Hilbert Problems (or Any Other Empirical Research)
articles.authors: Daniel Major-Smith
articles.abstract: "Hilbert problems" are a great idea to galvanise research in the scientific study of religion, yet how do we go about answering these – or any other scientific questions of interest – empirically? This "meta-scientific" methodological aspect of research was largely missing from the original Hilbert problems and the 10 year follow-ups. Here, I want to focus on the importance of a clear and unambiguous estimand – the target quantity a study wants to estimate – and how this shapes all aspects of research, from synthesising existing research, data collection, statistical analysis and interpretation of results. At present, this is often vague or left unspecified, yet making progress on these Hilbert problems requires that researchers can clearly and unambiguously answer the question: "What is your estimand?"

articles.title: A General Framework for Tax Shield Valuation
articles.authors: Woongki Lee
articles.abstract: This study develops a general valuation framework that delivers internally consistent valuations for all forms of firm capital and for the tax shield associated with their combination. This consistency is achieved by incorporating the interdependence among the components of a levered firm’s cash flows. The study reexamines classical tax shield valuation models within the same framework and clarifies the conditions under which each arises as a special case. A central finding is that these models depend not only on stated assumptions but on an implicit assumption that debt is risk-free. This hidden assumption is more restrictive than it may appear.

articles.title: Cellular automata coupled with Bayesian MCMC reveal the evolutionary history of diffusion processes
articles.authors: Takuya Takahashi; Nico Neureiter; Geneviève Hannes; Peter Ranacher
articles.abstract: Spatial diffusion is a fundamental topic in geographic information science, relevant to various phenomena such as urban sprawl, pathogen dispersal, and the spread of innovation. When studying these processes, we often work with incomplete data. We may know the geographic distribution of the phenomenon at some specific points in time, while the full history of its diffusion is unknown. Alternatively, we may have data for certain regions but not the entire area where the diffusion occurs. We present sBread, a novel Bayesian model which infers the history of a diffusion process from temporally or spatially incomplete data. Like a stochastic cellular automaton, sBread uses probabilistic local updating rules to model how the geographic distribution of a phenomenon changes over time through local interactions. However, unlike cellular automata, which focus on forward simulation starting from a known initial state, sBread employs Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) to sample multiple plausible diffusion histories from the posterior distribution, given the observed data. Thus, sBread reconstructs the most likely past histories consistent with any observed data. We apply sBread to both simulated data and a case study on the diffusion of Indo-European languages in South America, which displaced the indigenous languages following European colonisation.

articles.title: Price Setting, Free Riding, and Equilibrium
articles.authors: Woongki Lee
articles.abstract: We analyze strategic interaction among investors by distinguishing between price taking and price setting. The analysis shows that as price setting becomes more prevalent, equilibrium prices fall. Because this lower price benefits price takers as well as price setters, price taking can be understood as free riding on price setting. The gains from the lower price are distributed more heavily toward price takers. This asymmetry creates relative-comparison concerns, which can distort incentives and discourage price setting even when it would increase aggregate utility. We examine this problem through a pricing game and derive implications for strategic behavior and equilibrium outcomes.

articles.title: A Macroeconomic Theory of Value Conversion
articles.authors: Woongki Lee
articles.abstract: This study develops a theory of value conversion in which conversion depends on realized consumption growth. By governing value conversion over time, consumption growth becomes a key determinant of output’s market value and a driver of broader economic expansion. The theory differs from conventional macroeconomic frameworks in two respects. First, it redefines production as an internal technological process combined with an external valuation process, so market-valued output depends not only on production but also on converting latent value into market value. Second, it reinterprets macroeconomic relations by treating household consumption as the starting point of causality.

articles.title: Comparative Analysis of Employee Compensation in Allegheny County, Pennsylvania, Before and After the COVID-19 Pandemic (2019-2020)
articles.authors: Sohel Sarwar; Robert King; Guelord Gabibulu
articles.abstract: The COVID-19 pandemic, which commenced in early 2020, significantly affected worldwide economies, labor markets, and employment conditions. Allegheny County, home to Pittsburgh and its surrounding areas, provides a critical case study examining how the pandemic affected local government employee compensation. Paired t-tests of salary data between 2019 and 2020 (pre- and post-COVID-19 pandemic) demonstrate a significant increase in average gross salaries for all employees of Allegheny County. While overall employee gross pays increased, the distribution of salaries became less concentrated, with a greater emphasis on higher-earning individuals. Within specific job categories, Nursing Assistants had a significantly greater salary in 2020; however, Deputy Sheriffs showed no significant change. Nursing Assistants likely worked more overtime to support the healthcare response to the pandemic. Law enforcement officers typically receive paid overtime to provide security for public events such as professional football, baseball, hockey games, and public concerts. With restrictions on these events, law enforcement officers likely faced reductions in their overtime pay in 2020. Forecasting employee salaries from 2023 to 2027 revealed a wide range in the intervals, reflecting increasing uncertainty further in the future. Due to potential variability, the forecasting results were, therefore, inconclusive.

articles.title: BLACK LGBTI+ PENTECOSTAL FAMILIES AND AFFECT OF RESISTANCE: DECOLONIAL PERSPECTIVES FROM THE BRAZILIAN PERIPHERY
articles.authors: Átila Augusto dos Santos
articles.abstract: This paper presents key results from doctoral research in Religious Studies on Black LGBTI+ Pentecostal families in Brazil, conceptualized herein as quilombo families (famílias aquilombadas), viewed as ethical-affective expressions of resistance within the religious field. Utilizing an intersectional, decolonial, and affective framework, engaging critical scholars such as Joe Coyle, E. Patrick Johnson, and Beatriz Nascimento, the study deploys the metaphor of the Pentecostal quilombo to analyze inclusive churches as urban territories of affection, freedom, and the restoration of social bonds. Grounded in semi-structured qualitative interviews with 33 Black LGBTI+ individuals and families across inclusive congregations, the findings reveal how these family units challenge traditional Christian heterocisnormative dogmas and articulate a counter-hegemonic spirituality. This framework demonstrates both the transformative potential of affective-political reconstruction and the structural limits of inclusion when racial, moral, and gender hierarchies remain unbroken.

articles.title: Guerreiro Ramos and sociological  reduction: dilemmas and prospects for Brazilian Economic Development
articles.authors: Isaias Albertin de Moraes
articles.abstract: This   article   examines   Alberto   Guerreiro   Ramos’s  contributions  to  understanding  the  dilemmas  and  prospects  of  Brazilian  economic  development,  em-phasizing  the  originality  and  relevance  of  his  thought.  The methodological approach is based on a bibliographic review, aiming to identifying the State of the Art on the subject.  The  analysis  is  structured  around  four  axes:  i)   biographical   context,   ii)   theoretical-methodological   foundations,  iii)  critiques  of  structural  obstacles,  and  iv)  proposals  for  a  national-developmental  project  in  Brazil.  The  study  concludes  that  Guerreiro  Ramos’s  work  rep-resents a landmark in Critical Sociology and Sociology of Development, in Brazil and should be further explored in contemporary economic studies.

articles.title: Causal Beliefs about the Economic Effects of AI among Politicians and the Public
articles.authors: Sophie Borwein; Beatrice Magistro
articles.abstract: Political disagreement over artificial intelligence may reflect different expectations about its economic consequences or judgments about appropriate government responses. Using parallel surveys of local Canadian politicians (n=1,100) and the public (n=5,510), and latent class analysis, we identify four causal theories of AI’s economic effects. Politicians are much more likely to view AI as complementing workers, while the public more often sees it a substitutionary, even after compositional adjustment. Causal theories further organize policy preferences: those with substitutionary beliefs favour policies restricting AI, while those with complementary beliefs favour adaptation. Yet politicians and citizens with similar causal theories also emphasize different policies, and these within-class differences account for a substantial share of policy gaps. Elite-public policy disagreement therefore reflects both different economic diagnoses and responses to shared diagnoses. Finally, politicians in communities shaped by past economic shocks hold more substitutionary views, suggesting political responses may change as AI’s distributional consequences become visible.

articles.title: Intelligence as a Partial Order: Why g Compresses a Structure It Cannot Rank
articles.authors: Aaron Hoegn
articles.abstract:
The general intelligence factor "g" is one of the most, if not the most replicated constructs in
psychology, and its predictive validity is not in question. The question here is its interpretation. The
positive manifold is the current popular proof that intelligence is a scalar, a quantity along which
people can in principle be ranked. This review argues that such an inference is wrong. Brains that
have similar functionality differ significantly in architecture, and the properties they differ on
(efficiency, specialization, cost, resilience) are particular trade-offs which form a Pareto front
instead of a single optimum. On this front each different architecture that "excels" in different
environments is incomparable to the others, as ranking them would require privileging a specific set
of abilities to reward, and for human life none is favored. Intelligence, thus, is better described as a
partial order rather than a line. Ranking remains legitimate between widely separated scores, where
a whole-life average lets a large gap dominate; within a band of equal g, it does not. This account
returns a prediction a scalar model cannot make: equally scoring individuals should cross over in
performance as demands change. It also names the core assumption whose failure would reinstate g
- that for a human life, no environment is privileged.

articles.title: The Value Core of Student Sustainability: Verification Methodology (Author’s English Translation)
articles.authors: Inna Gazieva
articles.abstract:
In the context of a deep transformation of the socio-cultural environment and fragmentation of value orientations, the task of moving from a declarative description of youth values to the identification of their stable, behaviorally realizable core is actualized. Existing approaches often fix only normative ideals, ignoring the gap between attitudes and actual practices, which reduces the effectiveness of social design. The purpose of this study is to identify the value core of student youth's resilience, based on the results of an analysis of the degree of interiorization of values among student youth. The methodology of the work is based on the author's four-component empirical model, which evaluates value according to the parameters: "ideal", "significance", "readiness" and "action". The empirical basis was based on data from a mass survey (n = 3864) of students from leading Russian universities. Spearman's correlation analysis was used to identify structural relationships. The criterion for selection to the value core was the high intra-value consistency of all four components and the presence of stable inter-value clusters. It is revealed that the stable core is formed by state-patriotic (patriotism, service to the Fatherland, historical memory) and spiritual and moral values (family, charity, priority of the spiritual), characterized by high internal integration. The values of personal growth and universal norms (rights, justice, health) remain predominantly declarative, demonstrating the gap between ideal and action.

Author's English translation of the article published in Russian: Society and Security Insights, 2026, vol. 9, no. 2, pp. 104-121. DOI: 10.14258/ssi(2026)2-06. The Russian original is the version of record. Archived translation: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.21828746

articles.title: Inventory and Evaluation of Metrics for a Sustainability Indicator Framework in the Northeast U.S. Food System
articles.authors: Christopher Donovan; Tessa Lawler; Isabella Loconte; Polly Ericksen; Gillian Galford; Matthew McIntosh
articles.abstract:
CONTEXT: Food systems support the nutritional needs and livelihoods of a growing population. Sustainably managing food systems within social and ecological bounds requires accessible and accurate data. Sustainability indicator frameworks provide a structure for curating these data, and regional approaches are particularly relevant for decision making at the state and local levels.
    
OBJECTIVE: To assess data availability, quality, and trends in the Northeast food system, we conducted an inventory and analysis of publicly available datasets representing five dimensions of sustainability.
    
METHODS: Data were sourced from federal, academic, and non-profit repositories, and metrics were selected to best represent the region at the county level. We used correlations and spatial regressions to assess interactions among metrics and trends over time.
    
RESULTS AND CONCLUSIONS: We found key gaps in the Economic, Production, and Social dimensions. Some data were only available at state level, while monitoring for some metrics began recently, precluding analysis of trends over time. We identified 62 metrics to represent the framework indicators, but only 31 were available at the county level with multiple time points. Of these, half were improving, and one third were declining. Trends in the Production and Economic dimensions were neutral to positive, while the other dimensions were mixed.

SIGNIFICANCE: Access to data is critical in improving regional food system sustainability. The gaps we identified should serve as a road map in developing monitoring programs. The curation of datasets that are consistent, interoperable, and accessible, is crucial in monitoring food systems and developing policies and interventions to support sustainability.

articles.title: Predictability in Strategic Asset Allocation
articles.authors: Woongki Lee
articles.abstract: The benchmark chosen under strategic asset allocation serves as the fund’s long-term target, while the actual portfolio composition fluctuates around that target over time. When active managers adjust portfolio weights in response to forecasts of benchmark returns, return predictability becomes valuable because it creates opportunities for effective short-term tactical adjustment. Predictability therefore enters utility as a distinct source of benefit. This role of predictability is not captured by the traditional mean-variance framework. The study therefore extends that framework by introducing predictability directly into the analysis. The resulting mean-variance-predictability framework defines the benchmark choice problem and reshapes the associated pricing relation.

articles.title: Price Dynamics and Investor Mobility
articles.authors: Woongki Lee
articles.abstract: This study develops an equilibrium framework for asset price dynamics under heterogeneous investor beliefs. It shows that price changes admit three equivalent representations, each linked to a distinct channel: group dominance, order imbalance, and participation tilt. As an application of the third representation, the study introduces investor mobility as a measure of how actively investors shift their participation across belief groups over time. Higher mobility indicates greater changes in investor composition and, for a given level of forecast dispersion, larger price movements. The study implements this concept empirically by constructing and analyzing a market-wide series of investor mobility.

articles.title: SOBRE LOS REGÍMENES POLÍTICOS EN EL MUNDO Y SU EVOLUCIÓN (1900-2025)
articles.authors: RICARDO DE LA PEÑA MENA
articles.abstract: Este ensayo analiza la evolución histórica de los regímenes políticos mundiales desde 1900 hasta 2025 empleando las bases de datos del proyecto Varieties of Democracy (V-Dem). Revisa los fundamentos teóricos de la democracia y la autocracia, destacando que la tercera ola de autocratización contemporánea no opera mediante golpes de Estado tradicionales, sino a través de una erosión interna y sutil de los contrapesos institucionales. Mediante índices como el de regímenes en el mundo y el de democracia electoral, la investigación examina la distribución bimodal global, las disparidades regionales y la correlación entre elecciones competitivas y garantías liberales, concluyendo que la preservación de la libertad requiere instituciones sólidas y una actuación institucional temprana.

articles.title: Who Reaches the NBA Draft? Dual Concentration in College and High-School Pathways (2016–2026)
articles.authors: Dharit Shah
articles.abstract: Public debate about who reaches the NBA draft still mixes anecdote about prep factories, suburban publics, and “kids from nowhere.” We assemble a complete finishing-school panel of 656 NBA draft picks (2016–2026)—typed into US public, local private, elite prep, and international pathways—and document dual concentration at both ends of the same file: Duke and Kentucky alone account for 9.5% of picks, the top ten college priors for 25.0%, and four elite prep feeders (Montverde, IMG, Oak Hill, Link) for 8.5%. Only 34.0% of picks finish at a US public high school; elite prep (24.8%) and local private (20.3%) together account for 45.1%, and with international pathways (20.9%) nearly two-thirds of draftees do not finish at a US public school. Formal indices sharpen the picture: the 656 picks trace to an effective field of only 83 prior institutions, and high-school feeder concentration nearly doubles between 2016–2019 and 2023–2026 (top-5 feeder share 9.0% → 16.9%; effective feeders 145 → 83) as purpose-built academies such as Link and Overtime Elite consolidate the pathway. As a supporting ecological finding—not a claim about family poverty—under a transparent rule (public finishing school in a Census place below 0.85× state median household income), 60 / 656 = 9.1% of picks follow a clearly poor-town public path (Layer A). Broader below-state public towns raise the share to 17.8% (Layer B); private/prep campuses in poor Census places (13.6%, Layer C) are context only. Place income is an ecological proxy, not family income; finishing school is not the full developmental pathway.

articles.title: Putting Street Justice into Practice: Insights from London Boroughs
articles.authors: Enrica Papa; Sabina Cioboata
articles.abstract:
Street transformations are not merely technical responses to climate, health and liveability goals. They are political interventions that redistribute public space, mobility, environmental quality and decision-making authority. Yet justice rarely appears as an explicit concept in everyday street planning. This paper investigates why justice is invoked as a principle but seldom used as an operational category, how it nevertheless shapes practice, and which institutional and political conditions determine its influence. Conducted within the 32-partner Horizon Europe JUST STREETS programme, the study combines documentary analysis with 10 semi-structured interviews undertaken between October and December 2025 with practitioners working across several London borough contexts. We develop a street-specific framework integrating distributive, procedural, recognition and epistemic justice across streets’ dual functions as links and places and across the transformation project cycle.
The findings show that practitioners usually articulate justice through administratively established concepts such as safety, accessibility, health, equality, air quality and inclusion. These concepts connect more readily than justice to statutory duties, departmental responsibilities, funding criteria, technical standards and measurable outcomes. Explicit justice language becomes most salient when practitioners question the inherited allocation of street space, challenge car-centred assumptions or adjudicate between competing claims. Justice is therefore not absent from practice, but operates principally as a normative basis for determining whose needs should receive priority.
Its dimensions are, however, unevenly institutionalised. Distributive and recognition concerns shape spatial prioritisation, kerbside reallocation, accessibility and child-centred design. Procedural justice remains largely confined to consultation rather than shared authority, while epistemic justice is constrained by the continuing dominance of professional and quantitative evidence. This unevenness is politically consequential: more specific policy language can enable intervention while obscuring redistribution, normalising inherited inequalities and weakening accountability. We conclude that street justice must be embedded throughout problem definition, design, implementation and evaluation, with explicit scrutiny of benefits, burdens, participation, recognition and evidentiary authority.

articles.title: Ethical Influence of Behaviourally Targeted Political Advertising on Young  Adults in Edo State, Nigeria
articles.authors: Adriel Ekozin; Yamah Abdul; Faith Ozikor Amah
articles.abstract:
The study was designed to investigate the ethical implications of behaviourally targeted political advertisements on young adults in Edo State, Nigeria, within the context of the rising trend of digital platforms and personal data use in political communications. The study was guided by Privacy and Surveillance Theory, which explains how personal data
are gathered, tracked, and exploited, often against personal autonomy, privacy and democratic choice. The study used survey research as its design, and data were collected from young adults between the ages of 18 and 35 from Etsako West Local Government Area of Edo State, Nigeria. Using the Taro Yamane formula, the study established a sample size of 399, from which 396 valid copies of questionnaire were retrieved for analysis using SPSS. The findings revealed that behaviourally targeted political advertisements are not effective in promoting political participation and that the influence of the advertisements on political opinions is limited. Nevertheless, there are ethical concerns associated with behaviourally targeted political advertising. The major ethical concern was related to the invasion of privacy by political actors. Therefore, the study concluded that behaviourally targeted political advertising has a weak impact on the opinions of young adults but has ethical concerns related to privacy and data misuse. It recommended data protection and digital campaign regulations and the promotion of transparent and credible political communication.

articles.title: Seeing Amsterdam through Google Maps: Uneven visibility and crowd-based mapping
articles.authors: Reza Ardekani Shaker; Justus Uitermark
articles.abstract: How is the city represented and shaped through Google Maps? Through a computational analysis of over 106,000 places in Amsterdam, this paper examines how Google Maps represents and creates urban hierarchies and differences. Drawing on critical cartography and platform studies, we examine how Google Maps’ affordances and modes of crowd-sourced data collection generate uneven platform geographies: consumption-oriented places, scenes, and neighbourhoods stand out while others are pushed to the background. However, we also show that Google Maps intervenes into processes of segregation and gentrification in complex ways; we do not find straightforward platform-promoted displacement. Through a granular analysis of one street, we show that there are synergistic connections between places that may seem to be in competition and that different communities use Google Maps to appraise the street in culturally specific ways. Both our city-wide and street-level analyses demonstrate that Google Maps functions as a constitutive urban infrastructure that creates platform geographies by spawning hierarchies of visibility and marking differences.

articles.title: The City Multiple: Comparing Geographies of Digital Visibility across Google Maps, Instagram, Facebook, and TikTok
articles.authors: Reza Ardekani Shaker; Justus Uitermark
articles.abstract: Digital platforms have become key geospatial infrastructures through which cities are discovered, experienced, and evaluated. Whereas the extant literature has often focused on single platforms or assumed an undifferentiated platform urbanism, we know very little about how different platforms produce distinct geographies of urban visibility. To address this lacuna, we examine the spatially differentiated regimes of visibility that emerge when platforms mediate urban environments. In doing so, we distinguish between three dimensions of platforms’ geographies of digital visibility: (1) spatial inequality—how each platform distributes visibility across places; (2) spatial articulation—how platform visibilities map onto local urban geographies; and (3) spatial representation—the kinds of places and content that achieve visibility on each platform. Combining computational, geographic, and interpretive methods, we analyse how 6,682 eating and drinking establishments in Amsterdam are represented on TikTok, Instagram, Google Maps, and Facebook, and find strikingly weak correlations between their visibility on the four platforms. We find that each platform produces distinct structures of unequal visibility, with algorithmic-discovery platforms concentrating visibility more intensely than review-based systems. Neighbourhood-level analyses further show that platform-specific spatial articulations correspond to the gentrification and touristification of specific areas. Our findings contribute to the literatures on digital geography and platform urbanism by demonstrating that digital platforms generate multiple instantiations of the same city.

articles.title: Assessment of Gender Digital Divide and Participation in Public Discourse  Online
articles.authors: Adriel Ekozin; Onyeoma Osife-Kurex; Igbafe A. Alonge
articles.abstract:
The study assessed the gender digital divide and participation in online public discourse among internet users in Benin City, Edo State, Nigeria. The objectives of the study were to examine the level of digital access among males and females, identify factors contributing to the gender digital divide, determine patterns of participation in online public discourse, examine challenges limiting women’s participation and assess the implications of the gender digital divide on democracy and public discourse. The study adopted the Digital Divide Theory as its theoretical framework. A descriptive survey
research design was employed, while the population comprised internet users in Benin City. A sample size of 400 respondents was selected using a multistage sampling technique involving stratified and simple random sampling methods. Questionnaire served as the instrument for data collection, while data were analysed using frequency
tables and simple percentages. Findings revealed that males had greater digital access and participated more actively in online public discourse than females. The study also found that poor infrastructure, high cost of data, lack of digital literacy, cultural restrictions, online harassment, and cyberbullying were major factors contributing to the gender
digital divide and limiting women’s participation in online discussions. The study concluded that the gender digital divide negatively affects inclusive democratic participation and reduces women’s visibility and influence in online public discourse. The study recommended improved digital infrastructure, affordable internet access, enhanced digital literacy programmes for women, and stronger measures against online harassment.

articles.title: The affective bases of socialized preferences
articles.authors: Tamkinat Rauf
articles.abstract: Research on family socialization suggests that the drivers of preferences (such as values and attitudes) are rooted in early life experiences. But the cognitive process that connects past experiences to present thought processes is not well understood or theorized. In this article, I draw on recent cognitive science research on the role of affectively-valenced memories in shaping preferences, and the sensitivity of the involved cognitive processes to top-of-mind concerns. Revisiting socialization theories in light of these ideas suggests that while rooted in affective memories, socialized preferences are results of probabilistic predictions of the brain and are malleable to priming. Across 3 related studies, including a preregistered survey experiment, I examine the empirical case of socialization of inclinations towards parenthood.

articles.title: Same Facts, Different Meanings: Factual Information, Interpretation, and Attitude Change
articles.authors: Martín Opertti
articles.abstract:
A key puzzle in the political information literature is why factual information reliably updates citizens’ beliefs about the fact in question but rarely shifts downstream political attitudes. Using two preregistered survey experiments (N ≈ 3,250) covering eleven issues across economic indicators and misstatements by prominent political figures, this paper makes two contributions. First, we test whether the muted effect of factual information on downstream attitudes holds for outcomes that are less entrenched and more proximate to the information than
those tested in prior work—such as economic evaluations and perceptions of politicians’ honesty and competence—and find that even these outcomes respond only modestly. Second, we develop and empirically test a framework of six adjacent belief dimensions—regarding causes,
relevance, and intent—through which factual information may be reinterpreted in ways that reshape its political meaning. We find evidence of adjacent belief updating, although concentrated on specific dimensions rather than widespread. The strongest finding is that individuals
who learn that a favored politician made an inaccurate claim concede the inaccuracy but shift toward viewing the statement as figurative, with sizable effects across two independent studies. Importantly, where adjacent belief adjustment occurs, its direction is contingent on individuals’ predispositions. Uncongenial information triggers adjustment that attenuates the political implications of the fact, while congenial information triggers no such adjustment or small shifts in the opposite direction. Together, the results illustrate how parallel trends in factual accuracy can coexist with divergent trends in how those facts are politically interpreted.

articles.title: When Government Uses AI: Experimental Evidence of Selective Trust Decline and Algorithmic Nimbyism
articles.authors: Daniel Juhász Vigild; Andreas Bjerre-Nielsen; Laust Hvas Mortensen; Vedran Sekara
articles.abstract:
Artificial intelligence is increasingly being used in government, changing the ways in which citizens
relate to public institutions. One important aspect, the impact of AI on trust in public institutions, has
been the subject of substantial efforts that document an "AI penalty" on trust in public institutions when
they use AI. However, little is known about why or how such a penalty arises. In two preregistered survey
experiments (N=6 084) we measure the effect of AI on trust across four real-life use cases of governmental
AI. First, we find large differences across the four domains—disclosing AI usage in social services
and health care settings decreases trust, while trust is unaffected for policing and unemployment use
cases. Second, we experimentally test a specific mechanism (algorithmic nimbyism) that considers personal
exposure to the decision-making outcomes as a driver of the negative impact of AI on trust. Despite
not finding any causal evidence for the notion of algorithmic nimbyism, we used rich administrative data
on survey participants’ medical history and labour force participation to explore heterogeneous treatment
effects that revealed descriptive and suggestive evidence of algorithmic nimbyism. Future work
could consider further exploring the combination of experimental and observational data to empirically
examine explanations of the impact AI has on relations between citizens and public institutions.

articles.title: One Policy, Many Publics: Central Bank Communication and the National Politics of Trust
articles.authors: Björn Bremer; Lucio Baccaro
articles.abstract: Central bank decisions have become politically contested. In response, central banks communicate more with the public, since their effectiveness rests on public trust. Yet whether they reach ordinary citizens is largely unknown. We exploit the European Central Bank’s unexpected announcement of the Pandemic Emergency Purchase Programme (PEPP) during the fieldwork of a March 2020 survey in Germany and Italy. Our results show that the same decisive intervention was rewarded only where it aligned with the perceived national interest: in Italy, trust in the ECB rose, strongest among news-followers and the left; in Germany, trust in the ECB did not move at all, even as trust in national institutions surged. Preferences for central bank goal independence moved in neither country. Citizens thus notice exceptional monetary policy decisions, but their responses are mediated by national interests and discourses, with asymmetric consequences for a central bank that makes one policy for many publics.

articles.title: Legal Threats and Online Dissent: Evidence from Social Media Regulation in Turkey
articles.authors: Arvind Magesan; Juan S. Morales; Arieda Muço
articles.abstract:
We study how legal threats to social media platforms shape online political communication. We exploit the sharp implementation of a 2020 Turkish law that required social media companies
to establish local offices and provide user data to the government on request. Assembling a panel of over 700 Twitter users and 7 million posts, we use a differences-in-differences design
to compare dissenters, individuals publicly critical of the reform when announced, to other groups unlikely to be affected, such as celebrities. We find that dissenters and political exiles
post 15-20 percent fewer tweets following implementation, and engagement with their content falls sharply. These short-run chilling effects emerge despite limited platform compliance, indicating
that anticipated enforcement risk, rather than actual enforcement, drives the effect. In the long run, the chilling effects dissipate. Our findings suggest that states can govern online
speech indirectly, by regulating platforms rather than users, but that such effects may be self-limiting in the absence of visible enforcement.

articles.title: Coding choices and short-sequence artefacts undermine claims of a conventional Palaeolithic sign system – a comment on Bentz and Dutkiewicz (2026)
articles.authors: Alexander Koplenig
articles.abstract: In this comment, I show that methodological and statistical flaws undermine the central conclusions of Bentz and Dutkiewicz (2026).

articles.title: Children’s Art Experiences: Interactive Digital Art
articles.authors: Emilie Bossens; Bieke Zaman; Priscilla Van Even
articles.abstract: Art invites exploratory, multisensory, emotionally rich and context-shaped forms of engagement, yet these experiences are sometimes difficult to capture. This challenge becomes especially pronounced with children, whose meaning-making relies on movement, sensation and play, rather than verbal reflection or evaluative judgements. Because most cultural spaces are designed around adult norms and expectations, children’s distinctive ways of engaging with art often remain overlooked or under supported. This raises questions about how cultural settings can better accommodate what children themselves experience as meaningful aesthetic encounters. In this chapter, we first review research on children’s art engagement from perceptual, cognitive, emotional, bodily, spatial, and social perspectives. We then present a case-study of 215 children aged 3 to 12 years old engaging with an interactive digital artwork at a family arts festival. Through systematic observations, we identify three recurring interaction patterns, demonstrate how social dynamics and contextual factors shape children’s unfolding engagement, and show how children exert agency through their exploratory actions and the artwork’s responsive features. Building on these insights, the chapter concludes with future directions for art research and practice, calling for child-centered methodologies, stronger attention to embodiment and emotion, and closer art-science collaboration to better support meaningful art experiences for children.

articles.title: Predatism and Predocracy: A Conceptual Framework for Emergent Predator-Prey Politics
articles.authors: Kenneth Syring
articles.abstract: This paper introduces the theoretical constructs of predatism and predocracy to describe an emerging authoritarian ideology and its corresponding mode of governance. Predatism is defined as a convergent far-right ideology from the fusion of white nationalism, male supremacism, Christian nationalism, anti-democratic populism, and online conspiracy subcultures into an increasingly unified worldview. This consolidation is argued to be uniquely catalyzed by the contemporary digital ecosystem, in which the dynamics of moral contagion confer a systematic transmission advantage on predator-prey framings, accelerating the migration of disparate fringe conspiracy theories and hate ideologies into the political mainstream. Within this context, distinct grievances coalesce around a shared moral logic, in which the in-group views itself as the collective victim of status theft, justifying a predatory social dynamic which celebrates cruelty and domination as both a righteous self-defense and a seek-to-destroy offense. When this movement captures state institutions, it establishes a predocracy: a system characterized by visible cruelty as a tool of rule, the weaponization of law against opponents, systemic impunity for the in-group, and the spectacular reinforcement of hierarchy through routine public displays of domination. By distinguishing predatism from classical fascism, this paper argues that predocracy is a distinct 21st-century phenomenon driven by the affective mobilization of its online base, the gamification of state violence, and the consumption of out-group anguish as in-group catharsis.

articles.title: Rural-Urban Differences in Student Journalism Performance Metrics
articles.authors: Kallen Zhou; Benjamin Cooley
articles.abstract: This paper examines rural-urban differences in student journalism performance among higher education institution (HEI) student produced news outlets. With journalism quality frameworks, three article-level dimensions serve as comparisons: textual distinctiveness, Critical Information Needs (CIN) coverage, and localeness. Using a dataset of approximately 15,000 student articles, we utilized outlet-level soft cosine similarity, validated LLM-assisted binary coding, and logistic regression. Our results suggest three findings within our dataset: 1) the textual patterns of articles are not strongly structured by locale, 2) rural articles had substantially higher descriptive rates and odds of addressing a CIN than urban articles, and 3) rural articles had higher descriptive rates and odds of being coded as local. These results suggest that student journalism’s local-news role varies more in their civic ability, corroborating that being locally engaged is not synchronous with addressing CINs and that rural-urban differences could extend beyond institutional capacities into HEIs informational role in surrounding communities.

articles.title: Aid Cuts and the Politics of Refugee Hosting
articles.authors: Mae MacDonald
articles.abstract:
In 2025, U.S. aid cuts drove the fastest contraction of foreign aid on record.
These cuts threaten the cooperative arrangement underpinning the refugee regime,
in which low- and middle-income countries host most refugees while high-income
countries finance assistance. As host communities lose aid-related jobs, services,
and infrastructure, does citizens’ willingness to host refugees decline? I examine
this question in Kenya using two nationwide surveys, a high-frequency panel and
vignette experiment near Kakuma camp, and 52 interviews with local leaders,
all conducted as the cuts unfolded. Support for hosting declined in refugee-
hosting areas as economic losses and insecurity grew, driven by households that
lost camp-based benefits. By contrast, national support remained stable, and
exploratory evidence suggests that humanitarian concern limited backlash. Yet
because refugee policy often responds to pressures in hosting regions, continued
cuts may weaken the local foundations of asylum in the countries that host most
of the world’s refugees.

articles.title: Chaotic Dynamics of Asset Prices
articles.authors: Woongki Lee
articles.abstract: This study offers a new perspective on asset price dynamics by showing that seemingly irregular price movements are governed by a common structure. It separates the forces underlying these movements and develops three equivalent representations that make this structure more transparent. A central construct in the study is a time-varying parameter that classifies price dynamics into interpretable regimes. In the empirical analysis of aggregate stock prices, periods of higher parameter values, indicating more turbulent regimes, align closely with major economic downturns. This evidence supports the parameter’s use as a diagnostic tool for detecting regime shifts and periods of macro-financial turbulence.

articles.title: Arbitrage-Induced Mispricing
articles.authors: Woongki Lee
articles.abstract: Contrary to common belief, arbitrageurs and mean-variance optimizers are not direct counterparts in trading. Their portfolio positions may instead overlap, amplifying fluctuations in aggregate demand for assets with particular positioning signals and pushing prices away from fundamental values. These deviations, in turn, create additional hedging demand. This study examines whether overlap in position setting between arbitrageurs and mean-variance optimizers generates mispricing and whether this mispricing becomes a priced source of risk. The empirical findings support both possibilities: they confirm the presence of such mispricing and show that additional pricing factors are needed to account for it.

articles.title: DE LA MAREA ROSA A SOMOS MÉXICO: EL ESFUERZO PARA CREAR UN PARTIDO
articles.authors: RICARDO DE LA PEÑA MENA
articles.abstract: El texto analiza el surgimiento de la organización política Somos México (derivada de la Marea Rosa y opositora a la autodenominada Cuarta Transformación). Examina el contexto histórico de las reformas electorales impulsadas por Andrés Manuel López Obrador (Planes A, B y C) y el proceso de obtención de su registro como partido político nacional ante el INE en 2026, enfrentando impugnaciones jurídicas y observaciones sobre su denominación y emblema.

articles.title: SOBRE LOS REGÍMENES POLÍTICOS EN EL MUNDO Y SU EVOLUCIÓN (1900-2025)
articles.authors: RICARDO DE LA PEÑA MENA
articles.abstract: Este ensayo analiza la evolución histórica de los regímenes políticos mundiales desde 1900 hasta 2025 empleando las bases de datos del proyecto Varieties of Democracy (V-Dem). Revisa los fundamentos teóricos de la democracia y la autocracia, destacando que la tercera ola de autocratización contemporánea no opera mediante golpes de Estado tradicionales, sino a través de una erosión interna y sutil de los contrapesos institucionales. Mediante índices como el de regímenes en el mundo y el de democracia electoral, la investigación examina la distribución bimodal global, las disparidades regionales y la correlación entre elecciones competitivas y garantías liberales, concluyendo que la preservación de la libertad requiere instituciones sólidas y una actuación institucional temprana.

articles.title: LA CUESTIÓN DEL GÉNERO EN LAS ELECCIONES PARA GUBERNATURAS EN MÉXICO DE 2021 A 2024
articles.authors: RICARDO DE LA PEÑA MENA
articles.abstract: El objetivo central de este ensayo es aproximarse al estado de las condiciones de paridad de género en material electoral en México a partir de la celebración de los comicios federales y locales de 2021 y hasta los de 2024. En particular, se pondrá énfasis en los resultados de los esfuerzos por establecer regulaciones y vigilar la paridad en materia de nominaciones por género en el ejercicio del sufragio de la ciudadanía en las elecciones a las gubernaturas durante 2021-2024. Al respecto, la revisión de la evidencia empírica permite afirmar que en las elecciones para gubernaturas lo novedoso de los intentos de normar y sancionar las inequidades ha tenido un éxito que se queda mayormente en lo formal y no logra avanzar hacia el encuentro de un sufragio ciudadano equilibrado, por lo que permanecen inequidades contra las mujeres que apuntan a la necesidad de mayores esfuerzos, menos formales y más orientados hacia incidir en cuestiones de cultura cívica y política del electorado y en la creación de nuevas lógicas de la ciudadanía para el enfrentamiento de los potenciales de gestión pública de las personas.

articles.title: The Spread of High-Speed Internet and Gender-Based Violence within Families in Mexico
articles.authors: Daniela R Urbina; Julia A Behrman
articles.abstract: The relationship between internet access and gender-based violence (GBV) remains contested: theories of global diffusion sustain that online media spreads gender-egalitarian norms and condemns violence against women, whereas digital platforms can also normalize misogyny and enable coercive control. To test these hypotheses, we exploit temporal and geographic variation in the rollout of high-speed internet across Mexican municipalities between 2011 and 2021, distinguishing violence by intimate partners from that by other family members. Combining three waves of Mexico’s ENDIREH survey, with time-varying georeferenced coverage measures, we estimate two-way fixed-effects, difference-in-differences, and triple-difference models. We find that rapid internet expansion reduced family-perpetrated violence—particularly emotional and physical violence —but had no effect on intimate-partner violence. Further analyses reveal that one pathway through which increased digital access decreased family-level GBV was by enhancing women’s decision-making power, especially among those living with their parents. Our findings highlight the value of adopting a broad definition of GBV that reaches beyond intimate partners, particularly in contexts where multigenerational households are common.

articles.title: Role differentiation as ignition of a collective information engine
articles.authors: Maximilian Puelma Touzel
articles.abstract: Informational active matter research has shown how measurement-informed decisions produce collective order, so far in systems that reach consensus. We identify a collective information engine that orders by differentiation instead, and construct a minimal instance using anti-coordination games, the simplest game class in which differentiated role information has value. Agents infer their role from a noisy social signal, and role-following action feeds back into that signal, shaping the incentive to follow roles. The schemas prescribing roles are themselves dynamic: resources accrued through coordinated role-play combine with population variability to shape and reinforce the schemas that generated them. The model thereby operationalizes Sewell's duality of schemas and resources, the influential but hitherto qualitative resolution of sociology's structure--agency debate. The engine ignites when a loop gain $\Lambda$---the product of identity persistence, cognitive capacity, and social feedback channel fidelity---exceeds one. For a repertoire of such schemas, roles emerge with increasing gain in a bifurcation cascade whose functional form is fixed by the repertoire's eigenvalue spectrum, ranging from monitorable logarithmic sequences to deceptive spike-then-avalanche onsets. Resource accumulation turns schema competition into a replicator dynamics that, in mean field, selects the cascade type endogenously. Subcritical behavioral covariance reveals that type before onset, enabling early detection, and feedback channel parameters bias which type is selected. For agents interacting on a platform, adaptive platform design then becomes a control lever to throttle emergent coordination, e.g. for mitigating risks from distributional AI. Joining game theory, collective dynamics, and information engines, we open a route to an information thermodynamics of agent populations.

articles.title: Writing the Situated Self: Intersectional and Geographic Patterning in College Admissions Essays
articles.authors: AJ Alvero; anthony lising antonio; Leslie Luqueño; Francis Pearman
articles.abstract: Written language is often considered a reflection of the author's internal thoughts, states, and characteristics. This is why writing is used in evaluation to make inferences about authors but also why social scientists use text as a lens into psychological states. We present a complementary perspective: that writing systematically reflects the social environments of authors. We explore these dynamics in a large corpus of college admissions essays (n = 232,838 essays submitted by 76,510 self-identified Hispanic applicants from 2015-2017) and metadata about author sociodemographics, including the ZIP code of their high school. We find that intersectional demographic markers are highly salient. We further demonstrate that ZIP code level socioeconomic measures are strongly correlated with the writing style and content of local applicants. Finally, we show that misclassification rates vary geographically and are modestly associated with local demographic composition and social capital, indicating that writing is influenced both socially and geographically. By documenting strong alignment between text and authors, observable through machine reading, our findings clarify how author demographics and context structure what is written and, stylistically, how. Framing text as an external process rather than purely internal creates opportunities to bridge psychological and sociological data, methods, and theories to better understand the connections between language, evaluation, and social stratification. Because these texts were produced before the popularization of large language models (LLMs), our results serve as useful benchmarks for archival work and generate new questions as LLMs mediate written self-presentation.

articles.title: Resistance to territorial stigmatization: the mechanisms linking place-based social movement engagement and people's perceptions of place
articles.authors: Nunnally Zou
articles.abstract: Scholars of territorial stigma have assumed that resistance efforts should improve how stigmatized neighborhoods are perceived. Findings from a two-and-a-half-year ethnographic study of a place-based social movement in Baton Rouge, Louisiana, challenge this assumption: the same organization's resistance efforts can produce fundamentally different effects depending on how audiences are positioned to encounter the neighborhood. For those with little direct contact, a consistent counternarrative reshaped how the neighborhood was symbolically imagined. For occasional visitors, direct exposure introduced complexity that secondhand accounts could not provide. For residents who engaged deeply with the organization, material and relational support gradually reshaped how the neighborhood was experienced from within. And for residents with high neighborhood familiarity but low organizational engagement, none of these mechanisms took hold. These findings reveal that resistance to territorial stigma and perception change are distinct processes, connected by mechanisms that vary with the nature and depth of contact between people and place, which shows how inequality is reproduced not only through material conditions but also through unequal processes of knowing place.

articles.title: Climate Adaptation as Evolvability
articles.authors: Michael Weisberg; Rachael Brown; Christopher H. Lean
articles.abstract: Standard approaches to climate adaptation, commonly understood as the protection of infrastructure, social systems, and ecosystems from adverse climate impacts,are too closely tied to the biological concept of adaptation and the ecological notion of stability. Instead, we argue that climate adaptation is better articulated by analogy to the concept of evolvability. Adaptation thus understood emphasizes the need for internal capacities of restoration and self-maintenance, preserves flexibility and options for the future, addresses the social, political, and psychological impacts of climate change, and promotes transboundary strategies.

articles.title: A Contract-Based Healthcare Ecosystem for Depopulated Rural Communities: Residential Risk Visibility and Incentive-Linked Health Monitoring
articles.authors: Atsushi Hisayuki
articles.abstract:
Debates on healthcare sustainability in depopulated rural communities have focused on technological solutions — telemedicine, drone delivery, remote monitoring. This paper addresses the structural problems technology alone cannot solve: helicopter emergency medical services (HEMS) cannot fly at night or in bad weather; severe emergencies admit no alternative to physical transport; and the healthcare costs generated by rural residence remain invisible to both residents and society. We propose a "contract-based healthcare ecosystem": (a) quantifying and visualizing the relationship between residence location and medical access as individual risk; (b) making participation in continuous health monitoring a contractual condition of new residency; and (c) linking participation and risk-management attainment to basic-income-style payments. On ethical grounds the scheme applies only to new residents, with existing residents guaranteed conventional arrangements. Extending the external-balance model of our companion paper (SocArXiv, doi:10.31235/osf.io/rcsq9_v1), we estimate that if 60 high-risk residents of a 500-person community participate in monitoring and severe events fall by 15-35%, incentive payments of 2,500-11,700 yen per person per month are offset by reduced external medical expenditure alone (break-even). This range is realistic for behavior-change incentives, implying that a scheme in which health-risk management directly contributes to community economic self-sufficiency is institutionally feasible. Ethical limits concerning privacy, stigmatization, and freedom of choice are examined from a clinician's perspective.

Note: The full manuscript is written in Japanese; an English abstract is provided above.

articles.title: What Citizens Mean by Democracy: Partisan Differences in Open-Ended Survey Responses
articles.authors: Mirko Wegemann; Elena Leuschner; Tim Lars Allinger; Daniel Bischof; Kristian Frederiksen; Morgan Le Corre Juratic
articles.abstract: Do voters from different partisan camps understand democracy in the same way? We analyze more than 25,000 open-ended survey responses from representative samples in 14 countries, classifying answers with a fine-tuned language model and sentence embeddings. Citizens most often define democracy through individual and civil rights; multidimensional definitions are rare, and elections are mentioned by only 17% of respondents. Yet shared vocabulary masks partisan divergence. Far-right voters and non-voters are less likely to mention civil rights, elections, and horizontal accountability, while far-right voters more often invoke majoritarian principles. Among respondents mentioning rights, left voters connect rights to equality and citizenship, whereas right voters emphasize freedom of speech. Democratic contestation thus unfolds within democratic language, creating openings for selective elite reframing.

articles.title: The impact of product placement on sales of plant-based meat alternatives: A controlled interrupted time series analysis of an in-store intervention
articles.authors: Alice Rose Kininmonth; Francesca Pontin; Victoria Jenneson; William Young; Alison Fildes; Michelle Morris
articles.abstract:
Background: Reducing meat consumption and substituting red and processed meats with plant-proteins could have positive health and environmental impacts. This study examined the impact of an in-store product positioning intervention on sales of plant-based meat alternatives (PBMA) and meat-based products. 

Methods: Between September 2021 and January 2022, a major UK supermarket retailer implemented a product placement intervention that moved 25 chilled PBMAs from a separate dedicated PBMA bay within the meat aisle to being shelved next to their meat-based counterparts and the original dedicated PBMA bay was removed. No changes were made in control stores. To examine the effectiveness of the intervention on sales of PBMAs and meat-based products, controlled interrupted time series analysis was conducted using 538 days of sales data from 6 intervention stores and 6 matched control stores. 

Results: Overall, there was a significant difference between intervention and control stores in the change in sales of PBMAs attributable to the intervention (-51.18 units, 95% CI: -97.15, -5.21, indicating that positioning PBMAs next to their meat-based counterparts led to a measurable reduction in PBMA sales in intervention stores. There was no difference between the intervention and control stores in sales of other meat-free products, meat-based products, or products within the protein Eatwell category, indicating that the intervention had no measurable effect on sales of products other than the relocated PBMAs. Price-point comparison analysis revealed that PBMA products were significantly more expensive than their meat-based counterparts.

Conclusion: This study revealed that positioning PBMAs next to their meat-based counterparts was not effective at increasing sales of PBMAs and in fact led to a significant reduction in sales of the repositioned PBMAs. The reduction observed may have resulted from regular PBMA customers not being able to find the relocated PBMAs or from the higher price of PBMAs compared to their meat-based counterparts or both. Future research in real-world settings is needed to better understand the behavioural levers that encourage customers towards healthier and more sustainable purchases. Future research should also examine whether placement-based interventions, such as dual-placement coupled with price promotions, can support meaningful behavioural shifts towards more sustainable choices.

articles.title: Effect of financial satisfaction on life satisfaction among older adults in Finland
articles.authors: Ilari Ilmakunnas; Liisa-Maria Palomäki
articles.abstract: As populations age, it is increasingly important to understand the factors that shape life satisfaction among older adults. Financial security is widely considered one of the major life domains that contributes to life satisfaction. However, there is a scarcity of longitudinal studies examining how financial satisfaction affects overall life satisfaction among older adults. Previous analyses have mainly focused on cross-sectional associations rather than causal designs. This study addresses several existing research gaps by using longitudinal survey data on Finnish old-age pensioners aged 64 or over. Fixed effects linear regression models are used to help isolate the effect of financial satisfaction. A sensitivity analysis is conducted to determine whether unobserved confounders could explain the results. In addition, to contextualize the observed effect of financial satisfaction, we compare that effect with the effects of changes in major life-course events. The study finds that financial satisfaction has a considerable effect on overall life satisfaction. Sensitivity analysis suggests it is unlikely that the effect of financial satisfaction is explained by unobserved confounders, lending further support to the idea that there is a causal relationship. Changes in financial satisfaction are more relevant to life satisfaction than changes in self-rated health. Changes in partnership status or work status had no effect on life satisfaction. Overall, the study shows that changes in financial satisfaction influence life satisfaction among older adults. Improving financial security in retirement can therefore be expected to also improve subjective well-being among aging populations.

articles.title: Communication Repertoires in Hybrid Office Work: Mediated Channels, Face-to-Face Interaction, and Formal and Informal Exchange
articles.authors: Kai-David Klärner; Sophie-Charlotte Meyer; Anita Tisch
articles.abstract: Research on communication in hybrid work often focuses on individual channels or remote work intensity rather than the broader communication repertoires through which employees interact. This study examines whether the composition of these repertoires is associated with formal and informal collegial exchange beyond employees’ overall communication frequency. Using data from the 2024 DiWaBe 2.0 survey of 7,587 employees, we distinguish overall work-related communication frequency from its distribution across face-to-face interaction and four mediated channels: email, chat, telephone, and video conferencing. A joint five-mode model separates overall communication frequency from mode-specific deviations rela-tive to face-to-face interaction. Parallel measures enable a direct comparison of formal and informal exchange. The findings suggest that greater relative reliance on mediated channels is associated with lower reported formal and informal collegial exchange relative to face-to-face interaction. By contrast, voice/video and text-based channels do not differ significantly in their average associations with either outcome. The mediated-channel deviations also do not differ significantly between formal and informal exchange. Robustness analyses yield sub-stantively similar results across alternative samples, additional controls, and model specifications. The study demonstrates the analytical value of a communication-repertoire perspective on hybrid work. Overall communication frequency and communication-mode composition represent distinct dimensions of employees’ communication repertoires. The findings therefore shift attention from workplace location or individual channels alone to how communication is organised across co-present and mediated forms.

articles.title: Testing the water: Importance of surface water resources for settlement installation in various climatic contexts using a machine learning approach
articles.authors: Mathias Bellat; Biel Soriano Elias
articles.abstract: Past human spatial dynamics are strongly influenced by water availability. Since the development of agrarian sedentary societies, water is seen as an essential ressource. Yet quantifying its influence on past populations across different environmental and chronological contexts remains methodologically challenging. This study investigates the relative importance of thirteen water-related variables alongside five additional environmental covariates in shaping archaeological site distributions. Using machine learning model of Maximum Entropy (MaxEnt), a total of 461 Bronze Age and Iron Age (3,500 - 50 BCE) sites from four regions with contrasting climatic conditions - the Rhine Valley, Lazio, the Shephelah, and the Kurdistan region of Iraq - were analysed. Results show that distance to water flow and stable topographic variables consistently emerge as the strongest predictors of settlement location. Palaeoclimatic variables, particularly precipitation seasonality and precipitation of the wettest quarter, outperform modern remote sensing indices. Despite contrasting environmental conditions, the four regions share broadly comparable settlement trajectories, with a consistent shift toward greater site density and spatial dispersion from the Bronze Age to the Iron Age. These findings highlight the value of temporally robust environmental proxies for modelling past human-landscape interactions and offer a replicable framework for water-focused archaeological predictive modelling across diverse climatic settings.

articles.title: How Schools Organize the Standard Life Course and Translate It into Relations to the Self
articles.authors: Vance Byun
articles.abstract:
This paper analyzes why the educational success narrative and standard life-course pathway continue to organize Korean schools despite their uneven efficacy, and how this structure is translated into students' self-relations and differentiated suffering. The educational success narrative is defined as the entry point into a standard life-course narrative linking good grades and university admission to stable employment, economic independence, housing, family formation, and old age. It gained institutional distribution during industrialization and educational expansion by organizing experiences of social mobility and stability. Yet higher-education massification, credential expansion, and changes in labor and housing markets have made its efficacy more conditional. School evaluation, family investment, university and labor-market selection, and textbook life-planning representations do not adjust at the same pace. This paper interprets this as a nonsynchronous breakdown rather than its disappearance.

The paper reconstructs mechanisms between macro-level structure and individual suffering often compressed into “internalization.” School structure appears as a distributive grammar in which time, attention, information, opportunities, recognition, and sanctions are attached to particular performances. Through repeated experiences of action and outcome, students develop a practice grammar organizing attention, time, and the body. When external evaluative standards are recursively applied to the self, self-interpellation emerges; when a pathway is experienced as the only route preserving safety, relationships, recognition, dignity, and the future, acute affective linkage forms. Yet structural coercion need not become a criterion of self-worth. Structural entrapment occurs when actors continue to perform because institutional distribution is high and resources for exit are limited even without believing the narrative.

These dimensions are assembled into V-Q-C coordinates to derive five mechanisms of suffering: suffering within the narrative, the double bind, anomie, structural coercion, and guilt induced by attacks on legitimacy. Distributive grammar itself is not treated as an error or violence to be eliminated, but as the institutional and phenomenological horizon through which schools allocate limited time and opportunities and students encounter worldly possibilities and risks. The problem arises when one distributive grammar monopolistically links performance evaluation to love, belonging, dignity, and the whole of life while foreclosing revision, retrying, and alternative pathways. Accordingly, Bildung is redefined as a phenomenological process of self-formation in which one is protected enough to revise one’s horizon of expectation in response to experience. Schools and teachers should limit the scope of evaluation, distinguish institutional advantage from human worth, and preserve the reversibility of failure and relational respect.

articles.title: Epistemic Intolerance Toward Outpartisans
articles.authors: Seo-young Silvia Kim; Taegyoon Kim; Jeong Hyun Kim; Youngdeuk Park
articles.abstract: We identify and operationalize epistemic intolerance, the belief that outgroup members are epistemically incompetent, violate epistemic norms, and are unworthy of epistemic engagement. In particular, we measure epistemic intolerance toward outpartisans using an original 18-item battery fielded in two U.S. surveys (December 2025 and April 2026; N = 3,386, of whom 2,525 partisans are analyzed). We show that epistemic intolerance is widespread and distinct from affective polarization and that, when measured with the full battery, it predicts democratic norm erosion, outparty dehumanization, and anti-intellectualism toward outparty elites, even when benchmarked against both affective polarization and political sectarianism. Moreover, its overall level is bipartisan, and prevalent even among leaners across both the Democratic and Republican parties. These findings identify epistemic intolerance as a consequential and previously underappreciated dimension of partisan hostility, with downstream implications for designing effective depolarization strategies.

articles.title: Barriers to disclosing school-based sexual harassment for racially-minoritised girls in the UK
articles.authors: Vanita Sundaram; Beth Bell; Nadia Jessop; Emma Louise Jackson
articles.abstract:
Abstract
This paper focuses on barriers to disclosing school-based sexual harassment for racially-minoritised girls in the UK. The data are derived from the first UK study of racially minoritised girls’ experiences of public sexual harassment; in this paper we focus specifically on sexual harassment experiences in school. We adopted a qualitative research design that used co-produced, participatory methods to elicit the voices of racially-minoritised girls and young women.
